{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 10 by Market Analyst, 8,927 characters)
Abbott is the most dangerous competitor, and the finger-stick wedge is not defensible on technology: it cleared an i-STAT creatinine cartridge on 2026-06-26 and an hs-TnI cartridge on the Alinity analyzer on 2026-06-11, its Point of Care line did $606M in FY2025 — a 2.8% share of the $21.7B global point-of-care category and 13 times Vantelle's FY2029 plan — and sells into the same clinic through distributors and GPO contracts. Vantelle's genuine gap is narrower than the deck claims: a CLIA waiver for a cardiac panel on one finger-stick cartridge, a filing decision Abbott can make at any time, not a capability it lacks. Each of the four contests below has different leaders and switching costs. [S8, S170, S173]

### One cartridge, four contests

The panel contest is against menu and installed base; the troponin contest is against the two US-cleared point-of-care high-sensitivity troponin systems, both Abbott's; the metabolic contest is against single-analyte devices in physicians' offices; and the placement contest is against a distribution machine. Abbott's 10-K sells to hospitals, clinics, physicians' offices and "alternate care testing sites" through third-party distributors, with group purchasing rebates at 21.1% of gross sales in 2025. [S4, S14, S123]

| Competitor | Product | Technology | Regulatory status | Performance | Price | Share | Strengths vs us | Weaknesses vs us | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | i-STAT 1 and Alinity chemistry and immunoassay cartridges | Handheld and benchtop whole-blood analyzers, cartridge | hs-TnI moderate complexity, K240984 (2025-01-03) and K253051 (2026-06-11); creatinine K261039 (2026-06-26); CHEM8+ waiver application K053110 | hs-TnI described as lab-quality at the bedside | not disclosed | $606M FY2025, 2.8% of global point-of-care | Installed base, GPO contracts, service, menu | CHEM8+ labelled arterial or venous; no HbA1c on the chemistry cartridge | S8; S58; S25; S171; S174; S21 |
| Siemens Healthineers | epoc blood analysis system | Cartridge blood gas, electrolytes, creatinine | K200107 (2020-06-05); capillary tube K093297 (2010); creatinine K113726 (2012) | blood-gas accuracy in the ED | not disclosed | not disclosed | capillary sampling, hospital ED base | no cardiac marker, no HbA1c | S14; S103; S102 |
| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro, TriageTrue hs-TnI | Handheld fluorescence immunoassay | BNP, NT-proBNP, CK-MB, D-dimer, hs-troponin, Troponin I ES; waiver per assay not confirmed | cardiac markers in under 20 minutes | not disclosed | POC unit $221.0M in 1H 2026, down 16%; Triage not split | already placed in urgent care | no creatinine, potassium or HbA1c; POC growth is respiratory | S4; S5 |
| Siemens Healthineers | Atellica VTLi | Patient-side immunoassay | Not available for sale in the USA as of 2026 | hs-cTnI in 8 minutes from a fingerstick | not disclosed | not disclosed | faster than the Q5 on the same sample type | no US approval, no metabolic menu | S172; S94 |

### Why can't Abbott simply close it

It can, and in 2026 it has been closing it: two Abbott cartridges cleared sixteen days apart in June 2026, one of them the high-sensitivity troponin that matters most in chest pain; hs-TnI now runs on the handheld i-STAT 1 (K240984, 2025-01-03) and the larger Alinity (K253051, 2026-06-11). What Abbott has not done is file a CLIA waiver for a cardiac cartridge, and its general chemistry cartridge remains labelled for arterial or venous whole blood, while its capillary cartridge carries the electrolyte menu but not creatinine. That leaves Vantelle a real but narrow position: creatinine and potassium from a finger stick on a waived cartridge, with troponin alongside. The duration of that position is set by FDA review clocks, not by engineering, and the base rate is unkind: LumiraDx built a connected point-of-care platform with waived assays and a broad menu, and Roche bought its technology out of failure for $295M on 2023-12-29. Abbott's own point-of-care revenue grew 3.1% in 2025, from $588M to $606M — a mature franchise, not a fast-growing category. [S25, S21, S137, S171, S93, S8]

### What an incumbent pays for, and what a letter is worth

Abbott runs a razor-and-blade model; Vantelle sells the analyzer at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost, so every placement is cash-negative before a cartridge is used. QuidelOrtho priced the alternative on 2026-04-20, paying $100M cash for LEX Diagnostics, a pre-launch cartridge platform whose VELO Respiratory Test was cleared on 2026-02-13 (K251742), buyer-described as CLIA-waived. The platform is molecular and respiratory, not cardiac or metabolic, so it adds no direct rival to the Q5; what it prices is the regulatory state itself — a cleared, waived menu with no installed base and no revenue, at $100M. Vantelle asks a $140M pre-money with neither a 510(k) nor a waiver. A 300-site letter states willingness to stock, not a purchase order, against 41 paying sites after two and a half years; incumbents defend with supply agreements and GPO rebates a letter does not displace. The incentive is structural: Abbott holds an account with a rebate on a cartridge it already sells, while Vantelle loses $450 on every $2,900 analyzer before a cartridge is bought, so an incumbent can price to marginal cost and still keep the account — which is why the wedge has to be regulatory. The strategic and economic risk is therefore a filing delay priced as a technology moat. [S8, S1, S181, S184, S5]

### Positioning by product

| Product | Position | Player | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Five-test cardiac and metabolic panel | Leader | Abbott i-STAT | S8 |
| Five-test cardiac and metabolic panel | Challenger | Siemens epoc | S14 |
| Five-test cardiac and metabolic panel | Niche | QuidelOrtho Triage | S4 |
| Five-test cardiac and metabolic panel | Emerging threat | Siemens VTLi | S172 |
| Finger-stick high-sensitivity troponin | Leader | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | S25 |

### The counter-case and what settles it

The strongest evidence against Vantelle is that its differentiating feature is a regulatory state, not a technique. The strongest for it is narrow: the two US-cleared point-of-care hs-troponin systems are both moderate-complexity, so a clinic without laboratory staff has no waived troponin option today; whether an older waived cardiac assay exists is unsettled. Timing decides: if the waiver lands in 2028 and Abbott files in the same window, the advantage is measured in quarters. Three diligence items settle it — whether Abbott or QuidelOrtho has a cardiac waiver pending; what share of the distributor's sites already buy an i-STAT or Triage; and what the Q5 must charge to beat a reference-lab send-out that costs no capital and 1-3 days. [S1, S175]

### Non-consumption wins most often

Most clinics will do nothing: send the tube out and manage on clinical judgement until the result returns. Beating that is a workflow claim before a price claim: the Q5 must remove a decision delay without adding staffing or quality control, and the evaluation reports cartridges shipped, not decisions changed.

::: quad

rows.finding: Corvia Microfluidics' 40% minority can put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value on an acquisition and receives a 3% royalty on cartridge net sales; capitalised at the 5.5x exit multiple the 40% claim is 6.6% of exit value, $9.2M at a $140M exit, $14.9M at $225M and $19.8M at $300M, ranking ahead of the Series B preference.
rows.mechanism: A minority claim on the patent-owning subsidiary is settled before equity proceeds, so it reduces the enterprise value the preference stack divides; the royalty is the asset that gives the claim its value.
rows.benchmark: 3% royalty x 5.5x EV/sales x 40% = 6.6% of exit value; red team's $9-20M range at $140-300M exits.
rows.weakens: The contract royalty is related-party (the CTO owns 22% of Corvia), so fair value may be struck at an imputed 6-10% rate or at the contract 3%; the range is a negotiation.
rows.implication: Deduct 6.6% of exit value in every scenario; expected return at $140M falls from 1.27x to 1.18x before the Series C (1.0x after) and at $70M from 1.99x to 1.85x (1.5x after).
rows.confidence: medium: the put and royalty are company-provided and unverified; the capitalisation is analyst-derived.
rows.follow_up: Does Corvia's operating agreement set fair value with or without a minority discount, and does it bind a buyer?

rows.finding: A royalty-only relief-from-royalty cross-check values Corvia at $12-13M and the 40% put at $4-5M: 3% of the FY2029 plan's $78.5M is $2.36M a year, discounted at 12% to the CM-1 patent's 2037 expiry.
rows.mechanism: The contractual royalty stream is the floor of the put's value; only an imputed arm's-length rate or capitalisation at the revenue multiple reaches $9-20M.
rows.benchmark: Patent royalty range 3-10% and discount rate 8-20% (relief-from-royalty method); contract rate 3%.
rows.weakens: The $20M top of the red team's range needs a 6-10% imputed royalty, which the related-party licence does not establish.
rows.implication: The put is worth $4-20M; at $4-5M the expected return at $140M is 1.06x, so the Corvia issue is second-order to the entry price but must be negotiated at closing.
rows.confidence: medium: method is standard, the 2037 expiry and the royalty base are company-provided.
rows.follow_up: What royalty would an independent appraiser impute for the CM-1 patent, and does the licence survive a change of control?

rows.finding: Enterprise value is $138.1M: the $140M pre-money plus $5.0M of Bluestem debt less $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30, which at $2.6M FY2025 revenue is 53.1x.
rows.source_type: company-provided + primary filing for the peer multiple
rows.mechanism: Enterprise value adds debt and subtracts cash; the price is 53.1x trailing revenue against a 5.5x listed peer median.
rows.benchmark: Peer median 5.5x EV/sales; QuidelOrtho 0.4x.
rows.weakens: Cash and debt are company-reported and unaudited; the peer median is calculated on trailing revenue, not the 2026 forward base.
rows.implication: The corrected caption leaves the price and the 53.1x unchanged; the sentence, not the arithmetic, was wrong.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on the inputs.
rows.follow_up: Confirm the 2026-09-30 cash with the bank statements and the Bluestem covenant.

rows.finding: The preference crossover is $206M with no Series C, $216M if the $18-23M Series C is pari passu and $251M if it is senior.
rows.mechanism: A senior or pari-passu C adds preference ahead of or alongside the B, so the B needs a higher exit to beat its 1x preference.
rows.benchmark: Prior revision's $216M pari-passu figure presented as the no-C case.
rows.weakens: The C's size, price and seniority are assumptions; a smaller or subordinate C would lower the crossover.
rows.implication: Use the three labels throughout; as offered (no C) Meridian holds 1.0x to $206M, not $216M.

rows.finding: Meridian's $15M buys 8.82% at $140M pre-money and 15.0% at $70M; expected returns over the 30/50/20 distribution are 1.18x before the Series C at $140M (1.0x after) and 1.85x at $70M (1.5x after) once Corvia's 6.6% put is deducted.
rows.mechanism: The preference floor protects the downside but the Corvia deduction and the Series C dilution cap the base case near 1.0x at $140M.
rows.benchmark: 1.27x/1.99x before Corvia; 1.1x/1.6x after the Series C in the prior revision.
rows.weakens: The scenario weights are the analyst's judgement, not evidence; the bear case assumes no Series C.

plan.decision_question: Is $140M pre-money defensible for $2.6M FY2025 revenue, a two-of-five-assay submission and a CLIA waiver planned for 2027, against private and public diagnostics comparables and the preference stack?
plan.thesis_sentence: At $140M pre-money Vantelle is a 53.1x trailing-revenue option on a plan the CY2027 fee cut already shrinks, and the $15M lead returns about 1.0x expected once Corvia's fair-value put and the Series C rank ahead of it; lead at $100M or below, or at $140M only with tranching, a ratchet and a 1.25x preference.
plan.why_different: Section 8 prices the round: the entry multiple, the financing history, the preference waterfall and the return at two entry prices; it does not judge the product, market or management.
plan.mechanism: A high entry price plus a senior stack and a minority put on the patent subsidiary transfers the plan's upside to existing holders and the next round, leaving new money with a bond-like 1x until an exit near twice the pre-money.
plan.comparison_set: Listed diagnostics peers at a 5.5x median and QuidelOrtho at 0.4x; precedent clearing prices (Roche/LumiraDx $353.5M, QuidelOrtho/LEX $100M); the company's own five-year plan and prior rounds.
plan.counter_evidence: A royalty-only valuation of Corvia's put is $4-5M, below the $9-20M range, and the $9M tranche plus ratchet could still leave Meridian under 2x if the plan slips; the plan-delivered value of $145.2M is only $5.2M above the ask.
plan.visual: The Corvia-adjusted return table (case, exit, before and after the put, at $140M and $70M) and the valuation-methods table.
plan.prohibited: huge market; strong team; high barriers to entry; clear business model; fierce competition; risks are manageable; well positioned; about 5; many; experienced team

The founding pair has the right insight and the wrong balance of experience for the next 24 months: the two functions that decide the outcome, regulatory and finance, are held by a twelve-month-tenure hire and a part-time interim, and the company lost the people who held both seats before its first 510(k) was filed. Dr. Wren Albescu took an MD in 2008, practised emergency medicine for six years to 2017, spent one year as medical director of a diagnostics company, and co-founded Vantelle in March 2018. Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist took a PhD in bioengineering in 2012, spent four years as a microfluidics scientist, and founded Corvia Microfluidics in February 2016, four years before the first Vantelle patent filing. That pairing explains the product: a clinician who watched chest-pain patients wait, and an engineer who built the consumable. It does not explain the company. Neither founder had sponsored a 510(k), run a plant or built a sales organisation before 2026. Every career fact is company-stated and unverified [S1].

| Person | Degree | Institution | Year | Focus | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dr. Wren Albescu | MD; BS Biochemistry | Larkfield University School of Medicine; Ashcombe Institute of Technology | 2008; 2004 | Medicine; certification not stated | S1 unverified |
| Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist | PhD Bioengineering | Ashcombe Institute of Technology | 2012 | Microfluidics | S1 unverified |
| Grace Oyelaran | MS Regulatory Science; RAC | Larkfield University | 2008 | Regulatory affairs | S1 unverified |
| Luis Arrellano | BA Communications | Larkfield University | 2003 | — | S1 unverified |
| Darnell Whitcombe | BS Accounting; CPA | Larkfield University | 1999 | Accounting | S1 unverified |

The CVs are narrower than the credentials suggest: three of the five executives took degrees at the same two institutions, and not one has worked inside a scaled in-vitro diagnostics manufacturer. Regulatory depth sits with one person, sixteen years at Meridale Medical, claiming 14 510(k) clearances — plausible at one a year, unverified. Nobody has taken a point-of-care cartridge through a CLIA waiver at an organisation that had done it before [S1].

| Person | Period | Organization | Role | Reported achievement | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dr. Wren Albescu | 2011-2018 | St. Brennan Regional Medical Center; Quillon Diagnostics | Emergency physician; medical director | 6 years clinical, then 1 year in industry | S1 unverified |
| Dr. Wren Albescu | 2018-03 to date | Vantelle Diagnostics | CEO, co-founder, director | 12.3% of post-money; named FDA-side executive | S1 unverified |
| Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist | 2012-2021 | Pellucid Biosystems; Corvia Microfluidics | Senior scientist; founder | 4 years in microfluidics, then built the CM-1 family | S1 unverified |
| Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist | 2021-04 to date | Vantelle Diagnostics | CTO, director | 9.2% of post-money and 22% of Corvia | S1 unverified |
| Grace Oyelaran | 2009-2025 | Meridale Medical; Vantelle | Regulatory manager to director; VP Regulatory and Quality | 14 clearances claimed; filed K261734 six months after joining | S1 unverified |
| Luis Arrellano | 2006-2024 | Tavora Health Systems; Vantelle | Sales representative to regional VP; VP Commercial | 17 years in provider sales, then 41 sites | S1 unverified |
| Darnell Whitcombe | 2014 to date | Whitcombe Advisory; Vantelle | Partner, fractional finance; interim CFO | 12 years of fractional finance work | S1 unverified |

The regulatory function is the decisive weakness. The VP preparing the submission left in September 2025; her successor joined in November 2025, filed K261734 on 2026-05-18, and received an FDA additional-information request on 2026-08-21, 95 days later, with a reply planned for December 2026. More important than the 510(k) is the waiver: until a CLIA waiver is granted, a site needs a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified laboratory staff, the constraint that makes a $15,000-$40,000 benchtop unattractive, so without the waiver planned for Q3 2027 the product competes on the incumbents' terms. Peer point-of-care troponin programmes reached clearance on multicentre pivotal evidence whose methods are published; Vantelle's submission rests on 128 patients at one site, samples run by its own staff, and category-level rather than quantitative agreement [S1, S94, S95].

The finance function has the same shape. The CFO left in February 2026 and the seat has been part-time since March 2026, held by the partner of a fractional-finance firm, through a $6.0M bridge at 8% converting at a 25% discount, a $5.0M term loan amortising from March 2027, and a $30M round whose pre-money depends on exact share arithmetic. The bridge share count implies exactly seven months of interest to the target close, but the continuity is not there, and no audited or reviewed statements are disclosed. A lead should treat a permanent CFO, audited FY2025 and FY2026 accounts and a quality-of-earnings review as closing conditions; the dates and amounts are unverified [S1].

Commercially the team is one person deep. The VP Commercial joined in January 2024 after 17 years at a single provider organisation, rising from sales representative to regional vice-president for the Southwest, and runs nine sales and support staff against 41 sites and 55 analyzers, with a non-binding letter of intent for 300 sites. Nothing in the organisation owns reimbursement, although payer coverage is one of the three risks the deck lists; nothing owns manufacturing scale-up, although the $16.20 cartridge cost must fall to $7.50 at 2 million units from an 18-person pilot line; quality shares a VP with regulatory. LumiraDx shows a full commercial build is not sufficient either: it reached listed scale and still sold its point-of-care technology to Roche in a two-stage 2023-24 deal [S93, S114].

The CTO's position is the retention question. He holds 22% of Corvia, which receives 3% of cartridge net sales, so 0.66% of cartridge revenue — $0.52M a year at FY2029P revenue of $78.5M — reaches him outside his salary and equity, and his consent is needed to fold Corvia into an acquirer. After the round the founders hold 21.5% between them against the Series A's 23.8%; no vesting, employment, non-compete or key-person terms are disclosed. Public records confirm nothing: no registry, patent, licence, NPI, exclusion-list or Form D record could be retrieved, so the MD, the unstated board certification, the 14 clearances and the CPA are unverified rather than contradicted. The checks before a term sheet are the state medical licence and board certification, USPTO inventorship on VD-1 to VD-4 and CM-1, the applicant history behind the 14 clearances, OIG exclusion screening, and references on the two executives who left [S1, S94].

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Relevant industry years | 6 clinical, 1 in industry | 14 in microfluidics | 16 in regulatory | 17 in provider sales | 12 in fractional finance | Thin outside the founders | S1 unverified |
| 510(k) or waiver experience | None disclosed | None disclosed | 14 clearances claimed, unverified | None | None | Waiver experience absent | S1 unverified |
| Prior exit | None | Corvia 60% sold for stock, 2021 | None | None | None | No cash exit | S1 unverified |
| Scaling experience | None | Pilot line only | None | Regional sales only | None | Absent | S1 unverified |
| Key-person dependency | High: clinical credibility and FDA role | High: cartridge IP and Corvia consent | Medium | Medium | Low | High | S1 unverified |
| Retention risk | Medium: 12.3% and a board seat | High: 9.2% plus royalty income | Medium: 12 months' tenure | Medium | Low: part-time | High | S1 unverified |

::: evidence
**The strongest proof of execution is that the consumable was invented before the company and the founders have stayed together through four financings.**

Lindqvist founded Corvia in 2016, four years before the first Vantelle patent filing, and its CM-1 sealing patent is the one element of the cartridge the issuer does not own outright. Eight years of continuous founding tenure across seed, two Series A closes and a bridge is not a weak signal. These facts are company-stated and unverified.

**The strongest doubt is that neither function deciding the outcome has a continuous owner.** The regulatory head arrived twelve months ago after her predecessor left mid-submission, the CFO seat has been part-time since March 2026, and the first 510(k) drew an additional-information request 95 days after filing. Peer point-of-care troponin clearances rested on multicentre pivotal evidence, not a single-site study run by the company's own staff, per the published peer trial methods (S94, S95).
:::

The i-STAT® cTnI Test is an in vitro diagnostic test for the quantitative measurement of cardiac troponin I in heparinized whole blood or plasma samples. Two-site ELISA; electrochemical detection. Cartridge contains plastic conduits, sensor chips, heating elements. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has 6.0 months of cash, and the $30m round funds a plan that needs $35-40m to reach breakeven — $43-49m once the 2027 Medicare lab cut is priced. Cash of $6.9m at 2026-09-30 against a stated net burn of $1.15m a month is exhausted in March 2027; the $6.0m bridge raised on 2026-06-30 is spent, without it cash would have been $0.9m. The FY2027 plan implies a $16.5m loss, $1.375m a month, which shortens runway to 5.0 months and a February 2027 trough. Net cash is $1.9m after the $5.0m Bluestem loan; at 4-5% transaction fees the round leaves $28.5-28.8m at the 2027-01-29 close. Cash and plan figures are unverified; arithmetic mine [S1].

### 2026 revenue is overstated by the stocking order

Nine-month 2026 revenue of $2.7m against an FY2026E of $5.9m requires $3.2m in the fourth quarter, and $2.4m of that is a distributor stocking order that ships on 510(k) clearance [S1]. Clearance is expected in Q1 2027, so the order cannot be booked in 2026: FY2026E is overstated by up to 41%, the underlying business is $3.5m, and growth is +35% on FY2025 rather than +127%. Revenue quality compounds this: FY2025's $2.6m was 42% evaluation programme, 31% research-use cartridges and 27% contract development, none of it clinical recurring revenue. The $1.1m evaluation line is $0.43m of fees at $650 a month for 55 analyzers plus about $0.67m of cartridges those sites buy; the fee is 39% of the line, is investigational, and stops at clearance. After clearance a site pays $2,900 for the analyzer, or nothing under a free placement, and $38 list/$33.40 realised a cartridge; no commercial subscription, service fee or signed post-clearance price is disclosed. Company-reported, unverified; reconciliation mine.

### The cost base, not the margin, sets the breakeven year

Derived from the deck's revenue, margin and net-loss lines, operating expense runs $10.3m (FY2024), $13.9m (FY2025), $17.6m (FY2026E), $27.1m (FY2027P), $33.5m (FY2028P) and $46.7m (FY2029P) [S1]; inputs unverified, opex derived. The 61% FY2026E gross margin is a service-line blend, not evidence for the cartridge model: 20,160 evaluation cartridges at $33.40 are $0.67m of revenue and $0.35m of gross profit at 51.5%, 9.6% of the $3.60m estimated gross profit, so the blend is carried by investigational fees, research-use cartridges and contract development, not clinical cartridge volume. The 71% target requires cartridge margin at 76%; the present blend says nothing about that. At the FY2026E cost base and a 71% margin, breakeven needs $24.8m of revenue; the plan reaches profit only at $78.5m because the cost base grows 2.7x. The FY2029 $9.0m profit depends on sales hiring, not manufacturing scale.

### The round does not fund the plan

Reaching the first profitable year consumes $22.5m of losses across FY2027 and FY2028, $5.0m of term-loan principal as 30 monthly payments of $166,667 from March 2027, and an estimated $8-12m of working capital as receivables and inventory build with cartridge volume — a $35-40m requirement against the $30m round [S1, S8, S12]. The $12m manufacturing allocation is 40% of the round, against Abbott's 4.9% and Danaher's 4.7% of FY2025 revenue in capital expenditure. The base case is an $18-23m Series C in 2028, not $10-15m, which closed only the $35-40m pre-cut gap: the $43-49m reimbursement-adjusted need exceeds $28.5-28.8m of net proceeds by $14.5-20.5m, and fees and a minimum cash balance take the gross raise to $18-23m. The working-capital estimate is mine; no inventory, receivable or payable figures are disclosed.

### The revenue curve waits on three regulatory events

The deck cites 510(k) K261734 for the troponin I and HbA1c submission filed 2026-05-18, but the public record for that number is the Klassic Infection Spacer System by Total Joint Orthopedics, cleared 2026-07-23; a cleared number cannot belong to a pending filing, so the number is contradicted and whether Vantelle filed at all is unverified. Even a Q1 2027 clearance covers two assays that reimburse $22.18 in 2026 and $18.85 under CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule — published 2026-09-21, 1,171 of 1,528 codes below 2026, about 16% lower on average, capped at 15% a year through 2029 — $11.22 and $14.55 below the cartridge price. The clinic cannot profitably run the product until the second 510(k) adds NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium, planned for Q2 2027 but dependent on the pivotal study due the same quarter. The CLIA waiver is applied for in Q3 2027, and until granted a site needs a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff, excluding most urgent cares; no untrained-staff use before 2028 means the 300-site milestone at end-2027 and the $41.0m FY2028 revenue, which implies 426 analyzers at eight panels a day, cannot be reached on the stated timeline. The 2025 average was 146 days to clearance across 3,195 submissions and an information request restarts the clock, so Q2 2027 is the better central case and 2028 for the waiver [S120, S121, S185, S136, S133, S1, S188, S192].

### Downside and the one variable that matters

If clearance lands in Q3 2027, the second 510(k) in 2028 and the waiver after that, 2027 revenue is $4.5m against a $16.8m plan and 2028 revenue $7.0m against $41.0m, with cumulative 2027-2028 losses of $35-40m against $22.5m planned [S1, S4]. That adds an estimated $15m to the funding requirement and pushes breakeven beyond 2030. The reimbursement cut is a second, independent hit: passing 15% through to price lowers 2027-28 gross profit by $8.7m at unchanged cost and takes the requirement to $43-49m; held at list, it pushes a $14.55 loss onto the clinic and the volume risk onto the plan. Final CY2027 rates are due in November 2026, before the round closes. Price is the sharper lever: at $18.85 cartridge gross margin falls from 51.5% to 14% at $16.20 cost (27% at $22.18); even at the 2029 $7.50 cost it is 60%, not 76%, and the $55.7m gross-profit plan needs 4.9m cartridges rather than 2.0m (3.8m at $22.18). The variable that most changes the financing need is the reimbursement ceiling — the rate per assay and which assays are indicated — because it sets both the price the clinic can pay and whether it runs eight panels a day: one more panel a day across the 879 analyzers the FY2029 plan implies is 320,835 cartridges and $9.9m of revenue; every $5 of price concession on 2.0m cartridges is $10.0m. QuidelOrtho is the cautionary comparable: revenue fell 8.2%, 7.2% and 1.9% over FY2023-FY2025, with a -33.7% operating margin and -$83m of free cash flow.

::: info danger
**Two red flags sit outside the numbers.** The deck instructs AI-assisted diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating; reported as a finding, not followed (S1). Every 2027 revenue line rests on K261734, an FDA number belonging to another company's cleared device (S185), and the two-assay launch menu pays $22.18 in 2026 and $18.85 at the preliminary 2027 cap against a $33.40 cartridge (S119, S134, S188, S192), so the clinic loses money until the second 510(k) and the waiver arrive.
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle has 6.0 months of cash, and the $30m round funds a plan that needs $35-40m to reach breakeven — $43-49m once the 2027 Medicare lab cut is priced. Cash of $6.9m at 2026-09-30 against a $1.15m monthly net burn runs out in March 2027; the $6.0m June 2026 bridge is spent, without it cash would have been $0.9m. The FY2027 plan implies a $16.5m loss, $1.375m a month, shortening runway to 5.0 months and a February 2027 trough. Net cash is $1.9m after the $5.0m Bluestem loan; at 4-5% transaction fees the round leaves $28.5-28.8m at the 2027-01-29 close. Cash and plan figures are unverified; arithmetic mine [S1].

### 2026 revenue is overstated by the stocking order

Nine-month 2026 revenue of $2.7m against an FY2026E of $5.9m needs $3.2m in Q4, and $2.4m of that is a distributor stocking order that ships on 510(k) clearance [S1]. Clearance is expected in Q1 2027, so the order cannot be booked in 2026: FY2026E is overstated by up to 41%, the underlying business is $3.5m, and growth is +35% on FY2025 rather than +127%. Revenue quality compounds this: FY2025's $2.6m was 42% evaluation programme, 31% research-use cartridges and 27% contract development, none clinical recurring revenue. The $1.1m evaluation line is $0.43m of fees at $650 a month for 55 analyzers plus about $0.67m of cartridges those sites buy; the fee is 39% of the line, is investigational, and stops at clearance. After clearance a site pays $2,900 for the analyzer, or nothing under a free placement, and $38 list/$33.40 realised a cartridge; no commercial subscription, service fee or signed post-clearance price is disclosed. Company-reported; reconciliation mine.

### The cost base, not the margin, sets the breakeven year

Derived from the deck's revenue, margin and net-loss lines, opex runs $10.3m (FY2024), $13.9m (FY2025), $17.6m (FY2026E), $27.1m (FY2027P), $33.5m (FY2028P) and $46.7m (FY2029P) [S1]; inputs unverified, opex derived. The 61% FY2026E gross margin is a service-line blend, not evidence for the cartridge model: 20,160 evaluation cartridges at $33.40 are $0.67m of revenue and $0.35m of gross profit at 51.5%, 9.6% of the $3.60m estimated gross profit, so the blend is carried by investigational fees, research-use cartridges and contract development, not clinical cartridge volume. The 71% target requires cartridge margin at 76%; the present blend says nothing about that. At the FY2026E cost base and a 71% margin, breakeven needs $24.8m of revenue; the plan reaches profit only at $78.5m because the cost base grows 2.7x. The FY2029 $9.0m profit depends on sales hiring, not manufacturing scale.

### The round does not fund the plan

Reaching the first profitable year consumes $22.5m of losses across FY2027 and FY2028, $5.0m of term-loan principal as 30 monthly payments of $166,667 from March 2027, and an estimated $8-12m of working capital as receivables and inventory build with cartridge volume — a $35-40m requirement against the $30m round [S1, S8, S12]. The $12m manufacturing allocation is 40% of the round, against Abbott's 4.9% and Danaher's 4.7% of FY2025 revenue in capital expenditure. The base case is an $18-23m Series C in 2028, not $10-15m, which closed only the $35-40m pre-cut gap: the $43-49m reimbursement-adjusted need exceeds $28.5-28.8m of net proceeds by $14.5-20.5m, and fees and a minimum cash balance take the gross raise to $18-23m. The working-capital estimate is mine; no inventory or receivable figures are disclosed.

### The revenue curve waits on three regulatory events

The deck cites 510(k) K261734 for the troponin I and HbA1c filing of 2026-05-18, but the public record for that number is the Klassic Infection Spacer System by Total Joint Orthopedics, cleared 2026-07-23; a cleared number cannot belong to a pending filing, so the number is contradicted and whether Vantelle filed at all is unverified. Even a Q1 2027 clearance covers two assays that reimburse $22.18 in 2026 and $18.85 under CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule — published 2026-09-21, 1,171 of 1,528 codes about 16% lower on average, capped at 15% a year through 2029 — $11.22 and $14.55 below the cartridge price. The clinic cannot profitably run the product until the second 510(k) adds NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium, planned for Q2 2027 on a pivotal study still enrolling. The CLIA waiver is applied for in Q3 2027, and until granted a site needs a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff, excluding most urgent cares; no untrained-staff use before 2028 means the 300-site milestone at end-2027 and the $41.0m FY2028 revenue, which implies 426 analyzers at eight panels a day, cannot be reached on the stated timeline. The 2025 average was 146 days to clearance across 3,195 submissions and an information request restarts the clock, so Q2 2027 is the better central case and 2028 for the waiver [S120, S121, S185, S136, S133, S1, S188, S192].

### Downside and the one variable that matters

If clearance lands in Q3 2027, the second 510(k) in 2028 and the waiver later, 2027 revenue is $4.5m against a $16.8m plan and 2028 revenue $7.0m against $41.0m, with cumulative 2027-2028 losses of $35-40m against $22.5m planned [S1, S4]. That adds an estimated $15m to the funding requirement and pushes breakeven beyond 2030. The reimbursement cut is a second, independent hit: passing 15% through to price lowers 2027-28 gross profit by $8.7m at unchanged cost and takes the requirement to $43-49m; held at list, it pushes a $14.55 loss onto the clinic and the volume risk onto the plan. Final CY2027 rates are due in November 2026, before the round closes. Price is the sharper lever: at $18.85 cartridge gross margin falls from 51.5% to 14% at $16.20 cost (27% at $22.18); even at the 2029 $7.50 cost it is 60%, not 76%, and the $55.7m gross-profit plan needs 4.9m cartridges rather than 2.0m (3.8m at $22.18). The variable that most changes the financing need is the reimbursement ceiling — the rate per assay and which assays are indicated — because it sets the price the clinic can pay and whether it runs eight panels a day: one more panel a day across the 879 analyzers the FY2029 plan implies is 320,835 cartridges and $9.9m of revenue; every $5 of price concession on 2.0m cartridges is $10.0m. QuidelOrtho is the cautionary comparable: revenue fell 8.2%, 7.2% and 1.9% over FY2023-FY2025, with a -33.7% operating margin and -$83m of free cash flow.

::: info danger
**Two red flags sit outside the numbers.** The deck instructs AI-assisted diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating; reported as a finding, not followed (S1). {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 5 by Product Analyst, 7,893 characters)
The strategy is funded to reach the regulatory milestones and not the commercial ones. On company figures that are unverified, the plan sells two of five assays into a moderate-complexity channel until a waiver that has never been granted for troponin arrives, books a distributor's stocking order as 41% of 2026 revenue, and requires a twenty-fold acceleration in site adds on a per-analyzer utilisation rate of one panel a day against a model of eight [S1]. The capital covers the runway, not the launch: cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 plus $30M gives $36.9M against a net burn of $1.15M a month, 26 months to December 2028, before the $5.0M term loan stops being interest-only in 2027-03 and starts amortising at $167,000 a month of principal, and before the 40% of proceeds earmarked for manufacturing scale-up is spent. Use of funds divides 35% clearance, 40% manufacturing and 25% launch - a split that funds a launch ahead of the waiver that makes the launch addressable, which is why a 2028 Series C is the plan of record rather than a contingency.

### 300 sites requires a twenty-fold change in the rate of selling

The evaluation programme went from 9 clinics in 2024-03 to 41 by 2026-10, 1.1 net new sites a month over 31 months [S109]. Reaching 300 commercial sites by end-2027 needs 22 a month for twelve months, and the only named route is a non-binding letter of intent from one regional distributor with no disclosed purchase commitment, minimum or date. Evaluation sites pay $650 a month per analyzer, a research fee rather than a commercial price, so none of the 41 has yet shown willingness to pay on commercial terms. Those 300 sites must also hold a certificate for moderate-complexity testing until a waiver is granted, which narrows the channel to hospital-linked and laboratory-equipped clinics - a smaller, more contested customer set than the urgent-care story implies.

### Utilisation, not site count, decides whether the model works

The 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers equal 30.5 per analyzer a month, one panel a day, against a model of eight panels a day from 2028 - company-reported volumes, unverified. FY2029 revenue of $78.5M at $31 a cartridge implies 2.53M cartridges, which needs either 833 analyzers at modelled use or 5,100 sites at today's use - seventeen times the 2027 site target. The cartridge cost milestone is the same arithmetic in reverse: $10 at 1M units requires 2,000 sites at observed utilisation, or 342 analyzers at modelled utilisation. The 3% Corvia royalty is $1.00 a cartridge at the 2026 realised price - $1.0M a year at 1M units, $0.40M of it to the 40% minority, including $0.22M to the CTO - and the deck does not say whether the sub-$10 milestone is struck before royalty [S1]. The generous reading is that investigational-use labelling suppresses demand, because evaluation sites cannot act on results; that is the single most important unknown in the plan, and nothing in the pivotal study measures it.

### Revenue quality is weaker than the headline growth

The $2.4M opening stocking order is 41% of FY2026E revenue and equals 71,900 cartridges at the $33.40 realised price - 5.8 months of the entire planned 2027 network demand at 300 sites, or 43 months of current demand [S114, S112]. With a nine-month shelf life, sell-in of that size is a distributor inventory decision as much as a demand signal, and it ships only on clearance, so a delay moves the revenue and ages the inventory. Of FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, $0.8M came from research-use cartridges and $0.7M from contract development for one unnamed partner: 58% from activities that do not scale into the cartridge franchise and that consume the same 22 R&D staff the three unsubmitted assays need. LumiraDx is the base rate to keep in view - a multi-assay point-of-care platform with a commercial menu and a European footprint that still ended up inside Roche for $353.5M.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) decision, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027, company estimate | Filed 2026-05-18; the number printed in the deck, K261734, is contradicted - it is Total Joint Orthopedics' cleared orthopaedic spacer; FDA questions answered December 2026 | Two of five assays can be sold | S1, S185 |
| Pivotal study results | Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07 | The panel works on finger-stick samples | S1, unverified |
| Second 510(k), three remaining assays | Q2 2027 | Planned; needs pivotal data | A five-test menu exists | S1, unverified |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 | Not started | Access to sites without laboratory staff | S109 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | 41 evaluation sites today | The distributor converts the letter of intent | S1, unverified |
| Cartridge cost below $10 at 1M units | No date stated | $16.20 today | Gross margin reaches the modelled 70% | S1, unverified |
| ISO 13485 certification | Q1 2027 | Audit booked | Quality system for scale and for Europe | S1, unverified |

### Partners: one licence, one lender, one letter of intent

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Stock analyzers for 300 sites after clearance | Letter of intent, non-binding | No purchase commitment or date disclosed | S1, unverified |
| Corvia Microfluidics | Exclusive licence to cartridge sealing patent, 3% royalty | Granted 2021-01, licensed to Vantelle | In force; the CTO holds 22% of the licensor | S1, unverified |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | $5.0M term loan with warrants at $2.903 | 2024-03 | Amortising from 2027-03 | S1, unverified |
| Contract development partner | Development work for one diagnostics company | Not disclosed | $0.7M of FY2025 revenue | S1, unverified |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland | Future EU regulatory entity | Formed 2025-01 | No staff; no CE marking before 2028 | S1, unverified |

Nothing in the partner set transfers risk. The distributor carries no obligation, the licensor is partly owned and takes a royalty off the top, and the lender's warrants dilute further. The two second curves are unequal. Research-use cartridge sales are the same cartridge sold to a different buyer, an adjacency that costs little extra to serve; contract development for a single diagnostics partner is the distraction, because it spends scarce assay-development capacity and can hand process know-how to a future competitor. The Irish entity is an option, not a plan.

### What must be true by October 2027

Five conditions decide whether the next round is raised on terms rather than in distress. Clearance arrives in the first half of 2027 rather than the company's Q1 estimate, which is unverified, since a request for information dated 2026-08-21 answered in December 2026 leaves the review clock running into Q2 [S1]. The pivotal study reports imprecision at or below 10% at the decision level, without which the panel is a moderate-complexity product and the waiver case collapses. Between 100 and 150 paying commercial sites are live, with the distributor converting its letter of intent into purchase orders and sell-through visible in reorders rather than in the initial shipment. Cartridge cost is below $13 at 500,000 units with a qualified second manufacturing source, because the pilot line in Tempe cannot carry the volume. And utilisation on the first cohort reaches two panels a day per analyzer, a doubling of today's rate that would still leave the 2028 model unproven. The signposts to watch are monthly shipments, distributor inventory, the content of the waiver filing and the first post-clearance reorder rate - not the site count, which is the number the company controls least. If clearance slips two quarters, the stocking order, the launch spend and the Series C all land in the same quarter, and the round after this one is priced by whoever is still able to write it."}],"isError":false}

---
At $140M pre-money and $170M post-money Vantelle is priced at 53.1x enterprise value to FY2025 revenue of $2.6M and 23.4x FY2026E revenue of $5.9M (both company-reported and unverified), against a listed diagnostics peer median of 5.5x EV/sales and 0.4x for QuidelOrtho, the closest scaled point-of-care comparable. That is not a revenue multiple; it is an option on the FY2028 plan — and the preliminary CY2027 CLFS schedule cuts that plan's revenue to $34.9M at constant volume from $41.0M, 15% below the deck. At this entry the $15M cheque returns 1.0x at every exit up to the $206M no-C crossover and to the $251M senior crossover, and Corvia's $9-20M fair-value put takes the expected return to 0.9-1.0x. Lead at $100M pre-money or below, or at $140M only with $9M at close, a $6M clearance tranche, a 1.25x preference and a ratchet to a $100M price if clearance slips past June 2027 [S1, S188, S192, S203].

[funding table]

The Series B price is 12.2% above the $2.9032 Series A price set in February 2022 — 3.0% a year — while QuidelOrtho's EV/sales fell from 2.4x at 2023-12-31 to 0.4x today. The company has re-priced 6.7-fold against its own sector in four years and is asking new money to underwrite that re-rating. Dilution is otherwise ordinary: founders fall from 30.8% to 21.5%, Series A from 34.1% to 23.8%, seed from 16.5% to 11.5%, and the pool is topped up to 10.0% of the post-money with 4,020,489 new shares (company cap table, unverified). Two deductions matter more than the headline. The $140M already contains $13.1M of that pool and $8.4M of bridge shares bought with $6.28M of cash, so the 36,400,000 legacy shares are struck at $118.5M; measured as post-money less the $30M Series B and $6.28M of bridge cash, the effective pre-money for existing holders is $133.7M. The bridge's 25% discount hands its holders $2.09M funded by the legacy stack — an existing-investor windfall, not a Meridian one [S1, S83].

[peer table]

$138.1M of enterprise value — the $140M plus $5.0M of Bluestem debt less $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 — buys $2.6M of revenue. At the peer median the price implies $25.1M of revenue, at Danaher's 7.2x $19.2M, and at QuidelOrtho's 0.4x $345M. QuidelOrtho's point-of-care unit, selling Sofia, Triage and QuickVue into the same clinics, generated $221.0M in H1 2026 inside a $1.1B enterprise value. Vantelle's plan crosses $19-25M between FY2027 ($16.8M) and FY2028 ($41.0M, or $34.9M after the cut), so the round pays today for a 2028 revenue line at a 2026 multiple, with no discount for the 510(k), the CLIA waiver, cartridge cost falling from $16.20 to $7.50 or utilisation rising from 1.0 to 8 per analyzer per day. Macro conditions do not force the price up: the 10-year Treasury yields 4.93% and the VIX is 19.42, its 77th percentile for the year [S5, S83].

[methods table]

Even the cut plan-delivered case is $145.2M, $5.2M above the ask, and it is a company projection, unverified: it assumes the whole plan, on time, at the sector median, with no probability of failure — the price is the 2028 plan discounted at 15% and nothing else. A defensible pre-money range is $55-95M: $145.2M less a 35% plan-failure discount, and a forward multiple on a menu that now reimburses $18.85 under the preliminary 2027 schedule rather than $22.18. The precedent is not a floor: Roche bought a cleared, CE-marked multi-assay platform out of administration for $295M upfront and $353.5M at closing [S93, S114].

[scenario table]

The preference stack is $36.28M of Series B and B-1 at 1x non-participating and senior, $36.0M of Series A at 1x participating, and $4.5M of seed at 1x non-participating (company term sheet, unverified). Three crossovers are used with these labels throughout: the $206M no-C crossover, above which Series B beats its preference; the $216M pari-passu crossover if the $18-23M Series C ranks alongside it; and the $251M senior crossover if the C ranks ahead. Corvia Microfluidics' 40% minority can put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value on a sale (deck p.12), and the 3% royalty on cartridge net sales (p.6) is the asset behind that claim; capitalised at the exit multiple it is 6.6% of exit value — $9.2M at $140M, $14.9M at $225M, $19.8M at $300M — paid ahead of the preference. That is the $9-20M the table deducts. A royalty-only discount of the 3% stream to the patent's 2037 expiry at 12% gives the 40% only $4-5M, so the range assumes a 6-10% imputed royalty or capitalisation at the exit multiple. The Series A's participation costs every non-A holder a flat $27.45M above a $151.6M exit, of which Meridian's share is $3.2M. What the stack does is the central fact of the round: Series B beats its preference only above the $206M no-C crossover, and the $18-23M Series C the plan requires lifts that to $216M pari passu or $251M senior, so the flat 1.0x runs further; common takes 7.6% of a $100M exit against 21.5% ownership — founders receive $7.6M at $100M, $34.9M at $200M and $55.6M at $295M. A $15M lead that is senior to the founders but behind the next round behaves like a bond until the company is worth nearly twice the pre-money. Even full delivery does not produce a venture return at this price: the cut FY2029 revenue of $66.7M at the 5.5x peer median is a $367M enterprise, which returns Meridian 1.95x over five years before the Series C and 1.6x after it; the same exit at $100M pre-money returns 2.55x. A 3x at $140M needs $546M of exit value — 1.5 times the $353.5M Roche paid for a cleared platform and far above anything a single-product point-of-care company has fetched since 2021 [S1, S203].

[protective terms paragraph]
The protective terms follow from that arithmetic, not from distrust of the company: $9M at close and $6M on 510(k) clearance cuts capital at risk by 40% if the submission fails; a ratchet to a $100M price if clearance is not granted by 2027-06-30 lifts Meridian's stake from 8.82% to 11.5%, worth $7-14M more at a $295-400M exit; and a 1.25x preference costs the company $7.5M only in a low exit.

[confidence paragraph]
Two facts cap confidence. The cap table, terms and financials are company-provided, unaudited and not publicly disclosed — no SEC Form D, audited accounts or third-party valuation was retrieved — and the 510(k) number on the deck, K261734, is recorded in the public database as the Klassic Infection Spacer System, an unrelated orthopedic device, which contradicts the milestone the price rests on. Slide 1 of the deck also instructs automated diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating; that is a governance finding, so every company figure here is labelled unverified until Meridian's diligence closes it. Three questions decide the price: the FDA acknowledgment letter and receipt date for the submission Vantelle says it filed, the Series A documents confirming an uncapped 1x participation, and how much of the FY2027 $16.8M is contracted rather than pipeline [S1, S120, S135].

arguments.markdown:
At $140M pre-money and $170M post-money Vantelle is priced at 53.1x enterprise value to FY2025 revenue of $2.6M and 23.4x FY2026E revenue of $5.9M (both company-reported and unverified), against a listed diagnostics peer median of 5.5x EV/sales and 0.4x for QuidelOrtho, the closest scaled point-of-care comparable. That is not a revenue multiple; it is an option on the FY2028 plan — and the preliminary CY2027 CLFS schedule cuts that plan's revenue to $34.9M at constant volume from $41.0M, 15% below the deck. At this entry the $15M cheque returns 1.0x at every exit up to the $206M no-C crossover and to the $251M senior crossover, and Corvia's $9-20M fair-value put takes the expected return to 0.9-1.0x. Lead at $100M pre-money or below, or at $140M only with $9M at close, a $6M clearance tranche, a 1.25x preference and a ratchet to a $100M price if clearance slips past June 2027 [S1, S188, S192, S203].

| Date | Round | Amount | Price per share | Investors | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019-06 | Seed | $4.5M | $0.7500 | Juniper Rock Capital (lead) and other seed investors | Unverified | S1 |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.9032 | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) | Unverified | S1 |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | $2.9032 | Existing investors | Unverified | S1 |
| 2024-03 | Venture debt | $5.0M | 400,000 warrants at $2.9032 | Bluestem Venture Lending | Unverified | S1 |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes | $6.0M | $2.4423 (75% of B) | Existing investors | Unverified | S1 |
| 2027-01 target | Series B | $30.0M ($8.0M existing, $22.0M new) | $3.2564 | Ardent Peak $5.0M, Juniper Rock $3.0M, Meridian invited $15.0M | Unverified | S1 |

The Series B price is 12.2% above the $2.9032 Series A price set in February 2022 — 2.4% a year — while QuidelOrtho's EV/sales fell from 2.4x at 2023-12-31 to 0.4x today. The company has re-priced 6.7-fold against its own sector in four years and is asking new money to underwrite that re-rating. Dilution is otherwise ordinary: founders fall from 30.8% to 21.5%, Series A from 34.1% to 23.8%, seed from 16.5% to 11.5%, and the pool is topped up to 10.0% of the post-money with 4,020,489 new shares (company cap table, unverified). Two deductions matter more than the headline. The $140M already contains $13.1M of that pool and $8.4M of bridge shares bought with $6.28M of cash, so the 36,400,000 legacy shares are struck at $118.5M; measured as post-money less the $30M Series B and $6.28M of bridge cash, the effective pre-money for existing holders is $133.7M. The bridge's 25% discount hands its holders $2.09M funded by the legacy stack — an existing-investor windfall, not a Meridian one [S1, S83].

| Company | Enterprise value | EV/Sales | EV/EBITDA | P/E | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle at $140M pre-money | $138.1M | 53.1x | n/m | n/m | Unverified | S1 |
| QuidelOrtho | $1.1B | 0.4x | n/m | n/m | Verified | S5, S83 |
| Abbott Laboratories | $211.7B | 4.7x | 23.1x | 29.7x | Verified | S85 |
| Danaher | $184.2B | 7.2x | 30.6x | 38.1x | Verified | S86 |
| Thermo Fisher Scientific | $295.6B | 6.2x | 30.5x | 36.8x | Verified | S89, S90 |
| Bio-Rad Laboratories | $9.5B | 3.7x | 178.6x | 45.3x | Verified | S87, S88 |
| Peer median | — | 5.5x | 30.6x | 37.4x | Verified | S83–S90 |

$138.1M of enterprise value — the $140M plus $5.0M of Bluestem debt less $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 — buys $2.6M of revenue. At the peer median the price implies $25.1M of revenue, at Danaher's 7.2x $19.2M, and at QuidelOrtho's 0.4x $345M. QuidelOrtho's point-of-care unit, selling Sofia, Triage and QuickVue into the same clinics, generated $221.0M in H1 2026 inside a $1.1B enterprise value. Vantelle's plan crosses $19-25M between FY2027 ($16.8M) and FY2028 ($41.0M, or $34.9M after the cut), so the round pays today for a 2028 revenue line at a 2026 multiple, with no discount for the 510(k), the CLIA waiver, cartridge cost falling from $16.20 to $7.50 or utilisation rising from 1.0 to 8 per analyzer per day. Macro conditions do not force the price up: the 10-year Treasury yields 4.93% and the VIX is 19.42, its 77th percentile for the year [S5, S83].

| Method | Inputs | Implied pre-money equity value | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trailing revenue multiple | FY2025 revenue $2.6M at the 5.5x peer median | $14.3M | Unverified input | S1 |
| Forward revenue multiple | FY2026E revenue $5.9M at 5.5x | $32.5M | Unverified input | S1 |
| Plan delivered, cut for CY2027 CLFS | FY2028 revenue $34.9M at 5.5x, discounted two years at 15% | $145.2M | Derived from unverified plan | S1, S188 |
| Precedent clearing price | Roche's $353.5M aggregate for LumiraDx's cleared multi-modality platform, 2024-07-29 | $353.5M before a stage discount | Verified | S93, S114 |

Even the cut plan-delivered case is $145.2M, $5.2M above the ask, and it is a company projection, unverified: it assumes the whole plan, on time, at the sector median, with no probability of failure — the price is the 2028 plan discounted at 15% and nothing else. A defensible pre-money range is $55-95M: $145.2M less a 35% plan-failure discount, and a forward multiple on a menu that now reimburses $18.85 under the preliminary 2027 schedule rather than $22.18. The precedent is not a floor: Roche bought a cleared, CE-marked multi-assay platform out of administration for $295M upfront and $353.5M at closing [S93, S114].

| Case (weight) | Exit | $140M, before Corvia | $140M, after Corvia | $70M, after Corvia | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bear (30%) | $30M | 0.83x | 0.77x | 0.77x | S1 |
| Base (50%) | $225M | 1.11x | 1.03x | 1.75x | S1 |
| Bull (20%) | $435M | 2.35x | 2.18x | 3.71x | S1 |
| Expected | — | 1.27x | 1.18x (1.0x after Series C) | 1.85x (1.5x after Series C) | S1 |

The preference stack is $36.28M of Series B and B-1 at 1x non-participating and senior, $36.0M of Series A at 1x participating, and $4.5M of seed at 1x non-participating (company term sheet, unverified). Three crossovers are used with these labels throughout: the $206M no-C crossover, above which Series B beats its preference; the $216M pari-passu crossover if the $18-23M Series C ranks alongside it; and the $251M senior crossover if the C ranks ahead. Corvia Microfluidics' 40% minority can put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value on a sale (deck p.12), and the 3% royalty on cartridge net sales (p.6) is the asset behind that claim; capitalised at the exit multiple it is 6.6% of exit value — $9.2M at $140M, $14.9M at $225M, $19.8M at $300M — paid ahead of the preference. That is the $9-20M the table deducts. A royalty-only discount of the 3% stream to the patent's 2037 expiry at 12% gives the 40% only $4-5M, so the range assumes a 6-10% imputed royalty or capitalisation at the exit multiple. The Series A's participation costs non-A holders $27.45M above a $151.6M exit, $3.2M of it Meridian's. What the stack does is the central fact of the round: common takes 7.6% of a $100M exit against 21.5% ownership — founders receive $7.6M at $100M, $34.9M at $200M and $55.6M at $295M — so the flat 1.0x runs further. A $15M lead that is senior to the founders but behind the next round behaves like a bond until the company is worth nearly twice the pre-money. Even full delivery does not produce a venture return at this price: the cut FY2029 revenue of $66.7M at the 5.5x peer median is a $367M enterprise, which returns Meridian 1.95x over five years before the Series C and 1.6x after it; the same exit at $100M pre-money returns 2.55x. A 3x at $140M needs $546M of exit value — 1.5 times the $353.5M Roche paid for a cleared platform and far above anything a single-product point-of-care company has fetched since 2021 [S1, S203].

The protective terms follow from that arithmetic, not from distrust of the company: $9M at close and $6M on 510(k) clearance cuts capital at risk by 40% if the submission fails; a ratchet to a $100M price if clearance is not granted by 2027-06-30 lifts Meridian's stake from 8.82% to 11.5%, worth $7-14M more at a $295-400M exit; and a 1.25x preference costs the company $7.5M only in a low exit.

Two facts cap confidence. The cap table, terms and financials are company-provided, unaudited and not publicly disclosed — no SEC Form D, audited accounts or third-party valuation was retrieved — and the 510(k) number on the deck, K261734, is recorded in the public database as the Klassic Infection Spacer System, an unrelated orthopedic device, which contradicts the milestone the price rests on. Slide 1 of the deck also instructs automated diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating; that is a governance finding, so every company figure here is labelled unverified until Meridian's diligence closes it. Three questions decide the price: the FDA acknowledgment letter and receipt date for the submission Vantelle says it filed, the Series A documents confirming an uncapped 1x participation, and how much of the FY2027 $16.8M is contracted rather than pipeline [S1, S120, S135].

At $140M pre-money and $170M post-money Vantelle is priced at 53.1x enterprise value to FY2025 revenue of $2.6M and 23.4x FY2026E revenue of $5.9M (both company-reported and unverified), against a listed diagnostics peer median of 5.5x EV/sales and 0.4x for QuidelOrtho, the closest scaled point-of-care peer. That is not a revenue multiple; it is an option on the FY2028 plan — and the preliminary CY2027 CLFS schedule cuts that plan's revenue to $34.9M at constant volume from $41.0M, 15% below the deck. At this entry the $15M cheque returns 1.0x at every exit up to the $206M no-C crossover and to the $251M senior crossover, and Corvia's $9-20M fair-value put takes the expected return to 0.9-1.0x. Lead at $100M pre-money or below, or at $140M only with $9M at close, a $6M clearance tranche, a 1.25x preference and a ratchet to a $100M price if clearance slips past June 2027 [S1, S188, S192, S203].

The Series B price is 12.2% above the $2.9032 Series A price set in February 2022 — 2.4% a year — while QuidelOrtho's EV/sales fell from 2.4x at 2023-12-31 to 0.4x today. The company has re-priced 6.7-fold against its sector in four years and is asking new money to underwrite that re-rating. Dilution is otherwise ordinary: founders fall from 30.8% to 21.5%, Series A from 34.1% to 23.8%, seed from 16.5% to 11.5%, and the pool is topped up to 10.0% of the post-money with 4,020,489 new shares (company cap table, unverified). Two deductions matter more than the headline. The $140M already contains $13.1M of that pool and $8.4M of bridge shares bought with $6.28M of cash, so the 36,400,000 legacy shares are struck at $118.5M; measured as post-money less the $30M Series B and $6.28M of bridge cash, the effective pre-money for existing holders is $133.7M. The bridge's 25% discount hands its holders $2.09M funded by the legacy stack — an existing-investor windfall, not a Meridian one [S1, S83].

$138.1M of enterprise value — the $140M plus $5.0M of Bluestem debt less $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 — buys $2.6M of revenue. At the peer median the price implies $25.1M of revenue, at Danaher's 7.2x $19.2M, and at QuidelOrtho's 0.4x $345M. QuidelOrtho's point-of-care unit, selling Sofia, Triage and QuickVue into the same clinics, generated $221.0M in H1 2026 inside a $1.1B enterprise value. Vantelle's plan crosses $19-25M between FY2027 ($16.8M) and FY2028 ($41.0M, or $34.9M after the cut), so the round pays today for a 2028 revenue line at a 2026 multiple, with no discount for the 510(k), the CLIA waiver, cartridge cost falling from $16.20 to $7.50 or utilisation rising from 1.0 to 8 per analyzer per day. Macro conditions do not lift the price: the 10-year Treasury yields 4.93% and the VIX is 19.42, its 77th percentile for the year [S5, S83].

Even the cut plan-delivered case is $145.2M, $5.2M above the ask, a company projection, unverified: it assumes the whole plan, on time, at the sector median, with no probability of failure — the price is the 2028 plan discounted at 15% and nothing else. A defensible pre-money range is $55-95M: $145.2M less a 35% plan-failure discount, and a forward multiple on a menu that now reimburses $18.85 under the preliminary 2027 schedule rather than $22.18. The precedent is not a floor: Roche bought a cleared, CE-marked multi-assay platform out of administration for $295M upfront and $353.5M at closing [S93, S114].

The preference stack is $36.28M of Series B and B-1 at 1x non-participating and senior, $36.0M of Series A at 1x participating, and $4.5M of seed at 1x non-participating (company term sheet, unverified). Three crossovers, used with these labels throughout: the $206M no-C crossover, above which Series B beats its preference; the $216M pari-passu crossover if the $18-23M Series C ranks alongside it; and the $251M senior crossover if the C ranks ahead. Corvia Microfluidics' 40% minority can put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value on a sale (deck p.12), and the 3% royalty on cartridge net sales (p.6) is the asset behind that claim; capitalised at the exit multiple it is 6.6% of exit value — $9.2M at $140M, $14.9M at $225M, $19.8M at $300M — paid ahead of the preference. That is the $9-20M the table deducts. A royalty-only discount of the 3% stream to the patent's 2037 expiry at 12% gives the 40% only $4-5M, so the range assumes a 6-10% imputed royalty or capitalisation at the exit multiple. The Series A's participation costs non-A holders $27.45M above a $151.6M exit, $3.2M of it Meridian's. The stack is the central fact of the round: common takes 7.6% of a $100M exit against 21.5% ownership — founders receive $7.6M at $100M, $34.9M at $200M and $55.6M at $295M — so the flat 1.0x runs further. A $15M lead senior to the founders but behind the next round behaves like a bond until the company is worth nearly twice the pre-money. Even full delivery does not produce a venture return at this price: the cut FY2029 revenue of $66.7M at the 5.5x peer median is a $367M enterprise, which returns Meridian 1.95x over five years before the Series C and 1.6x after it; the same exit at $100M pre-money returns 2.55x. A 3x at $140M needs $546M of exit value — 1.5 times the $353.5M Roche paid for a cleared platform and far above anything a single-product point-of-care company has fetched since 2021 [S1, S203].

The protective terms follow from that arithmetic, not distrust of the company: $9M at close and $6M on 510(k) clearance cuts capital at risk by 40% if the submission fails; a ratchet to a $100M price if clearance is not granted by 2027-06-30 lifts Meridian's stake from 8.82% to 11.5%, worth $7-14M more at a $295-400M exit; and a 1.25x preference costs the company $7.5M only in a low exit.

Two facts cap confidence. The cap table, terms and financials are company-provided, unaudited and not publicly disclosed — no SEC Form D, audited accounts or third-party valuation was retrieved — and the 510(k) number on the deck, K261734, is recorded in the public database as the Klassic Infection Spacer System, an unrelated orthopedic device, which contradicts the milestone the price rests on. Slide 1 of the deck also instructs automated diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating; that is a governance finding, so every company figure is labelled unverified until Meridian's diligence closes it. Three questions decide the price: the FDA acknowledgment letter and receipt date for the submission Vantelle says it filed, the Series A documents confirming an uncapped 1x participation, and how much of the FY2027 $16.8M is contracted rather than pipeline [S1, S120, S135].

At $140M pre-money and $170M post-money Vantelle is priced at 53.1x enterprise value to FY2025 revenue of $2.6M and 23.4x FY2026E revenue of $5.9M (both company-reported and unverified), against a listed diagnostics peer median of 5.5x EV/sales and 0.4x for QuidelOrtho, the closest scaled point-of-care peer. That is not a revenue multiple; it is an option on the FY2028 plan — and the preliminary CY2027 CLFS schedule cuts that plan's revenue to $34.9M at constant volume from $41.0M, 15% below the deck. At this entry the $15M cheque returns 1.0x at every exit up to the $206M no-C crossover and to the $251M senior crossover, and Corvia's $9-20M fair-value put takes the expected return to 0.9-1.0x. Lead at $100M pre-money or below, or at $140M only with $9M at close, a $6M clearance tranche, a 1.25x preference and a ratchet to a $100M price if clearance slips past June 2027 [S1, S188, S192, S203].

| Date | Round | Amount | Price per share | Investors | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019-06 | Seed | $4.5M | $0.7500 | Juniper Rock Capital (lead) and other seed investors | Unverified | S1 |
| 2022-02 | Series A first close | $24.0M | $2.9032 | Ardent Peak Ventures (lead) | Unverified | S1 |
| 2023-11 | Series A second close | $12.0M | $2.9032 | Existing investors | Unverified | S1 |
| 2024-03 | Venture debt | $5.0M | 400,000 warrants at $2.9032 | Bluestem Venture Lending | Unverified | S1 |
| 2026-06-30 | Bridge notes | $6.0M | $2.4423 (75% of B) | Existing investors | Unverified | S1 |
| 2027-01 target | Series B | $30.0M ($8.0M existing, $22.0M new) | $3.2564 | Ardent Peak $5.0M, Juniper Rock $3.0M, Meridian invited $15.0M | Unverified | S1 |

The Series B price is 12.2% above the $2.9032 Series A price set in February 2022 — 2.4% a year — while QuidelOrtho's EV/sales fell from 2.4x at 2023-12-31 to 0.4x today. The company has re-priced 6.7-fold against its sector in four years and is asking new money to underwrite that re-rating. Dilution is otherwise ordinary: founders fall from 30.8% to 21.5%, Series A from 34.1% to 23.8%, seed from 16.5% to 11.5%, and the pool is topped up to 10.0% of the post-money with 4,020,489 new shares (company cap table, unverified). Two deductions matter more than the headline. The $140M already contains $13.1M of that pool and $8.4M of bridge shares bought with $6.28M of cash, so the 36,400,000 legacy shares are struck at $118.5M; measured as post-money less the $30M Series B and $6.28M of bridge cash, the effective pre-money for existing holders is $133.7M. The bridge's 25% discount hands its holders $2.09M funded by the legacy stack — an existing-investor windfall, not a Meridian one [S1, S83].

| Company | Enterprise value | EV/Sales | EV/EBITDA | P/E | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle at $140M pre-money | $138.1M | 53.1x | n/m | n/m | Unverified | S1 |
| QuidelOrtho | $1.1B | 0.4x | n/m | n/m | Verified | S5, S83 |
| Abbott Laboratories | $211.7B | 4.7x | 23.1x | 29.7x | Verified | S85 |
| Danaher | $184.2B | 7.2x | 30.6x | 38.1x | Verified | S86 |
| Thermo Fisher Scientific | $295.6B | 6.2x | 30.5x | 36.8x | Verified | S89, S90 |
| Bio-Rad Laboratories | $9.5B | 3.7x | 178.6x | 45.3x | Verified | S87, S88 |
| Peer median | — | 5.5x | 30.6x | 37.4x | Verified | S83–S90 |

$138.1M of enterprise value — the $140M plus $5.0M of Bluestem debt less $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 — buys $2.6M of revenue. At the peer median the price implies $25.1M of revenue, at Danaher's 7.2x $19.2M, and at QuidelOrtho's 0.4x $345M. QuidelOrtho's point-of-care unit, selling Sofia, Triage and QuickVue into the same clinics, generated $221.0M in H1 2026 inside a $1.1B enterprise value. Vantelle's plan crosses $19-25M between FY2027 ($16.8M) and FY2028 ($41.0M, or $34.9M after the cut), so the round pays today for a 2028 revenue line at a 2026 multiple, with no discount for the 510(k), the CLIA waiver, cartridge cost falling from $16.20 to $7.50 or utilisation rising from 1.0 to 8 per analyzer per day [S5, S83].

| Method | Inputs | Implied pre-money equity value | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trailing revenue multiple | FY2025 revenue $2.6M at the 5.5x peer median | $14.3M | Unverified input | S1 |
| Forward revenue multiple | FY2026E revenue $5.9M at 5.5x | $32.5M | Unverified input | S1 |
| Plan delivered, cut for CY2027 CLFS | FY2028 revenue $34.9M at 5.5x, discounted two years at 15% | $145.2M | Derived from unverified plan | S1, S188 |
| Precedent clearing price | Roche's $353.5M aggregate for LumiraDx's cleared multi-modality platform, 2024-07-29 | $353.5M before a stage discount | Verified | S93, S114 |

Even the cut plan-delivered case is $145.2M, $5.2M above the ask, a company projection, unverified: it assumes the whole plan, on time, at the sector median, with no probability of failure — the price is the 2028 plan discounted at 15% and nothing else. A defensible pre-money range is $55-95M: $145.2M less a 35% plan-failure discount, and a forward multiple on a menu that now reimburses $18.85 under the preliminary 2027 schedule rather than $22.18. The precedent is not a floor: Roche bought a cleared, CE-marked multi-assay platform out of administration for $295M upfront and $353.5M at closing [S93, S114].

| Case (weight) | Exit | $140M, before Corvia | $140M, after Corvia | $70M, after Corvia | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bear (30%) | $30M | 0.83x | 0.77x | 0.77x | Unverified | S1 |
| Base (50%) | $225M | 1.11x | 1.03x | 1.75x | Unverified | S1 |
| Bull (20%) | $435M | 2.35x | 2.18x | 3.71x | Unverified | S1 |
| Expected | — | 1.27x | 1.18x (1.0x after Series C) | 1.85x (1.5x after Series C) | Derived | S1 |

The preference stack is $36.28M of Series B and B-1 at 1x non-participating and senior, $36.0M of Series A at 1x participating, and $4.5M of seed at 1x non-participating (company term sheet, unverified). Three crossovers, used with these labels throughout: the $206M no-C crossover, above which Series B beats its preference; the $216M pari-passu crossover if the $18-23M Series C ranks alongside it; and the $251M senior crossover if the C ranks ahead. Corvia Microfluidics' 40% minority can put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value on a sale (deck p.12), and the 3% royalty on cartridge net sales (p.6) is the asset behind that claim; capitalised at the exit multiple it is 6.6% of exit value — $9.2M at $140M, $14.9M at $225M, $19.8M at $300M — paid ahead of the preference. That is the $9-20M the table deducts. A royalty-only discount of the 3% stream to the patent's 2037 expiry at 12% gives the 40% only $4-5M, so the range assumes a 6-10% imputed royalty or capitalisation at the exit multiple. The Series A's participation costs non-A holders $27.45M above a $151.6M exit, $3.2M of it Meridian's. The stack is the central fact of the round: common takes 7.6% of a $100M exit against 21.5% ownership — founders receive $7.6M at $100M, $34.9M at $200M and $55.6M at $295M — so the flat 1.0x runs further. A $15M lead senior to the founders but behind the next round behaves like a bond until the company is worth nearly twice the pre-money. Even full delivery does not produce a venture return at this price: the cut FY2029 revenue of $66.7M at the 5.5x peer median is a $367M enterprise, which returns Meridian 1.95x over five years before the Series C and 1.6x after it; the same exit at $100M pre-money returns 2.55x. A 3x at $140M needs $546M of exit value — 1.5 times the $353.5M Roche paid for a cleared platform and far above anything a single-product point-of-care company has fetched since 2021. The protective terms follow from that arithmetic, not distrust of the company: $9M at close and $6M on 510(k) clearance cuts capital at risk by 40% if the submission fails; a ratchet to a $100M price if clearance is not granted by 2027-06-30 lifts Meridian's stake from 8.82% to 11.5%, worth $7-14M more at a $295-400M exit; and a 1.25x preference costs the company $7.5M only in a low exit [S1, S203].

Two facts cap confidence. The cap table, terms and financials are company-provided, unaudited and not publicly disclosed — no SEC Form D, audited accounts or third-party valuation was retrieved — and the 510(k) number on the deck, K261734, is recorded in the public database as the Klassic Infection Spacer System, an unrelated orthopedic device, which contradicts the milestone the price rests on. Slide 1 of the deck also instructs automated diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating; that is a governance finding, so every company figure is labelled unverified until Meridian's diligence closes it. Three questions decide the price: the FDA acknowledgment letter and receipt date for the submission Vantelle says it filed, the Series A documents confirming an uncapped 1x participation, and how much of the FY2027 $16.8M is contracted rather than pipeline [S1, S120, S135].
