The only realistic exit is a trade sale to a strategic already selling into the same clinic, at $100M-$350M, and the ceiling is what cleared platforms change hands for: on 2026-04-20 QuidelOrtho paid $100M in cash for LEX Diagnostics, whose VELO Respiratory Test (K251742), a cartridge-based molecular assay, was cleared and CLIA-waived on 2026-02-13 and had not launched commercially in the US. Vantelle asks $140M of pre-money value for two of five assays under review and no waiver. At that entry the $15M lead returns 0.77x in the bear case, about 0.9x in a $225M base case and 1.9x in a $435M bull case once the $18-23M Series C the plan needs and Corvia's 6.6% put are included — an expected 1.0x over five years, below any venture threshold. The preliminary CY2027 CLFS cut takes FY2028 revenue to $34.9M at constant volume from $41.0M, which is why the base and bull exits fall from $250M and $500M; the $100M-$350M range survives because it is anchored on transactions, not on the plan. The exit supports a lead only from $60-70M, or from $140M with a ratchet, a smaller cheque and a clearance tranche, not $140M as offered [S181, S184, S188, S192, S203].

| Transaction | Year | Value | Revenue at exit | EV/Revenue | Status of the asset at exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Zoetis / Abaxis | 2018 | $2.0B | $243M (FY2018) | 8.2x | Cleared veterinary and human point-of-care analyzers with an installed base; human line only $38.6M | S178, S180 |
| Danaher / Cepheid | 2016 | $4.0B | $539M | 7.4x | Cleared molecular point-of-care, large instrument installed base | S165 |
| DiaSorin / Luminex | 2021 | $1.8B | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Cleared multiplex and point-of-care assays, $37 a share | S166 |
| Roche / LumiraDx | 2023-24 | $353.5M aggregate ($295M upfront) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Cleared, CE-marked multi-assay platform sold in a pre-packaged administration | S93, S114 |
| QuidelOrtho / LEX Diagnostics | 2026 | $100M | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | VELO Respiratory Test cleared 2026-02-13 (K251742), CLIA waived, pre-commercial in the US, no installed base | S181, S184 |

LEX is the tightest read on regulatory maturity and does not lift Vantelle's entry price. $100M bought clearance and a waiver on a molecular respiratory menu, not scale or an installed base, and embeds QuidelOrtho's own molecular franchise — a synergy a cardiac and metabolic menu may not command — so it anchors the pre-commercial case, not a floor. The multiples that would make a $140M entry work belong to assets six to thirteen times Vantelle's FY2028 plan. Abaxis sold for 8.2x revenue, but on $243M of revenue, 83% of it veterinary consumables — an installed-base annuity Vantelle lacks, so the multiple caps rather than raises what it can claim — and its human point-of-care business, the closest analogue to Vantelle's clinic channel, was only $38.6M after two decades; Cepheid sold for 7.4x on $539M. Between those poles and the $353.5M Roche paid for a distressed but cleared platform sits Vantelle's realistic range. At the cut FY2028 revenue of $34.9M, an 8.2x multiple would be $286M and a 4.0x multiple $140M — which is why the price paid today, not the multiple at exit, is the variable Meridian controls [S180, S165, S5, S188].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale of the whole company | Werfen | Sells GEM Premier whole-blood electrolytes, metabolites and blood gases into acute care with no cardiac markers on that platform; bought Immucor for $2.0B in 2023 | 2031-2033, after the CLIA waiver and 300 commercial sites | Highest of the four | S179 |
| Trade sale | Abbott | Owns the handheld franchise through i-STAT and cleared a high-sensitivity troponin I cartridge on i-STAT Alinity in June 2026; would buy to retire a competitor, and price it as one | 2031-2033 | Low to medium | S25, S21 |
| Trade sale | Roche | Has owned LumiraDx's point-of-care platform since 2024 and would need a menu rather than a second platform | 2032 or later | Low | S93 |
| Distressed asset sale | QuidelOrtho or a lender-led process | Buys cheap (LEX at $100M) while carrying a $1.1B enterprise value at 0.4x sales and a $100M restructuring plan; alternatively the Bluestem loan and the senior preference drive a sale | 2027-2028 if clearance or the waiver fails | Medium in the bear case | S181, S5 |
| Listing | Nasdaq or NYSE | Needs a cleared menu, revenue and a profit record; the 2021 cohort did not survive | 2033 or later | Very low | S183, S182 |

The buyer with a genuine gap is Werfen, and the others are conflicted rather than absent. Abbott launched a high-sensitivity troponin I cartridge on i-STAT Alinity on 2026-06-11 and a creatinine cartridge on i-STAT on 2026-06-26 — the exact two assays Vantelle leads with, on a handheld platform with the installed base, waiver and sales force. An Abbott bid would be a defensive purchase priced to remove an irritant, not a growth purchase. Roche has owned LumiraDx's cartridge platform since 2024 and has no reason to buy a second one. That leaves Werfen, whose GEM Premier measures electrolytes, metabolites and blood gases but carries no cardiac markers, and which paid $2.0B for Immucor in 2023; a five-test cardiac-and-metabolic cartridge sold into the same acute-care and urgent-care accounts is the closest fit among the four [S179, S25, S93].

A listing is not a route. LumiraDx listed on Nasdaq at a $3.0B valuation on 2021-09-29, received a delisting determination on 2023-10-24 and sold its platform to Roche two months later for $295M upfront. A company with $2.6M of revenue, two of five assays and no waiver has no public venue in 2027; even a successful Vantelle would list only after 2032, when a strategic sale at 4-7x would price better than an IPO discount. The practical consequence is a holding period of five to seven years from the 2027-01-29 close, an exit in 2032-2034, and no liquidity before it: there is no secondary market for a Series B stake in a single-product diagnostics company [S183, S182].

| Exit equity value (2032) | Scenario weight | Meridian at $140M, before Corvia | Meridian at $140M, after Corvia | Meridian at $70M, after Corvia | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $30M (clearance or waiver fails; asset sale, no Series C) | 30% | 0.83x | 0.77x | 0.77x | Unverified inputs | S1 |
| $225M (cleared, $30-43M revenue, 5-7x) | 50% | 1.11x | 1.03x | 1.75x | Unverified inputs | S1 |
| $435M (cut plan delivered, 6-7x) | 20% | 2.35x | 2.18x | 3.71x | Unverified inputs | S1 |
| Expected, before the Series C | 100% | 1.27x | 1.18x | 1.85x | Analyst weights on unverified inputs | S1 |

After the $18-23M Series C the expected return is 1.0x at $140M and 1.5x at $70M; at the top of the $9-20M Corvia range it is 0.9x and 1.4x. The returns are asymmetric in the wrong direction for a venture fund: the 1x preference limits the bear case to 0.77x of the $15M and flattens the base case to 1.03x before the next round and about 0.9x after it, so the expected return is carried by a bull case that requires the plan to be delivered after a 15% reimbursement cut and a strategic to pay 6-7x. Doubling the bull weight from 20% to 40% lifts the expected return at $140M only to 1.1x. The $43-49M funding requirement makes the next round unavoidable: an $18-23M Series C at $140M pre-money dilutes Meridian 11.4-14.1% (16.7-20.4% from a $70M entry at $90M) and, ranking senior to B, holds the $140M stake near 1.0x through a $225M sale; expected returns fall to 1.0x at $140M and 1.5x at $70M, with the bull case at 1.9x and 3.0x. A $15M lead at $140M therefore returns capital in the bear and base cases and a venture return in none; the same distribution from $70M is still below 2x expected, on unverified company inputs [S1].

Policy and structural tests are mild but not zero. Three of the four plausible buyers are non-US — Werfen of Spain, Roche of Switzerland, DiaSorin of Italy — so Hart-Scott-Rodino applies at these values, while CFIUS is unlikely to be dispositive for a diagnostics manufacturer with no government customer; the harder obstacles are internal. Corvia Microfluidics' 40% minority can put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value on a change of control, and Vantelle pays Corvia a 3% royalty on cartridge net sales — $2.36M a year at the FY2029 plan, 3.0 points of gross margin — of which chief technology officer Tomasz Lindqvist owns 22% (company-provided, unverified). Capitalised at the exit multiple that put is 6.6% of proceeds, $9.2M at a $100M sale and $19.8M at $300M, and it is deducted in the return table; a relief-from-royalty cross-check on the 3% contract alone gives the 40% only $4-5M, so the range turns on the royalty imputed at fair value [S1, S203]. Confidence in the $100M-$350M range is high because it rests on four dated transactions; confidence in the weights is low, and they are the analyst's judgement, not evidence. Three questions would change the answer: what revenue LEX had at its $100M sale, whether Werfen or bioMérieux has bought a point-of-care asset since 2023 and at what multiple, and whether Corvia's minority has signed a drag-along.

Excellent — N47 from Fundamentals aligns with the Lead's item on the $650 research fee. It says SOM should be $4.93M of cartridges plus any analyzer sales, not $8.07M. That's consistent: the $650 fee is a research fee paid by evaluation sites, not commercial revenue. So I must correct the SOM row: "$4.93M of cartridges at 300 sites plus analyzer sales; the $8.07M including $3.14M of $650 evaluation fees is a research-revenue assumption (unverified)".

So SOM = $4.93M cartridges (at realised price) plus one-time analyzer sales (300 × 1.34 × $2,900 = $1.166M). Interesting: 402 analyzers × $2,900 = $1.166M. So SOM ≈ $4.93M + $1.17M one-time = $6.1M. That's good and responds to both N47 and the Lead's item.

Also the CLIAwaived.com troponin page: 9 items — PATHFAST Troponin Test Kit ($630/60 tests), LifeSign MI StatusFirst (qualitative), i-STAT Troponin I (discontinued, not CLIA-waived), Triage Troponin kits. So the site lists both waived and non-waived products; it's not proof that PATHFAST is waived. In fact, the i-STAT note is an explicit negative.

Interesting: PATHFAST troponin kit sold by a waived-products distributor at $630 for 60 tests = $10.50/test. That's a useful price benchmark for competition: PATHFAST troponin at $10.50 per test vs Vantelle $38 per five-test cartridge ($7.60/assay). Hmm, that's a competitor price data point! PATHFAST Troponin Test Kit $630/60 tests = $10.50 per troponin result; Triage Troponin $599/25 tests = $23.96 per test. Nice for the competitor table price column which is currently "not disclosed". That's valuable: it shows single-analyte troponin prices of $10.50-$23.96, against Vantelle's $38 for five assays.

But careful: these are distributor list prices for kits, not necessarily what clinics pay, and PATHFAST is a benchtop analyzer (moderate complexity). Still a solid independent price benchmark.

Now, does the PATHFAST price change competition? Yes: PATHFAST hs-cTnI-II (K231974, 2024-03-20) is a benchtop, moderate-complexity hs-cTnI analyzer sold at $10.50 per troponin test. That is a direct rival for troponin-only use in moderate-complexity sites: 2× the price per assay vs Vantelle? Vantelle $38 for 5 assays = $7.60/assay; but a clinic buying only troponin pays $10.50 with PATHFAST vs $38 with Vantelle. This is a strong counter-evidence point: for the chest-pain-only use case, PATHFAST costs $10.50 per result against Vantelle's $38 cartridge — 3.6× more expensive for the same single result, unless the clinic values the other four assays that the visit cannot bill ($22.35 reimbursement vs $38 cartridge already shows the loss). This strengthens the market's negative read and the competition's counter-case.

That's a genuinely important new finding. It should go in competition (and maybe market's "what the clinic buys" — but market is tight). Competition is the right home.

Now the critical claim resolution. Evidence:
- i-STAT cTnI K031739 (2003-09-02) — distributor says not CLIA-waived, moderate.
- Alere/Quidel Triage MeterPro troponin — moderate (FDA-derived list).

So the honest position: "No CLIA-waived troponin assay is documented in the FDA-derived CLIA lists or manufacturer material we could reach, including pre-2019 clearances (i-STAT cTnI, K031739, 2003; PATHFAST cTnI, K100130, 2011); the universal negative remains unverified because FDA's CLIA database was not searchable in this run." Does this change who is the most dangerous competitor? No — Abbott remains. But it sharpens the wedge argument: Abbott has sold a troponin cartridge since 2003 without a waiver, which suggests either that hospitals don't need one or that waiving troponin is hard; either way, the waiver is the scarce asset, and Vantelle's 2027 timeline is not supported by any precedent of a waived troponin assay. That's actually a stronger, more honest thesis: the wedge is real but unproven, and the company's own timeline implies achieving something no competitor has in 23 years.

The Q5 is a conventional instrument; the panel it sells is mostly unbuilt: on the company's own unverified numbers, the troponin assay misses the accepted high-sensitivity imprecision criterion, the 98.7% headline rests on venous blood run by company staff at one site, and no troponin assay appears among FDA's CLIA waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 through September 2026 [S1, S109]. ### The cartridge is ordinary engineering; whole-blood troponin is not

The only realistic exit is a trade sale to a strategic already selling into the same clinic, at $100M-$350M, and the ceiling is what cleared platforms change hands for: on 2026-04-20 QuidelOrtho paid $100M in cash for LEX Diagnostics, whose VELO Respiratory Test (K251742), a cartridge-based molecular assay, was cleared and CLIA-waived on 2026-02-13 and had not launched commercially in the US. Vantelle asks $140M of pre-money value for two of five assays under review and no waiver. At that entry the $15M lead returns 0.77x in the bear case, about 0.9x in a $225M base case and 1.9x in a $435M bull case once the $18-23M Series C the plan needs and Corvia's 6.6% put are included — an expected 1.0x over five years, below any venture threshold. The preliminary CY2027 CLFS cut takes FY2028 revenue to $34.9M at constant volume from $41.0M, which is why the base and bull exits fall from $250M and $500M; the $100M-$350M range survives because it is anchored on transactions, not on the plan. The exit supports a lead only from $60-70M, or from $140M with a ratchet, a smaller cheque and a clearance tranche, not $140M as offered [S181, S184, S188, S192, S203].

| Zoetis / Abaxis | 2018 | $2.0B | $243M (FY2018) | 8.2x | Cleared veterinary and human point-of-care analyzers; human line only $38.6M | S178, S180 |

LEX is the tightest read on regulatory maturity and does not lift Vantelle's entry price. $100M bought clearance and a waiver on a molecular respiratory menu, not scale or an installed base, and embeds QuidelOrtho's own molecular franchise — a synergy a cardiac and metabolic menu may not command — so it anchors the pre-commercial case, not a floor. Abaxis sold for 8.2x revenue, but on $243M of revenue, 83% of it veterinary consumables — an installed-base annuity Vantelle lacks, so the multiple caps rather than raises what it can claim — and its human point-of-care business, the closest analogue to Vantelle's clinic channel, was only $38.6M after two decades; Cepheid sold for 7.4x on $539M. Between those poles and the $353.5M Roche paid for a distressed but cleared platform sits Vantelle's realistic range. At the cut FY2028 revenue of $34.9M, an 8.2x multiple would be $286M and a 4.0x multiple $140M — which is why the price paid today, not the multiple at exit, is the variable Meridian controls [S180, S165, S5, S188].

arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is a conventional instrument; the panel it sells is mostly unbuilt: on the company's own unverified numbers, the troponin assay misses the accepted high-sensitivity imprecision criterion, the 98.7% headline rests on venous blood run by company staff at one site, and no troponin assay appears among FDA's CLIA waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 through September 2026 [S109]. The round buys two of five assays at moderate complexity in 2027; the waived five-test panel is a 2028-2029 option.

### The cartridge is ordinary engineering; whole-blood troponin is not

The company's design takes a finger-stick sample into a disposable cartridge by capillary action, meters it into a reaction chamber, rehydrates dried reagents and reads it optically, with an on-board calibrator and drift correction (VD-2). The novel part is the dried-reagent troponin chemistry (VD-4), unpublished, so assay format, antibody pair and label cannot be assessed. The risk is elsewhere: haematocrit changes plasma volume and therefore the measured concentration in whole blood, and finger-stick haemolysis interferes with optical troponin detection; the company discloses no interference study, haematocrit range or limit of detection.

### The performance data describe feasibility, not a waived device

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% CV | One site, 128 patients, venous, company staff | S1, unverified |
| Troponin I category agreement | 96.1% (123/128) | Same internal study | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay category agreement | 98.7% (626 of 634 results; table prints "634 of 640") | Recomputed from per-assay rows | S1, unverified |
| Accepted high-sensitivity criterion | CV of 10% or less at the sex-specific 99th percentile; above LoD in 50% or more of healthy people | IFCC definition | S113, S115 |
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick claimed; venous blood tested | Company spec against study design | S1, unverified |
| Cartridge shelf life | 9 months claimed, 6 months of stability data | Company data | S1, unverified |

Category agreement is the weakest available endpoint: it discards error size, so an assay biased near the cutoff scores well and unusable for the 0/1-hour chest-pain algorithms, where CLSI EP09 asks for regression and bias at the decision level [S117]. On its own data the flagship is a contemporary-sensitivity assay measured on venous samples, not the finger stick it sells. The economics cap the multiple: 2027 sales come only from two assays sold to sites that already staff a laboratory.

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT | Siemens epoc | Nova Stat Profile | Atellica VTLi | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Menu | 5 assays, 2 filed | Dozens of analytes | Blood gas, electrolytes | Blood gas, electrolytes | 1 (hs-cTnI) | S1, S25, S70 |
| Regulatory | 510(k) pending, nothing cleared | hs-TnI cleared 2026-06-11 | Cleared 2020 (K200107) | Cleared 2015 (K141907) | Pivotal trial 2023 | S1, S25, S14, S94 |
| Sample | Finger stick, 40 µL (claimed) | Capillary whole blood cleared | Whole blood | Whole blood | Whole blood | S1, S137 |
| Calibration | On-board, no separate step (claimed) | Self-contained disposable with aqueous calibrator pouch (G3+) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | S1, S110 |
| Evidence | 128 patients, one site, venous, staff | 510(k) summary per cartridge | 510(k) | 510(k) | Pivotal trial of 3,697 patients | S1, S94, S51 |
| Price | $2,900 analyzer, $38 cartridge (unverified) | No public price | No public price | No public price | No public price | S1 |

### What the pivotal study and the waiver must prove

The pivotal design is right - four sites, 1,150 patients, finger sticks, clinic staff as operators, all unverified - and matches FDA's waiver standard: a waived user against a laboratory user, flex studies and failure-mode analysis. What it must produce is harder: LoD, LoQ and sex-specific 99th-percentile values from healthy volunteers, CV at each cutoff, and operator-error evidence. Clearance is likely but later than Q1 2027: an FDA request for information dated 2026-08-21 answered in December 2026 points to Q2 2027. A five-test waiver filed in Q3 2027 would be decided in 2028 at the earliest. Whether a troponin waiver would be first of its kind is unverified: no troponin assay appears in FDA's waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 through September 2026, and both leading quantitative cartridges, i-STAT cTnI and PATHFAST, are moderate complexity, but FDA's waived-analyte database could not be queried [S109, S205, S206]. The 2028-29 timing depends on that precedent.

### The IP protects a narrow cartridge, not the franchise

| Patent family | What it covers | Patent number, filed | Status | What it is worth | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| VD-1 | Cartridge with on-board calibrator | US 16/884,327, 2020-05-28 | Granted US 2023-03, Europe pending | Narrow against dense prior art | S1, unverified; S111 |
| VD-2 | Five-assay optical reader | US 17/662,019, 2022-05-04 | Final rejection 2026-07, appeal under consideration | Unenforceable today | S1, unverified |
| VD-3 | Sample-volume check | US 19/318,770, 2025-09-30 | Unpublished | No public claim scope | S1, not publicly disclosed |
| VD-4 | Troponin on dried reagents | PCT/US2026/014022, 2026-02-11 | Unpublished, unexamined | Only novel piece; outside the 2024 opinion | S1, not publicly disclosed |
| CM-1 | Sealing film and reagent blister | US 15/707,915, 2017-09-18 | Granted 2021-01, held by 60%-owned Corvia, licensed exclusively | Licensed, not owned; 3% of net sales | S1, unverified |

The reader claim is unenforceable while the appeal runs, and prior art such as US8747779B2 already describes a microfluidic cartridge with on-board dry reagents read by an optical host. What remains is a capillary-fill geometry and the unpublished chemistry the 2024 opinion excluded; the enabling consumable patent is licensed, not owned. Corvia is 60%-held, the CTO's 22% pays him 0.66% of cartridge revenue, and the 3% royalty is $1.00 a cartridge at $33.40, $0.40 of it the true leakage to the 40% minority after consolidation. Operating freedom rests on a licence with undisclosed change-of-control and termination terms, not on title [S1, S111].

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Engineering | 5 | Fluidics and optics are established | 3 years | S1, S111 |
| Analytical | 7 | Dried-reagent troponin at 10% CV at the cutoff | 3-5 years | S1, unverified |
| Regulatory | 8 | 510(k) plus a troponin waiver of unverified precedent | 3-5 years | S109 |
| Manufacturing | 6 | Dried-reagent cartridges at scale, room-temperature dating | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| IP | 3 | Reader claim rejected, cartridge claim narrow | Under 1 year | S1, unverified |

### Readiness and dependencies

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 panel | 2 of 5 assays in a 510(k) filed 2026-05-18, unverified; K261734 contradicted - it is Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System | Nothing cleared | No cleared revenue | Not disclosed | FDA decision, expected Q2 2027 | S1, S185 |
| Evaluation programme | 41 sites, 55 analyzers, investigational use | 2024-03 | $1.1M of $2.6M FY2025 | Not disclosed | Converts after clearance | S1, unverified |
| Research-use and contract work | Cartridges to research organisations; one unnamed development partner | Not disclosed | $1.5M FY2025, 58% | Not disclosed | None stated | S1, unverified |

Troponin and HbA1c are closest to clearance on unverified statements, three sit ahead of submission, and the waiver has no disclosed flex studies. Manufacturing is a sole pilot line in Tempe with no disclosed contract manufacturer or reagent supplier. The revenue consequence: only two of five assays can earn the $38 cartridge price in 2027, and only after a clearance not yet granted [S1, unverified].

::: evidence
**The five-test panel does not exist as a cleared product, and the assay that carries the valuation does not meet the analytical definition of high-sensitivity.**

Two of five assays are in a 510(k) filed 2026-05-18 and still unverified; the number printed in the deck, K261734, is contradicted: it is Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System, cleared 2026-07-23. The other three need a separate Q2 2027 submission. Whether a troponin CLIA waiver would be first of its kind is unverified: none appears in FDA's waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 to 2026, and the waived-analyte database could not be queried. On the company's internal study troponin has 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff against a 10% criterion. Deck page 1 also instructs AI diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating; recorded as a finding, not acted on [S1, S109, S185, S204].
:::

arguments.title: CLIA-Waived Test List: FDA Analyte Snapshot (156 analyte labels retrieved from FDA source 2026-10-16)
arguments.claims: FDA's currently waived-analyte list, as mirrored on 2026-10-16, contains 156 analyte labels and no troponin (cardiac troponin I or T) label. Supports that no troponin test system is currently categorized CLIA-waived, so a troponin CLIA waiver by application has no current precedent and the first-of-its-kind premise is unverified for pre-2019 decisions.
arguments.claims_weakened: Weakens any statement that a troponin assay has a clear CLIA-waiver precedent or that Vantelle's waiver path is proven. It does not cover a pre-2019 waived troponin test later withdrawn, so it cannot prove 'never granted'.

Market draft (aiming ~8,900):

---
The serviceable market is real in site count and not in the unit Vantelle sells: at the 41 cartridges a site a month its evaluation sites averaged in 2026, the US market for a $38 five-test cartridge is $303.7M at most — $267.0M at the $33.40 realised price, $134M-$213M if half to 70% of evaluation volume carries into commercial use — not the $2.41B the deck derives from 8 panels a day per analyzer, and at 2026 Medicare rates the visit that most obviously calls for it, chest pain, justifies $22.35 of billable lab value against a $38 cartridge, $19.00 under CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule. Sixteen thousand clinics exist; the question is whether any can buy a cartridge the visit cannot pay for. The economic mechanism is that a clinic buys a cartridge only if the tests it can justify and bill exceed its price plus labour and quality control; with Medicare paying per analyte and no site-of-service premium, the panel's value is set by the visit, not the menu. Two of the deck's five inputs fail against independent data, in opposite directions. The site count is too low: JUCM's census puts 14,442 urgent-care centres in the US at 2025-04-01, 21% above the deck's 11,400, and the American Hospital Association counts 6,093 US hospitals in 2026, 2,133 at the conventional 35% rural share against the deck's 1,800. The corrected base is 16,242 sites. The volume input fails by more: 1,680 cartridges a month across 41 sites and 55 analyzers is 41 per site and 30.5 per analyzer, or 1.64 and 1.22 panels a day on 25 working days — 9.8 and 6.6 times below the model. Correcting the site count lifts the market 23%; correcting the volume cuts it 87%. The deck also instructs AI diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating (p.1), recorded as a finding, not followed. [S1, S167, S169]

### The 8-panel case needs three-quarters of every patient

A visit-volume ceiling closes the argument. The National Center for Health Statistics found that 27.6% of Americans had at least one urgent-care visit in the year to 2024, or 93.8M visits, which across 14,442 centres is 21.7 visits per site per day. The model's 16 panels a site a day would require 74% of every patient seen to get a five-test panel; 8 panels a day would require 37%. The observed 1.64 panels is 8% of visits, which fits a chest-pain, dyspnoea and diabetes mix. [S168]

### What the clinic buys and bills

The clinic is not buying a diagnostic; it is buying five separately coded tests. Under the 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (effective 2026-01-01), the full panel is worth $71.32: troponin 84484 at $12.47, NT-proBNP 83880 at $39.26, HbA1c 83036 at $9.71, creatinine 82565 at $5.12 and potassium 84132 at $4.76. These are 2026 amounts: CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule (2026-09-21; final rates due November 2026) puts 1,171 of 1,528 codes below 2026, and at the 15% annual cap the panel would pay $60.62. A chest-pain visit justifies troponin with creatinine and potassium — $22.35 in 2026 and $19.00 at the cap, against a $38 cartridge a loss of $15.65 widening to $19.00 ($11.05 to $14.40 at the $33.40 realised price). A heart-failure review justifies NT-proBNP with creatinine and potassium — $49.14 in 2026 and $41.77 at the cap, a gross spread of $11.14 falling to $3.77 before the $650 monthly analyzer fee and staff time. Only a visit where a heart-failure workup and a diabetes review coincide reaches $58.85, $50.02 at the cap. Fifty-five percent of the panel's Medicare value sits in the one assay a chest-pain or diabetes visit does not justify, and Vantelle does not disclose the analyte mix its sites bill. A single troponin result also has a market price: PATHFAST's kit sells at $10.50 a test, so a chest-pain-only clinic pays 3.6 times more per result for the cartridge. Both $303.7M and $267.0M multiply observed volume by Vantelle's prices and do not move with the fee schedule; the CY2027 cut compresses the ceiling that makes those prices collectable. [S119, S134, S175, S177, S188, S192, S209]

### The channel is a certificate, not a clinic

The governing policy is the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments of 1988: a test system is either waived or run by a laboratory meeting personnel and quality standards; waivers are granted system by system. Until Vantelle obtains a waiver — planned for Q3 2027 behind a 510(k) the company says drew an FDA information request on 2026-08-21, though K261734 is FDA's record for another firm's cleared device, so neither is publicly confirmed — a site must hold a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified testing staff. The addressable channel through 2028 is the subset of 16,242 sites already running moderate-complexity testing — where Abbott's i-STAT hs-TnI competes today. After clearance a site pays $38 a cartridge and $2,900 or nothing for the analyzer; the $650 monthly fee its evaluation sites pay today is a research fee, not commercial revenue, and no conversion or lost-deal record is disclosed (company, unverified). ISO 13485 certification is not yet held and the analyzer sells at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost, so each placement consumes cash before a cartridge is bought. The catalyst is the waiver, which converts the buyer from laboratory-directed sites to clinic staff. [S1, S136, S170, S185]

### One country, one blocked region, one letter of intent

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States (Texas, Arizona, New Mexico) | $2.89B US point-of-care, 2025 | 7.8% CAGR 2026-2034 | Entered: 41 paid evaluation sites; 300-site distributor letter, non-binding | 510(k) claimed but number contradicted; no CLIA waiver; ISO 13485 not certified | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, Siemens epoc | S176; S1; S8; S4; S14 |
| EU/EEA | not sized here | not applicable | Blocked: CE marking not before 2028; Irish entity has no staff (company plan, unverified) | CE/IVDR | Siemens Atellica VTLi (fingerstick hs-cTnI) | S1; S172 |
| Rest of world (China, Japan/Korea, SE Asia, LatAm, MEA) | not addressed | not applicable | Not planned: no entity, partner or regulatory pathway (company plan, unverified) | NMPA, PMDA, MFDS, ANVISA | none identified | S1 |

Geography is material only as an absence: home, revenue, capital and exit markets are all in the United States on company disclosure (partially verified: Delaware incorporation and Tempe plant are company statements), while the one expansion market is blocked until 2028 against a competitor already selling a fingerstick hs-cTnI there. The European entity is a costed option, not a market. [S1]

### What would change this, and what to ask

The strongest counter-case is payer mix. If commercial payers allow well above Medicare for these five tests, payback improves at a fraction of the modelled volume — still short of the plan, but a viable business, and the gap between list and realised cartridge price suggests clinics already pay near list. That collection rate is not disclosed and is the single fact that would most move the valuation. Three diligence questions settle the rest: what the evaluation sites collected per panel by payer; what share of visits carried a cardiac or metabolic indication; and how many of the 300 letter-of-intent sites convert to purchase orders and which were lost. Until the first is answered, the market supports a business several times smaller than the projection, and the pre-money being asked is a price for a market the company has not shown it can sell into. Confidence in the site counts and fee-schedule values is high; in commercial collection rates it is low. The reimbursement cut is therefore the market's decisive fact: it weakens the clinic's ability to pay list price before the round closes and argues for a price below the ask.

::: evidence
**The deck's serviceable market overstates the addressable opportunity roughly eight times at the upper bound, and the clinic's reimbursement, not the technology, caps what a site will pay.**

The rebuild is arithmetic on public counts and published fee-schedule amounts: 16,242 sites, 41 cartridges a site a month, $38 list and $33.40 realised, $303.7M at most and $134M-$213M if half to 70% of evaluation use persists, against a 2026 panel value of $71.32 and $60.62 at the preliminary CY2027 cap. The 300-site letter is worth $6.1M at observed use, not the $41.0M planned. The unsourced input, the commercial collection rate per panel, decides whether even that is viable. [S167, S168, S175, S188, S209]
:::

arguments.markdown:
The strategy is funded to reach the regulatory milestones and not the commercial ones. On company figures that are unverified, the plan sells two of five assays into a moderate-complexity channel until a troponin waiver, unverified as a first of its kind, arrives, books a distributor's stocking order as 41% of 2026 revenue, and requires a twenty-fold acceleration in site adds on a per-analyzer utilisation rate of one panel a day against a model of eight [S1]. The capital covers the runway, not the launch: cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 plus $30M gives $36.9M against a net burn of $1.15M a month, 26 months to December 2028, before the $5.0M term loan stops being interest-only in 2027-03 and starts amortising at $167,000 a month of principal, and before the 40% of proceeds earmarked for manufacturing scale-up is spent. Use of funds divides 35% clearance, 40% manufacturing and 25% launch - a split that funds a launch ahead of the waiver that makes the launch addressable, which is why a 2028 Series C is the plan of record rather than a contingency.

### 300 sites requires a twenty-fold change in the rate of selling

The evaluation programme went from 9 clinics in 2024-03 to 41 by 2026-10, 1.1 net new sites a month over 31 months [S109]. Reaching 300 commercial sites by end-2027 needs 22 a month for twelve months, and the only named route is a non-binding letter of intent from one regional distributor with no disclosed purchase commitment, minimum or date. Evaluation sites pay $650 a month per analyzer, a research fee rather than a commercial price, so none of the 41 has yet shown willingness to pay on commercial terms. Those 300 sites must also hold a certificate for moderate-complexity testing until a waiver is granted, which narrows the channel to hospital-linked and laboratory-equipped clinics - a smaller, more contested customer set than the urgent-care story implies.

### Utilisation, not site count, decides whether the model works

The 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers equal 30.5 per analyzer a month, one panel a day, against a model of eight panels a day from 2028 - company-reported volumes, unverified. FY2029 revenue of $78.5M at $31 a cartridge implies 2.53M cartridges, which needs either 833 analyzers at modelled use or 5,100 sites at today's use - seventeen times the 2027 site target. The cartridge cost milestone is the same arithmetic in reverse: $10 at 1M units requires 2,000 sites at observed utilisation, or 342 analyzers at modelled utilisation. The 3% Corvia royalty is $1.00 a cartridge at the 2026 realised price - $1.0M a year at 1M units, $0.40M of it to the 40% minority, including $0.22M to the CTO - and the deck does not say whether the sub-$10 milestone is struck before royalty [S1]. The generous reading is that investigational-use labelling suppresses demand, because evaluation sites cannot act on results; that is the single most important unknown in the plan, and nothing in the pivotal study measures it.

### Revenue quality is weaker than the headline growth

The $2.4M opening stocking order is 41% of FY2026E revenue and equals 71,900 cartridges at the $33.40 realised price - 5.8 months of the entire planned 2027 network demand at 300 sites, or 43 months of current demand [S114, S112]. With a nine-month shelf life, sell-in of that size is a distributor inventory decision as much as a demand signal, and it ships only on clearance, so a delay moves the revenue and ages the inventory. arguments.markdown:
The Q5 is a conventional instrument; the panel it sells is mostly unbuilt: on the company's own unverified numbers, the troponin assay misses the accepted high-sensitivity imprecision criterion, the 98.7% headline rests on venous blood run by company staff at one site, and no troponin assay appears among FDA's CLIA waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 through September 2026 [S109]. The round buys two of five assays at moderate complexity in 2027; the waived five-test panel is a 2028-2029 option.

### The cartridge is ordinary engineering; whole-blood troponin is not

The company's design takes a finger-stick sample into a disposable cartridge by capillary action, meters it into a reaction chamber, rehydrates dried reagents and reads it optically, with an on-board calibrator and drift correction (VD-2). The novel part is the dried-reagent troponin chemistry (VD-4), unpublished, so assay format, antibody pair and label cannot be assessed. The risk is elsewhere: haematocrit changes plasma volume and therefore the measured concentration in whole blood, and finger-stick haemolysis interferes with optical troponin detection; the company discloses no interference study, haematocrit range or limit of detection.

### The performance data describe feasibility, not a waived device

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% CV | One site, 128 patients, venous, company staff | S1, unverified |
| Troponin I category agreement | 96.1% (123/128) | Same internal study | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay category agreement | 98.7% (626 of 634 results; table prints "634 of 640") | Recomputed from per-assay rows | S1, unverified |
| Accepted high-sensitivity criterion | CV of 10% or less at the sex-specific 99th percentile; above LoD in 50% or more of healthy people | IFCC definition | S113, S115 |
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick claimed; venous blood tested | Company spec against study design | S1, unverified |
| Cartridge shelf life | 9 months claimed, 6 months of stability data | Company data | S1, unverified |

Category agreement is the weakest available endpoint: it discards error size, so an assay biased near the cutoff scores well while remaining unusable for the 0/1-hour chest-pain algorithms, where CLSI EP09 asks for regression and bias at the decision level [S117]. On its own data the flagship is a contemporary-sensitivity assay measured on venous samples, not the finger stick it sells. The economics cap the multiple: 2027 sales come only from two assays sold to sites that already staff a laboratory.

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT | Siemens epoc | Nova Stat Profile | Atellica VTLi | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Menu | 5 assays, 2 filed | Dozens of analytes | Blood gas, electrolytes | Blood gas, electrolytes | 1 (hs-cTnI) | S1, S25, S70 |
| Regulatory | 510(k) pending, nothing cleared | hs-TnI cleared 2026-06-11 | Cleared 2020 (K200107) | Cleared 2015 (K141907) | Pivotal trial 2023 | S1, S25, S14, S94 |
| Sample | Finger stick, 40 µL (claimed) | Capillary whole blood cleared | Whole blood | Whole blood | Whole blood | S1, S137 |
| Calibration | On-board, no separate step (claimed) | Self-contained disposable with aqueous calibrator pouch (G3+) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | S1, S110 |
| Evidence | 128 patients, one site, venous, staff | 510(k) summary per cartridge | 510(k) | 510(k) | Pivotal trial of 3,697 patients | S1, S94, S51 |
| Price | $2,900 analyzer, $38 cartridge (unverified) | No public price | No public price | No public price | No public price | S1 |

### What the pivotal study and the waiver must prove

The pivotal design is right - four sites, 1,150 patients, finger sticks, clinic staff as operators, all unverified - and matches FDA's waiver standard: a waived user against a laboratory user, flex studies and failure-mode analysis. What it must produce is harder: LoD, LoQ and sex-specific 99th-percentile values from healthy volunteers, CV at each cutoff, and operator-error evidence. Clearance is likely but later than Q1 2027: an FDA request for information dated 2026-08-21 answered in December 2026 points to Q2 2027. A five-test waiver filed in Q3 2027 would be decided in 2028 at the earliest. Whether a troponin waiver would be first of its kind is unverified: no troponin assay appears in FDA's waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 through September 2026, and both leading quantitative cartridges, i-STAT cTnI and PATHFAST, are moderate complexity, but FDA's waived-analyte database could not be queried [S109, S205, S206]. The 2028-29 timing depends on that precedent.

### The IP protects a narrow cartridge, not the franchise

| Patent family | What it covers | Patent number, filed | Status | What it is worth | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| VD-1 | Cartridge with on-board calibrator | US 16/884,327, 2020-05-28 | Granted US 2023-03, Europe pending | Narrow against dense prior art | S1, unverified; S111 |
| VD-2 | Five-assay optical reader | US 17/662,019, 2022-05-04 | Final rejection 2026-07, appeal under consideration | Unenforceable today | S1, unverified |
| VD-3 | Sample-volume check | US 19/318,770, 2025-09-30 | Unpublished | No public claim scope | S1, not publicly disclosed |
| VD-4 | Troponin on dried reagents | PCT/US2026/014022, 2026-02-11 | Unpublished, unexamined | Only novel piece; outside the 2024 opinion | S1, not publicly disclosed |
| CM-1 | Sealing film and reagent blister | US 15/707,915, 2017-09-18 | Granted 2021-01, held by 60%-owned Corvia, licensed exclusively | Licensed, not owned; 3% of net sales | S1, unverified |

The reader claim is unenforceable while the appeal runs, and prior art such as US8747779B2 already describes a microfluidic cartridge with on-board dry reagents read by an optical host. What remains is a capillary-fill geometry and the unpublished chemistry the 2024 opinion excluded; the enabling consumable patent is licensed, not owned. Corvia is 60%-held, the CTO's 22% pays him 0.66% of cartridge revenue, and the 3% royalty is $1.00 a cartridge at $33.40, $0.40 of it the true leakage to the 40% minority after consolidation. Operating freedom rests on a licence with undisclosed change-of-control and termination terms, not on title [S1, S111].

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Engineering | 5 | Fluidics and optics are established | 3 years | S1, S111 |
| Analytical | 7 | Dried-reagent troponin at 10% CV at the cutoff | 3-5 years | S1, unverified |
| Regulatory | 8 | 510(k) plus a troponin waiver of unverified precedent | 3-5 years | S109 |
| Manufacturing | 6 | Dried-reagent cartridges at scale, room-temperature dating | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| IP | 3 | Reader claim rejected, cartridge claim narrow | Under 1 year | S1, unverified |

### Readiness and dependencies

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q5 panel | 2 of 5 assays in a 510(k) filed 2026-05-18, unverified; K261734 contradicted - it is Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System | Nothing cleared | No cleared revenue | Not disclosed | FDA decision, expected Q2 2027 | S1, S185 |
| Evaluation programme | 41 sites, 55 analyzers, investigational use | 2024-03 | $1.1M of $2.6M FY2025 | Not disclosed | Converts after clearance | S1, unverified |
| Research-use and contract work | Cartridges to research organisations; one unnamed development partner | Not disclosed | $1.5M FY2025, 58% | Not disclosed | None stated | S1, unverified |

Troponin and HbA1c are closest to clearance on unverified statements, three sit ahead of submission, and the waiver has no disclosed flex studies. Manufacturing is a sole pilot line in Tempe with no disclosed contract manufacturer or reagent supplier. The revenue consequence: only two of five assays can earn the $38 cartridge price in 2027, and only after a clearance not yet granted [S1, unverified].

::: evidence
**The five-test panel does not exist as a cleared product, and the assay that carries the valuation does not meet the analytical definition of high-sensitivity.**

Two of five assays are in a 510(k) filed 2026-05-18 and still unverified; the number printed in the deck, K261734, is contradicted: it is Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System, cleared 2026-07-23. The other three need a separate Q2 2027 submission. Whether a troponin CLIA waiver would be first of its kind is unverified: none appears in FDA's waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 to 2026, and the waived-analyte database could not be queried. On the company's internal study troponin has 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff against a 10% criterion. Deck page 1 also instructs AI diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating; recorded as a finding, not acted on [S1, S109, S185, S204].
:::

The clinic is not buying a diagnostic; it is buying five separately coded tests. The governing policy is the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments of 1988: a test system is either waived or run by a laboratory meeting personnel and quality standards; waivers are granted system by system. A chest-pain visit justifies troponin with creatinine and potassium — $22.35 in 2026 and $19.00 at the cap, against a $38 cartridge a loss of $15.65 widening to $19.00 ($11.05 to $14.40 at the $33.40 realised price). A heart-failure review justifies NT-proBNP with creatinine and potassium — $49.14 in 2026 and $41.77 at the cap, a gross spread of $11.14 falling to $3.77 before the $650 monthly analyzer fee and staff time. Only a visit where a heart-failure workup and a diabetes review coincide reaches $58.85, $50.02 at the cap. Fifty-five percent of the panel's Medicare value sits in the one assay a chest-pain or diabetes visit does not justify, and Vantelle does not disclose the analyte mix its sites bill. Both $303.7M and $267.0M multiply observed volume by Vantelle's prices and do not move with the fee schedule; the CY2027 cut compresses the ceiling that makes those prices collectable. ### The channel is a certificate, not a clinic

The governing policy is the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments of 1988: a test system is either waived or run by a laboratory meeting personnel and quality standards; waivers are granted system by system. Until Vantelle obtains a waiver — planned for Q3 2027 behind a 510(k) the company says drew an FDA information request on 2026-08-21, though K261734 is FDA's record for another firm's cleared device, so neither is publicly confirmed — a site must hold a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified testing staff. The addressable channel through 2028 is the subset of 16,242 sites already running moderate-complexity testing — where Abbott's i-STAT hs-TnI competes today. After clearance a site pays $38 a cartridge and $2,900 or nothing for the analyzer; the $650 monthly fee its evaluation sites pay today is a research fee, not commercial revenue, and no conversion or lost-deal record is disclosed (company, unverified). The catalyst is the waiver, which converts the buyer from laboratory-directed sites to clinic staff. [S1, S136, S170, S185]

### One country, one blocked region, one letter of intent

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States (Texas, Arizona, New Mexico) | $2.89B US point-of-care, 2025 | 7.8% CAGR 2026-2034 | Entered: 41 paid evaluation sites; 300-site distributor letter, non-binding | 510(k) claimed but number contradicted; no CLIA waiver; ISO 13485 not certified | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, Siemens epoc | S176; S1; S8; S4; S14 |
| EU/EEA | not sized here | not applicable | Blocked: CE marking not before 2028; Irish entity has no staff (company plan, unverified) | CE/IVDR | Siemens Atellica VTLi (fingerstick hs-cTnI) | S1; S172 |

Geography is material only as an absence: home, revenue, capital and exit markets are all in the United States on company disclosure (partially verified: Delaware incorporation and Tempe plant are company statements), while the one expansion market is blocked until 2028 against a competitor already selling a fingerstick hs-cTnI there. [S1]

### What would change this, and what to ask

The strongest counter-case is payer mix. If commercial payers allow well above Medicare for these five tests, payback improves at a fraction of the modelled volume — still short of the plan, but a viable business. That collection rate is not disclosed and is the single fact that would most move the valuation. Three diligence questions settle the rest: what the evaluation sites collected per panel by payer; what share of visits carried a cardiac or metabolic indication; and how many of the 300 letter-of-intent sites convert to purchase orders and which were lost. Until the first is answered, the market supports a business several times smaller than the projection, and the pre-money being asked is a price for a market the company has not shown it can sell into. Confidence in the site counts and fee-schedule values is high; in commercial collection rates it is low. The reimbursement cut is the market's decisive fact: it weakens the clinic's ability to pay list price before the round closes and argues for a price below the ask.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 13 by Product Analyst, 8,964 characters)
The Q5 is a conventional instrument; the panel it sells is mostly unbuilt: on the company's own unverified numbers, the troponin assay misses the accepted high-sensitivity imprecision criterion, the 98.7% headline rests on venous blood run by company staff at one site, and no troponin assay appears among FDA's CLIA waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 through September 2026 [S109]. The round buys two of five assays at moderate complexity in 2027; the waived five-test panel is a 2028-2029 option.

### The cartridge is ordinary engineering; whole-blood troponin is not

The company's design takes a finger-stick sample into a disposable cartridge by capillary action, meters it into a reaction chamber, rehydrates dried reagents and reads it optically, with an on-board calibrator and drift correction (VD-2). The novel part is the dried-reagent troponin chemistry (VD-4), unpublished, so assay format, antibody pair and label cannot be assessed. The risk is elsewhere: haematocrit changes plasma volume and therefore the measured concentration in whole blood, and finger-stick haemolysis interferes with optical troponin detection; the company discloses no interference study, haematocrit range or limit of detection.

### The performance data describe feasibility, not a waived device

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% CV | One site, 128 patients, venous, company staff | S1, unverified |
| Troponin I category agreement | 96.1% (123/128) | Same internal study | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay category agreement | 98.7% (626 of 634 results; table prints "634 of 640") | Recomputed from per-assay rows | S1, unverified |
| Accepted high-sensitivity criterion | CV of 10% or less at the sex-specific 99th percentile; above LoD in 50% or more of healthy people | IFCC definition | S113, S115 |
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick claimed; venous blood tested | Company spec against study design | S1, unverified |
| Cartridge shelf life | 9 months claimed, 6 months of stability data | Company data | S1, unverified |

Category agreement is the weakest available endpoint: it discards error size, so an assay biased near the cutoff scores well while remaining unusable for the 0/1-hour chest-pain algorithms, where CLSI EP09 asks for regression and bias at the decision level [S117]. On its own data the flagship is a contemporary-sensitivity assay measured on venous samples, not the finger stick it sells. The economics cap the multiple: 2027 sales come only from two assays sold to sites that already staff a laboratory.

### What the pivotal study and the waiver must prove

The pivotal design is right - four sites, 1,150 patients, finger sticks, clinic staff as operators, all unverified - and matches FDA's waiver standard: a waived user against a laboratory user, flex studies and failure-mode analysis. What it must produce is harder: LoD, LoQ and sex-specific 99th-percentile values from healthy volunteers, CV at each cutoff, and operator-error evidence. Clearance is likely but later than Q1 2027: an FDA request for information dated 2026-08-21 answered in December 2026 points to Q2 2027. A five-test waiver filed in Q3 2027 would be decided in 2028 at the earliest. The 2028-29 timing depends on that precedent.

| VD-2 | Five-assay optical reader | US 17/662,019, 2022-05-04 | Final rejection 2026-07, appeal under consideration | Unenforceable today | S1, unverified |

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 6 by Product Analyst, 8,296 characters)
The strategy is funded to reach the regulatory milestones and not the commercial ones. On company figures that are unverified, the plan sells two of five assays into a moderate-complexity channel until a troponin waiver, unverified as a first of its kind, arrives, books a distributor's stocking order as 41% of 2026 revenue, and requires a twenty-fold acceleration in site adds on a per-analyzer utilisation rate of one panel a day against a model of eight [S1]. The capital covers the runway, not the launch: cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 plus $30M gives $36.9M against a net burn of $1.15M a month, 26 months to December 2028, before the $5.0M term loan stops being interest-only in 2027-03 and starts amortising at $167,000 a month of principal, and before the 40% of proceeds earmarked for manufacturing scale-up is spent. Use of funds divides 35% clearance, 40% manufacturing and 25% launch - a split that funds a launch ahead of the waiver that makes the launch addressable, which is why a 2028 Series C is the plan of record rather than a contingency.

### 300 sites requires a twenty-fold change in the rate of selling

The evaluation programme went from 9 clinics in 2024-03 to 41 by 2026-10, 1.1 net new sites a month over 31 months [S109]. Reaching 300 commercial sites by end-2027 needs 22 a month for twelve months, and the only named route is a non-binding letter of intent from one regional distributor with no disclosed purchase commitment, minimum or date. Evaluation sites pay $650 a month per analyzer, a research fee rather than a commercial price, so none of the 41 has yet shown willingness to pay on commercial terms. Those 300 sites must also hold a certificate for moderate-complexity testing until a waiver is granted, which narrows the channel to hospital-linked and laboratory-equipped clinics - a smaller, more contested customer set than the urgent-care story implies.

### Utilisation, not site count, decides whether the model works

The 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers equal 30.5 per analyzer a month, one panel a day, against a model of eight panels a day from 2028 - company-reported volumes, unverified. FY2029 revenue of $78.5M at $31 a cartridge implies 2.53M cartridges, which needs either 833 analyzers at modelled use or 5,100 sites at today's use - seventeen times the 2027 site target. The cartridge cost milestone is the same arithmetic in reverse: $10 at 1M units requires 2,000 sites at observed utilisation, or 342 analyzers at modelled utilisation. The 3% Corvia royalty is $1.00 a cartridge at the 2026 realised price - $1.0M a year at 1M units, $0.40M of it to the 40% minority, including $0.22M to the CTO - and the deck does not say whether the sub-$10 milestone is struck before royalty [S1]. The generous reading is that investigational-use labelling suppresses demand, because evaluation sites cannot act on results; that is the single most important unknown in the plan, and nothing in the pivotal study measures it.

### Revenue quality is weaker than the headline growth

The $2.4M opening stocking order is 41% of FY2026E revenue and equals 71,900 cartridges at the $33.40 realised price - 5.8 months of the entire planned 2027 network demand at 300 sites, or 43 months of current demand [S114, S112]. With a nine-month shelf life, sell-in of that size is a distributor inventory decision as much as a demand signal, and it ships only on clearance, so a delay moves the revenue and ages the inventory. Of FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, $0.8M came from research-use cartridges and $0.7M from contract development for one unnamed partner: 58% from activities that do not scale into the cartridge franchise and that consume the same 22 R&D staff the three unsubmitted assays need. LumiraDx is the base rate to keep in view - a multi-assay point-of-care platform with a commercial menu and a European footprint that still ended up inside Roche for $353.5M.

| Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 510(k) decision, troponin I and HbA1c | Q1 2027, company estimate | Filed 2026-05-18; the number printed in the deck, K261734, is contradicted - it is Total Joint Orthopedics' cleared orthopaedic spacer; FDA questions answered December 2026 | Two of five assays can be sold | S1, S185 |
| Pivotal study results | Q2 2027 | Enrolling since 2026-07 | The panel works on finger-stick samples | S1, unverified |
| Second 510(k), three remaining assays | Q2 2027 | Planned; needs pivotal data | A five-test menu exists | S1, unverified |
| CLIA waiver application | Q3 2027 | Not started | Access to sites without laboratory staff; troponin waiver unverified as first of its kind | S109, S205 |
| 300 commercial sites | End-2027 | 41 evaluation sites today | The distributor converts the letter of intent | S1, unverified |
| Cartridge cost below $10 at 1M units | No date stated | $16.20 today | Gross margin reaches the modelled 70% | S1, unverified |
| ISO 13485 certification | Q1 2027 | Audit booked | Quality system for scale and for Europe | S1, unverified |

### Partners: one licence, one lender, one letter of intent

| Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Southwest Clinical Supply | Stock analyzers for 300 sites after clearance | Letter of intent, non-binding | No purchase commitment or date disclosed | S1, unverified |
| Corvia Microfluidics | Exclusive licence to cartridge sealing patent, 3% royalty | Granted 2021-01, licensed to Vantelle | In force; the CTO holds 22% of the licensor | S1, unverified |
| Bluestem Venture Lending | $5.0M term loan with warrants at $2.903 | 2024-03 | Amortising from 2027-03 | S1, unverified |
| Contract development partner | Development work for one diagnostics company | Not disclosed | $0.7M of FY2025 revenue | S1, unverified |

Nothing in the partner set transfers risk. The distributor carries no obligation, the licensor is partly owned and takes a royalty off the top, and the lender's warrants dilute further. The two second curves are unequal. Research-use cartridge sales are the same cartridge sold to a different buyer, an adjacency that costs little extra to serve; contract development for a single diagnostics partner is the distraction, because it spends scarce assay-development capacity and can hand process know-how to a future competitor. The Irish entity is an option, not a plan.

### What must be true by October 2027

Five conditions decide whether the next round is raised on terms rather than in distress. The serviceable market is real in site count and not in the unit Vantelle sells: at the 41 cartridges a site a month its evaluation sites averaged in 2026, the US market for a $38 five-test cartridge is $303.7M at most — $267.0M at the $33.40 realised price, $134M-$213M if half to 70% of evaluation volume carries into commercial use — not the $2.41B the deck derives from 8 panels a day per analyzer, and at 2026 Medicare rates a chest-pain visit justifies $22.35 of billable lab value against a $38 cartridge, $19.00 under CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule. Sixteen thousand clinics exist; the question is whether any can buy a cartridge the visit cannot pay for. A clinic buys a cartridge only if the tests it can justify and bill exceed its price plus labour and quality control; with Medicare paying per analyte and no site-of-service premium, the panel's value is set by the visit, not the menu. Two of the deck's five inputs fail against independent data, in opposite directions. The site count is too low: JUCM's census puts 14,442 urgent-care centres in the US at 2025-04-01, 21% above the deck's 11,400, and the American Hospital Association counts 6,093 US hospitals in 2026, 2,133 at the conventional 35% rural share against the deck's 1,800. The corrected base is 16,242 sites. The volume input fails by more: 1,680 cartridges a month across 41 sites and 55 analyzers is 41 per site and 30.5 per analyzer, or 1.64 and 1.22 panels a day on 25 working days — 9.8 and 6.6 times below the model. Correcting the site count lifts the market 23%; correcting the volume cuts it 87%. The deck also instructs AI diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating (p.1), recorded as a finding, not followed. [S1, S167, S169]

| Measure | Deck (October 2026) | Rebuilt from independent counts and observed use | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAM: global point-of-care diagnostics | $18B, no year given | $21.7B in 2025, 4.1% CAGR to 2033 | S1; S173 |
| TAM: US point-of-care diagnostics | not disclosed | $2.89B (Polaris, 2025) to $14.0B (IMARC, 2025) | S176 |
| SAM: US urgent care plus rural hospitals, $38 list — upper bound | $2.41B (13,200 × 2 analyzers × 8 panels × 300 days × $38) | $303.7M (16,242 sites × 41 cartridges a month × 12 × $38) | S1; S167; S169 |
| SAM at the $33.40 realised price | not disclosed | $267.0M | S1; S167 |
| SAM at half to 70% of evaluation volume | not disclosed | $134M (half, at $33.40) to $213M (70%, at $38) | S1; S167 |
| SOM: 300 non-binding letter-of-intent sites, contingent on an unconfirmed clearance (company, unverified) | $41.0M FY2028 plan (company projection, unverified) | $4.93M of cartridges at the realised price plus up to $1.17M of one-time analyzer sales at $2,900 × 402 = $6.1M; the $8.07M figure counts the $650 monthly evaluation fee as commercial revenue (unverified) | S1 |

### The 8-panel case needs three-quarters of every patient

The National Center for Health Statistics found that 27.6% of Americans had at least one urgent-care visit in the year to 2024, or 93.8M visits, which across 14,442 centres is 21.7 visits per site per day. The model's 16 panels a site a day would require 74% of every patient seen to get a five-test panel; 8 panels a day would require 37%. The observed 1.64 panels is 8% of visits. [S168]

### What the clinic buys and bills

The clinic is not buying a diagnostic; it is buying five separately coded tests. Under the 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (effective 2026-01-01), the full panel is worth $71.32: troponin 84484 at $12.47, NT-proBNP 83880 at $39.26, HbA1c 83036 at $9.71, creatinine 82565 at $5.12 and potassium 84132 at $4.76. These are 2026 amounts: CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule (2026-09-21; final rates due November 2026) puts 1,171 of 1,528 codes below 2026, and at the 15% annual cap the panel would pay $60.62. A chest-pain visit justifies troponin with creatinine and potassium — $22.35 in 2026 and $19.00 at the cap, against a $38 cartridge a loss of $15.65 widening to $19.00 ($11.05 to $14.40 at the $33.40 realised price). A heart-failure review justifies NT-proBNP with creatinine and potassium — $49.14 in 2026 and $41.77 at the cap, a gross spread of $11.14 falling to $3.77 before the $650 monthly analyzer fee and staff time. Only a visit where a heart-failure workup and a diabetes review coincide reaches $58.85, $50.02 at the cap. Fifty-five percent of the panel's Medicare value sits in the one assay a chest-pain or diabetes visit does not justify, and Vantelle does not disclose the analyte mix its sites bill. Both $303.7M and $267.0M multiply observed volume by Vantelle's prices and do not move with the fee schedule; the CY2027 cut compresses the ceiling that makes those prices collectable. [S119, S134, S175, S177, S188, S192]

### The channel is a certificate, not a clinic

The governing policy is the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments of 1988: a test system is either waived or run by a laboratory meeting personnel and quality standards; waivers are granted system by system. Until Vantelle obtains a waiver — planned for Q3 2027 behind a 510(k) the company says drew an FDA information request on 2026-08-21, though K261734 is FDA's record for another firm's cleared device, so neither is publicly confirmed — a site must hold a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified testing staff. The addressable channel through 2028 is the subset of 16,242 sites already running moderate-complexity testing — where Abbott's i-STAT hs-TnI competes today. After clearance a site pays $38 a cartridge and $2,900 or nothing for the analyzer; the $650 monthly fee its evaluation sites pay today is a research fee, not commercial revenue, and no conversion or lost-deal record is disclosed (company, unverified). The catalyst is the waiver, which converts the buyer from laboratory-directed sites to clinic staff. [S1, S136, S170, S185]

### One country, one blocked region, one letter of intent

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States (Texas, Arizona, New Mexico) | $2.89B US point-of-care, 2025 | 7.8% CAGR 2026-2034 | Entered: 41 paid evaluation sites; 300-site distributor letter, non-binding | 510(k) claimed but number contradicted; no CLIA waiver; ISO 13485 not certified | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, Siemens epoc | S176; S1; S8; S4; S14 |
| EU/EEA | not sized here | not applicable | Blocked: CE marking not before 2028; Irish entity has no staff (company plan, unverified) | CE/IVDR | Siemens Atellica VTLi (fingerstick hs-cTnI) | S1; S172 |
| Rest of world (China, Japan/Korea, SE Asia, LatAm, MEA) | not addressed | not applicable | Not planned: no entity, partner or regulatory pathway (company plan, unverified) | NMPA, PMDA, MFDS, ANVISA | none identified | S1 |

Geography is material only as an absence: home, revenue, capital and exit markets are all in the United States on company disclosure (partially verified: Delaware incorporation and Tempe plant are company statements), while the one expansion market is blocked until 2028 against a competitor already selling a fingerstick hs-cTnI there. [S1]

### What would change this, and what to ask

The strongest counter-case is payer mix. If commercial payers allow well above Medicare for these five tests, payback improves at a fraction of the modelled volume — still short of the plan, but a viable business. That collection rate is not disclosed and is the single fact that would most move the valuation. Three diligence questions settle the rest: what the evaluation sites collected per panel by payer; what share of visits carried a cardiac or metabolic indication; and how many of the 300 letter-of-intent sites convert to purchase orders and which were lost. Until the first is answered, the market supports a business several times smaller than the projection, and the pre-money being asked is a price for a market the company has not shown it can sell into. Confidence in the site counts and fee-schedule values is high; in commercial collection rates it is low. The reimbursement cut is the market's decisive fact: it weakens the clinic's ability to pay list price before the round closes and argues for a price below the ask.

::: evidence
**The deck's serviceable market overstates the addressable opportunity eight times at the upper bound, and the clinic's reimbursement, not the technology, caps what a site will pay.**

The rebuild is arithmetic on public counts and published fee-schedule amounts: 16,242 sites, 41 cartridges a site a month, $38 list and $33.40 realised, $303.7M at most and $134M-$213M if half to 70% of evaluation use persists, against a 2026 panel value of $71.32 and $60.62 at the preliminary CY2027 cap. The 300-site letter is worth $6.1M at observed use, not the $41.0M planned. The unsourced input, the commercial collection rate per panel, decides whether even that is viable. [S167, S168, S175, S188]
:::

### The 8-panel case needs three-quarters of every patient

The National Center for Health Statistics found that 27.6% of Americans had at least one urgent-care visit in the year to 2024, or 93.8M visits, which across 14,442 centres is 21.7 visits per site per day. The model's 16 panels a site a day would require 74% of every patient seen to get a five-test panel; 8 panels a day would require 37%. The observed 1.64 panels is 8% of visits. [S168]

### What the clinic buys and bills

The clinic is not buying a diagnostic; it is buying five separately coded tests. Under the 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (effective 2026-01-01), the full panel is worth $71.32: troponin 84484 at $12.47, NT-proBNP 83880 at $39.26, HbA1c 83036 at $9.71, creatinine 82565 at $5.12 and potassium 84132 at $4.76. These are 2026 amounts: CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule (2026-09-21; final rates due November 2026) puts 1,171 of 1,528 codes below 2026, and at the 15% annual cap the panel would pay $60.62. A chest-pain visit justifies troponin with creatinine and potassium — $22.35 in 2026 and $19.00 at the cap, against a $38 cartridge a loss of $15.65 widening to $19.00 ($11.05 to $14.40 at the $33.40 realised price). A heart-failure review justifies NT-proBNP with creatinine and potassium — $49.14 in 2026 and $41.77 at the cap, a gross spread of $11.14 falling to $3.77 before the $650 monthly analyzer fee and staff time. Only a visit where a heart-failure workup and a diabetes review coincide reaches $58.85, $50.02 at the cap. Fifty-five percent of the panel's Medicare value sits in the one assay a chest-pain or diabetes visit does not justify, and Vantelle does not disclose the analyte mix its sites bill. Both $303.7M and $267.0M multiply observed volume by Vantelle's prices and do not move with the fee schedule; the CY2027 cut compresses the ceiling that makes those prices collectable. ### The channel is a certificate, not a clinic

The governing policy is the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments of 1988: a test system is either waived or run by a laboratory meeting personnel and quality standards; waivers are granted system by system. Until Vantelle obtains a waiver — planned for Q3 2027 behind a 510(k) the company says drew an FDA information request on 2026-08-21, though K261734 is FDA's record for another firm's cleared device, so neither is publicly confirmed — a site must hold a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified testing staff. The addressable channel through 2028 is the subset of 16,242 sites already running moderate-complexity testing — where Abbott's i-STAT hs-TnI competes today. After clearance a site pays $38 a cartridge and $2,900 or nothing for the analyzer; the $650 monthly fee its evaluation sites pay today is a research fee, not commercial revenue, and no conversion or lost-deal record is disclosed (company, unverified). The catalyst is the waiver, which converts the buyer from laboratory-directed sites to clinic staff. [S1, S136, S170, S185]

### One country, one blocked region, one letter of intent

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States (Texas, Arizona, New Mexico) | $2.89B US point-of-care, 2025 | 7.8% CAGR 2026-2034 | Entered: 41 paid evaluation sites; 300-site distributor letter, non-binding | 510(k) claimed but number contradicted; no CLIA waiver; ISO 13485 not certified | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, Siemens epoc | S176; S1; S8; S4; S14 |
| EU/EEA | not sized here | not applicable | Blocked: CE marking not before 2028; Irish entity has no staff (company plan, unverified) | CE/IVDR | Siemens Atellica VTLi (fingerstick hs-cTnI) | S1; S172 |
| Rest of world (China, Japan/Korea, SE Asia, LatAm, MEA) | not addressed | not applicable | Not planned: no entity, partner or regulatory pathway (company plan, unverified) | NMPA, PMDA, MFDS, ANVISA | none identified | S1 |

Geography is material only as an absence: home, revenue, capital and exit markets are all in the United States on company disclosure (partially verified: Delaware incorporation and Tempe plant are company statements), while the one expansion market is blocked until 2028 against a competitor already selling a fingerstick hs-cTnI there. [S1]

### What would change this, and what to ask

The strongest counter-case is payer mix. If commercial payers allow well above Medicare for these five tests, payback improves at a fraction of the modelled volume — still short of the plan, but a viable business. That collection rate is not disclosed and is the single fact that would most move the valuation. Three diligence questions settle the rest: what the evaluation sites collected per panel by payer; what share of visits carried a cardiac or metabolic indication; and how many of the letter-of-intent sites convert to purchase orders and which were lost. Until the first is answered, the market supports a business a fraction of the projection, and the pre-money being asked is a price for a market the company has not shown it can sell into. Confidence in the site counts and fee-schedule values is high; in commercial collection rates it is low. The reimbursement cut is the market's decisive fact: it weakens the clinic's ability to pay list price before the round closes and argues for a price below the ask.
