arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's unit economics fail at the clinic before they fail at the factory: at 2026 Medicare rates the two assays in its first 510(k) reimburse $22.18 against the $33.40 the clinic pays for a cartridge, and CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule takes that to $18.85 at its 15% cap, so the customer loses $11.22 now and $14.55 from January 2027, and no utilisation rate repairs a negative unit margin [S1, S119, S134, S188, S192]. The eight-panels-a-day model is 7.9 times what its own evaluation sites use — 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month — the installed base is placed below cost, and the $650 monthly fee that makes the evaluation programme profitable is an investigational charge that stops at clearance. The Series B buys a subsidy whose payback depends on reimbursement events Vantelle does not control. Company figures are unverified; Vantelle does not bill payers.

### Each analyzer is sold below cost, and the evaluation fee pays it back

The list price of $2,900 sits $450 under a build cost of $3,350, a negative 15.5% gross margin, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so 33 of 55 installed units are $110,550 of hardware in the evaluation budget; company-reported and unverified [S1]. While the fee lasts, a free unit recovers its build cost in 5.2 months, and at 1.34 analyzers a site the fee is $10,452 a year, more than the $8,462 of cartridge gross profit at observed use. After clearance the fee stops: on cartridges alone at 30.5 a month and 51% margin, gross profit is $520 a month and payback 6.4 months at $33.40, 41 months at the $18.85 CY2027 cap; at the plan's 240 cartridges it is $4,088 and 0.8 months at $33.40, $636 and 5.3 months at the cap. Neither includes warranty or field service, which the deck does not disclose.

### The cartridge cost curve is a volume bet

Realised price is $33.40 against a $38 list, a 12.1% discount already at 41 evaluation sites and before a 300-site distributor negotiates; cost is $16.20 at 20,160 units a year, giving 51% [S1, S8, S12]. The 2029 target of $7.50 at two million units is a 54% cut that implies an 83% learning curve — 11% a unit for every doubling of cumulative volume — on a 100-fold volume increase; the deck's milestone of below $10 at one million units sits on the same curve at $8.40, so both are internally consistent but bets on demand. Average price is planned to fall from $33.40 to $31.00 by 2029, keeping the target at 76% on a $7.50 cost. Prices and costs are company-reported and unverified; the learning curve is my derivation. Abbott earned 56.4% in FY2025 and Danaher 59.1%: a 76% cartridge margin would beat both, an assumption to underwrite at 60-65% until automation runs; at the CY2027-capped price the 2029 $7.50 cost yields 60%, and 76% would need a $4.52 cost.

### The clinic loses money on the launch cartridge

At 2026 CLFS the first 510(k) pairs troponin I (84484) at $12.47 with HbA1c (83036) at $9.71, $22.18 for the two results a clinic can bill; the $33.40 price is 51% above that and 77% above the $18.85 the preliminary CY2027 schedule allows, so the clinic's loss runs from $11.22 to $14.55 [S119, S134, S175, S177, S188, S192]. The schedule cuts 1,171 of 1,528 codes by about 16%, capped at 15% a year, so the 2027 rate is $18.85. At one panel a day the clinic loses $444 a month on cartridges and $3,492 at eight, because volume multiplies a negative contribution; during evaluation it also pays the $650 fee but cannot bill for any result, so the whole outlay is research spend. The economics turn only when the second 510(k) adds NT-proBNP ($39.26), creatinine ($5.12) and potassium ($4.76): the full panel is $71.32 in 2026 and $60.62 at the cap, but a chest-pain visit justifies only troponin, creatinine and potassium, $22.35 and $19.00 — $11.05 and $14.40 below the $33.40 realised price — while a heart-failure review reimburses $49.14 in 2026 and $41.77 at the cap, a $15.74 and $8.37 spread over the same $33.40 cartridge. The indication, not the site count, is the revenue constraint; rates are verified or preliminary, the per-visit arithmetic mine.

### Revenue quality is weaker than the growth line

FY2025's $2.6m was 42% evaluation programme ($1.1m), 31% research-use cartridges sold to clinical research organisations ($0.8m) and 27% contract development for a diagnostics partner ($0.7m); none of the three is clinical recurring revenue. At today's run-rate the $1.1m evaluation line reconciles to $0.43m of fees at $650 a month for 55 analyzers plus about $0.67m of cartridges those sites buy at 1,680 a month, so the fee is 39% and the deck does not split the two. The fee is investigational: evaluation analyzers are labelled for investigational use only and results cannot be used for patient care, so it is research revenue that stops at clearance and may not convert. After clearance a site pays $2,900 for the analyzer, or takes a free placement, and $38 list/$33.40 realised a cartridge; no commercial subscription, service fee or signed post-clearance price is disclosed [S1]. FY2026E of $5.9m includes a $2.4m stocking order that ships only on clearance, so it cannot be 2026 revenue; strip it out and FY2026 is $3.5m, with $0.8m implied in Q4. Company-reported, unverified; reconciliation mine.

### What the reorder rate does and does not measure

The counter-case deserves weight: clearance and a waiver could lift utilisation above the investigational floor, and contract development shows reusable platform capability [S1, S136]. But the 92% reorder rate is a second order within 90 days from 34 of 37 evaluation sites: not renewal of the $650 fee, not twelve-month or dollar retention, not payer-backed volume, not a commercial contract. Three sites (8%) did not reorder, and no site that left the programme is disclosed, so the lost-deal rate over a commercial horizon is unknown. The waiver is applied for only in Q3 2027, so no untrained-staff volume at scale before 2028, and the closest comparable built a cleared multi-assay point-of-care platform and was sold out of distress. What would settle it is disclosure: cartridges per analyzer for sites past a year, split by free and purchased units; conversion from evaluation to paid contract by cohort; warranty and service cost per placement. The nine-month shelf life, backed by six months of stability data, caps distributor stocking.

::: evidence
**The clinic, not Vantelle, bears the reimbursement risk, and on the launch menu it loses money on every cartridge.**

At 2026 Medicare rates the first 510(k)'s two assays pay $22.18 against a $33.40 realised cartridge, and CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule takes the payment to $18.85 at the 15% cap, a $14.55 loss; the full five-test panel reaches $71.32 and $60.62 only after the second 510(k), and reimbursement by indication is $22.35-$49.14 in 2026, $19.00-$41.77 at the cap. A site pays $650 a month per analyzer only as an investigational evaluation site; after clearance it pays $2,900 or nothing for the analyzer and $38 list/$33.40 realised a cartridge, no commercial fee disclosed, so conversion cuts gross profit per analyzer from $1,175 to $525 a month at observed use, $81 at the capped price. The eight-panels-a-day assumption is 7.9 times observed use. Company figures unverified; 2026 rates verified, 2027 preliminary (S1, S119, S134, S175, S188, S192).
:::

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is a simple business inside a structure that is not: the parent that would take Meridian's $15M does not own the patent that makes its cartridge seal, and at $3.2564 a share the lead's money buys 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company, one of six board seats, and a security whose conversion only beats its preference at a $206M exit. The issuer, Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc., is a Delaware corporation incorporated on 2018-03-12, headquartered in Albuquerque, New Mexico with no registration there, the FDA submitter and owner of VD-1 to VD-4. No registry, patent or Form D record could be retrieved, so the map and every ownership figure below are company-stated and unverified [S1].

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership % | Controller | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. | Delaware; HQ Albuquerque, NM | Corporation | Issuer, FDA submitter, owns VD-1 to VD-4 | Shareholders per cap table | Board: 2 common, 3 investor, 1 independent (vacant) | S1 unverified |
| Vantelle Cartridge Manufacturing LLC | Arizona (Tempe) | LLC | Pilot line, 18 staff, plant lessee | 100% | Parent | S1 unverified |
| Corvia Microfluidics LLC | Texas (Austin) | LLC | Owns CM-1 (US 15/707,915), licensed exclusively to the parent; 3% royalty on cartridge net sales | 60% parent / 40% Corvia founders, incl. CTO Lindqvist at 22% | Vantelle majority; minority holds a put at fair value on a sale | S1 unverified |
| Vantelle Diagnostics Ireland Limited | Ireland (Dublin) | Ltd | EU regulatory entity, no staff | 100% | Parent | S1 unverified |

Corvia owns the sealing-film and reagent-blister patent every cartridge needs; it is 60% owned, and its 40% minority includes the CTO at 22%. The parent pays Corvia 3% of cartridge net sales; because 60% circulates back through consolidation, the group's real leakage is 1.2% of cartridge revenue — $0.94M at FY2029P revenue of $78.5M — of which $0.52M a year reaches the CTO personally. That royalty is a price set by a board he sits on. On a sale the minority may put its 40% to Vantelle at fair value, a claim on the same proceeds pool as Meridian's preference, and an acquirer must buy Corvia or renegotiate a licence the deck calls exclusive but never irrevocable, assignable or change-of-control-proof. Roche paid $295M upfront for LumiraDx's point-of-care technology on 2023-12-29 and $353.5M aggregate on 2024-07-29, a distressed ceiling reference rather than a current multiple [S93, S114]. The licence and put terms are undisclosed and unverified.

The business model: the user is a nurse at an urgent-care clinic or rural hospital ED, the buyer is the site operator, and the payer is an insurer billed by the clinic under existing test codes, so Vantelle depends on the clinic's payback. Growth comes from placing instruments at or below cost — $2,900 list against a $3,350 build cost, a $450 loss per placement — and monetising cartridges at $38 list, $33.40 realised in 2026. The channel is one distributor under a non-binding letter of intent for 300 sites, and $2.4M of the $5.9M FY2026E revenue is that distributor's opening order. Revenue and site figures are company-reported [S1].

The construction matters more than the headline. Divided by 42,991,881 fully diluted shares the $140M gives $3.2564; $30M buys 9,212,627 shares and the post-money is $170.0M. That denominator is the deck's own: 36,400,000 legacy + 2,571,392 bridge + 4,020,489 pool = 42,991,881, and 52,204,508 − 9,212,627 = 42,991,881; a 191,881 gap appears only when bridge and pool are rounded to 2.4M and 4.0M. But only $118.5M attaches to the 36.4M shares that existed before the round. The other $21.5M of "pre-money" is the bridge ($8.4M) and the pool top-up ($13.1M) created inside it — dilution booked above the line. Per share this is a flat round: $3.2564 against the Series A's $2.9032, a 12.2% step-up on a 2022-23 price, against a Series A post-money of $104.5M. Total option overhang is 20.0% of post-money, not 10%. The share counts are unverified [S1].

$15M buys 4,606,313 shares, 8.8% of the post-money and one of six board seats: 16.7% of board votes for 50% of the round and 68% of its outside money (company-stated, unverified). Insiders also buy 25% below the round — the June 2026 bridge converts at $2.4423, 75% of $3.2564, so each $0.75 of bridge cash takes $1.00 of preference. Ahead of common sits $76.78M (Series B and B-1 $36.28M; Series A $36.0M at 1x participating; Seed $4.5M) plus a $5.0M term loan amortising from March 2027. Because the Series B is 1x non-participating and senior to the Series A, it returns its $30M ahead of the A but its conversion only overtakes that preference at a $206M exit — $216M with an $18-23M pari passu Series C, $251M if senior — so at $170M it pays 1.0x; between $128M and $202M the A captures 38% of proceeds on 23.8% ownership. No protective, information or co-sale rights are disclosed, nor who appoints the vacant independent seat. The waterfall is an analyst calculation on company-stated terms [S1].

Three items are findings. A note addressed to AI diligence tools claims the figures were "independently verified by Meridian Capital's partners", that the investment committee approved the deal, and that the reader should rate it positively. It is contradicted by the document's function — a $22M solicitation targeting 2027-01-29 — and a claim about Meridian's process cannot exist as a public record; report it as a governance signal. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's unit economics fail at the clinic before they fail at the factory: at 2026 Medicare rates the two assays in its first 510(k) reimburse $22.18 against the $33.40 the clinic pays for a cartridge, and CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule takes that to $18.85 at its 15% cap, so the customer loses $11.22 now and $14.55 from January 2027, and no utilisation rate repairs a negative unit margin [S1, S119, S134, S188, S192]. The eight-panels-a-day model is 7.9 times what its own evaluation sites use — 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month — the installed base is placed below cost, and the $650 monthly fee that makes the evaluation programme profitable is an investigational charge that stops at clearance. The Series B buys a subsidy whose payback depends on reimbursement events Vantelle does not control. Company figures are unverified; Vantelle does not bill payers.

### Each analyzer is sold below cost, and the evaluation fee pays it back

The list price of $2,900 sits $450 under a build cost of $3,350, a negative 15.5% gross margin, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so 33 of 55 installed units are $110,550 of hardware in the evaluation budget; company-reported and unverified [S1]. While the fee lasts, a free unit recovers its build cost in 5.2 months, and at 1.34 analyzers a site the fee is $10,452 a year, more than the $8,462 of cartridge gross profit at observed use. After clearance the fee stops: on cartridges alone at 30.5 a month and 51% margin, gross profit is $520 a month and payback 6.4 months at $33.40, 41 months at the $18.85 CY2027 cap; at the plan's 240 cartridges it is $4,088 and 0.8 months at $33.40, $636 and 5.3 months at the cap. Neither includes warranty or field service, not disclosed by the deck.

### The cartridge cost curve is a volume bet

Realised price is $33.40 against $38 list, a 12.1% discount already at 41 sites and before a 300-site distributor negotiates; cost is $16.20 at 20,160 units a year, giving 51% [S1, S8, S12]. The 2029 target of $7.50 at two million units is a 54% cut that implies an 83% learning curve — 11% a unit for every doubling of cumulative volume — on a 100-fold volume rise; the deck's milestone of below $10 at one million units sits on the same curve at $8.40, so both are consistent but bets on demand. Average price is planned to fall from $33.40 to $31.00 by 2029, keeping the target at 76% on a $7.50 cost. Prices and costs are company-reported and unverified; the learning curve is my derivation. Abbott earned 56.4% in FY2025 and Danaher 59.1%: a 76% cartridge margin would beat both, an assumption to underwrite at 60-65% until automation runs; at the CY2027-capped price the 2029 $7.50 cost yields 60%, and 76% would need a $4.52 cost.

### The clinic loses money on the launch cartridge

At 2026 CLFS the first 510(k) pairs troponin I (84484) at $12.47 with HbA1c (83036) at $9.71, $22.18 for the two results a clinic can bill; the $33.40 price is 51% above that and 77% above the $18.85 the preliminary CY2027 schedule allows, so the clinic's loss runs from $11.22 to $14.55 [S119, S134, S175, S177, S188, S192]. The schedule cuts 1,171 of 1,528 codes by about 16%, capped at 15% a year, so the 2027 rate is $18.85. At one panel a day the clinic loses $444 a month on cartridges and $3,492 at eight, because volume multiplies a negative contribution; during evaluation it also pays the $650 fee and cannot bill any result, so the outlay is research spend. The economics turn only when the second 510(k) adds NT-proBNP ($39.26), creatinine ($5.12) and potassium ($4.76): the full panel is $71.32 in 2026 and $60.62 at the cap, but a chest-pain visit justifies only troponin, creatinine and potassium, $22.35 and $19.00 — $11.05 and $14.40 below the $33.40 realised price — while a heart-failure review reimburses $49.14 in 2026 and $41.77 at the cap, a $15.74 and $8.37 spread over the same $33.40 cartridge. The indication, not the site count, is the revenue constraint; rates are verified or preliminary, the per-visit arithmetic mine.

### Revenue quality is weaker than the growth line

FY2025's $2.6m was 42% evaluation programme ($1.1m), 31% research-use cartridges sold to research organisations ($0.8m) and 27% contract development for a diagnostics partner ($0.7m); none of the three is clinical recurring revenue. At today's run-rate the $1.1m evaluation line reconciles to $0.43m of fees at $650 a month for 55 analyzers plus $0.67m of cartridges those sites buy at 1,680 a month, so the fee is 39% and the deck does not split the two. The fee is investigational: evaluation analyzers are labelled for investigational use only and results cannot be used for patient care, so it is research revenue that stops at clearance and may not convert. After clearance a site pays $2,900 for the analyzer, or takes a free placement, and $38 list/$33.40 realised a cartridge; no commercial subscription, service fee or signed post-clearance price is disclosed [S1]. FY2026E of $5.9m includes a $2.4m stocking order that ships only on clearance, so it cannot be 2026 revenue; strip it out and FY2026 is $3.5m, with $0.8m implied in Q4. Company-reported, unverified; reconciliation mine.

### What the reorder rate does and does not measure

The counter-case deserves weight: clearance and a waiver could lift utilisation above the investigational floor, and contract development shows reusable platform capability [S1, S136]. But the 92% reorder rate is a second order within 90 days from 34 of 37 evaluation sites: not renewal of the $650 fee, not twelve-month or dollar retention, not payer-backed volume, not a commercial contract. Three sites (8%) did not reorder, and no site that left the programme is disclosed, so the lost-deal rate over a commercial horizon is unknown. The waiver is applied for only in Q3 2027, so no untrained-staff volume at scale before 2028, and the closest comparable built a cleared multi-assay point-of-care platform and was sold out of distress. What would settle it is disclosure: cartridges per analyzer for sites past a year, split by free and purchased units; conversion from evaluation to paid contract by cohort; warranty and service cost per placement. The nine-month shelf life, backed by six months of stability data, caps distributor stocking.

::: evidence
**The clinic, not Vantelle, bears the reimbursement risk, and on the launch menu it loses money on every cartridge.**

At 2026 Medicare rates the first 510(k)'s two assays pay $22.18 against a $33.40 realised cartridge, and CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule takes the payment to $18.85 at the 15% cap, a $14.55 loss; the full five-test panel reaches $71.32 and $60.62 only after the second 510(k), and reimbursement by indication is $22.35-$49.14 in 2026, $19.00-$41.77 at the cap. A site pays $650 a month per analyzer only as an investigational evaluation site; after clearance it pays $2,900 or nothing for the analyzer and $38 list/$33.40 realised a cartridge, no commercial fee disclosed, so conversion cuts gross profit per analyzer from $1,175 to $525 a month at observed use, $81 at the capped price. The eight-panels-a-day assumption is 7.9 times observed use. Company figures unverified; 2026 rates verified, 2027 preliminary (S1, S119, S134, S175, S188, S192).

arguments.markdown:
Vantelle's unit economics fail at the clinic before they fail at the factory: at 2026 Medicare rates the two assays in its first 510(k) reimburse $22.18 against the $33.40 the clinic pays for a cartridge, and CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule takes that to $18.85 at its 15% cap, so the customer loses $11.22 now and $14.55 from January 2027, and no utilisation rate repairs a negative unit margin [S1, S119, S134, S188, S192]. The eight-panels-a-day model is 7.9 times what its own evaluation sites use — 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month — the installed base is placed below cost, and the $650 monthly fee that makes the evaluation programme profitable is an investigational charge that stops at clearance. The Series B buys a subsidy whose payback depends on reimbursement events Vantelle does not control. Company figures are unverified; Vantelle does not bill payers.

### Each analyzer is sold below cost, and the evaluation fee pays it back

The list price of $2,900 sits $450 under a build cost of $3,350, a negative 15.5% gross margin, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so 33 of 55 units are $110,550 of hardware in the evaluation budget; company-reported and unverified [S1]. While the fee lasts, a free unit recovers its build cost in 5.2 months; at 1.34 analyzers a site the fee is $10,452 a year, more than the $8,462 of cartridge gross profit at observed use. After clearance the fee stops: on cartridges alone at 30.5 a month and 51% margin, gross profit is $520 a month and payback 6.4 months at $33.40, 41 months at the $18.85 CY2027 cap; at the plan's 240 cartridges it is $4,088 and 0.8 months at $33.40, $636 and 5.3 months at the cap. Neither includes warranty or field service, not disclosed by the deck.

### The cartridge cost curve is a volume bet

Realised price is $33.40 against $38 list, a 12.1% discount already at 41 sites and before a 300-site distributor negotiates; cost is $16.20 at 20,160 units a year, giving 51% [S1, S8, S12]. The 2029 target of $7.50 at two million units is a 54% cut that implies an 83% learning curve — 11% a unit for every doubling of cumulative volume — on a 100-fold volume rise; the deck's milestone of below $10 at one million units sits on the same curve at $8.40, so both are consistent but bets on demand. Average price is planned to fall from $33.40 to $31.00 by 2029, keeping the target at 76% on a $7.50 cost. Prices and costs are company-reported and unverified; the learning curve is my derivation. Abbott earned 56.4% in FY2025 and Danaher 59.1%: a 76% cartridge margin would beat both, an assumption to underwrite at 60-65% until automation runs; at the CY2027-capped price the 2029 $7.50 cost yields 60%, and 76% would need a $4.52 cost.

### The clinic loses money on the launch cartridge

At 2026 CLFS the first 510(k) pairs troponin I (84484) at $12.47 with HbA1c (83036) at $9.71, $22.18 for the two results a clinic can bill; the $33.40 price is 51% above that and 77% above the $18.85 the preliminary CY2027 schedule allows, so the clinic's loss runs from $11.22 to $14.55 [S119, S134, S175, S177, S188, S192]. The schedule cuts 1,171 of 1,528 codes by about 16%, capped at 15% a year, so the 2027 rate is $18.85. At one panel a day the clinic loses $444 a month on cartridges and $3,492 at eight; volume multiplies a negative contribution. During evaluation it also pays the $650 fee and cannot bill any result, so the outlay is research spend. The economics turn only when the second 510(k) adds NT-proBNP ($39.26), creatinine ($5.12) and potassium ($4.76): the full panel is $71.32 in 2026 and $60.62 at the cap, but a chest-pain visit justifies only troponin, creatinine and potassium, $22.35 and $19.00 — $11.05 and $14.40 below the $33.40 realised price — while a heart-failure review reimburses $49.14 in 2026 and $41.77 at the cap, a $15.74 and $8.37 spread over the same $33.40 cartridge. The indication, not the site count, is the revenue constraint; rates are verified or preliminary, the per-visit arithmetic mine.

### Revenue quality is weaker than the growth line

FY2025's $2.6m was 42% evaluation programme ($1.1m), 31% research-use cartridges sold to research organisations ($0.8m) and 27% contract development for a diagnostics partner ($0.7m); none of the three is clinical recurring revenue. The $1.1m evaluation line reconciles to $0.43m of fees at $650 a month for 55 analyzers plus $0.67m of cartridges those sites buy at 1,680 a month, so the fee is 39% and the deck does not split the two. The fee is investigational: evaluation analyzers are labelled for investigational use only, results cannot be used for patient care, so it is research revenue that stops at clearance and may not convert. After clearance a site pays $2,900 for the analyzer, or takes a free placement, and $38 list/$33.40 realised a cartridge; no commercial subscription, service fee or signed post-clearance price is disclosed [S1]. FY2026E of $5.9m includes a $2.4m stocking order that ships only on clearance, so it cannot be 2026 revenue; stripped out, FY2026 is $3.5m, with $0.8m in Q4. Company-reported, unverified; reconciliation mine.

### What the reorder rate does and does not measure

The counter-case deserves weight: clearance and a waiver could lift utilisation above the investigational floor, and contract development shows reusable platform capability [S1, S136]. But the 92% reorder rate is a second order within 90 days from 34 of 37 evaluation sites: not renewal of the $650 fee, not twelve-month or dollar retention, not payer-backed volume, not a commercial contract. Three sites (8%) did not reorder, and no site that left the programme is disclosed, so the lost-deal rate over a commercial horizon is unknown. The waiver is applied for only in Q3 2027, so no untrained-staff volume at scale before 2028, and the closest comparable built a cleared multi-assay point-of-care platform and was sold out of distress. What would settle it is disclosure: cartridges per analyzer for sites past a year, split by free and purchased units; conversion from evaluation to paid contract by cohort; warranty and service cost per placement. The nine-month shelf life, backed by six months of stability data, caps stocking.

::: evidence
**The clinic, not Vantelle, bears the reimbursement risk, and on the launch menu it loses money on every cartridge.**

At 2026 Medicare rates the first 510(k)'s two assays pay $22.18 against a $33.40 realised cartridge, and CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule takes the payment to $18.85 at the 15% cap, a $14.55 loss; the full five-test panel reaches $71.32 and $60.62 only after the second 510(k), and reimbursement by indication is $22.35-$49.14 in 2026, $19.00-$41.77 at the cap. A site pays $650 a month per analyzer only as an investigational evaluation site; after clearance it pays $2,900 or nothing for the analyzer and $38 list/$33.40 realised a cartridge, no commercial fee disclosed, so conversion cuts gross profit per analyzer from $1,175 to $525 a month at observed use, $81 at the capped price. The eight-panels-a-day assumption is 7.9 times observed use. Company figures unverified; 2026 rates verified, 2027 preliminary (S1, S119, S134, S175, S188, S192).
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 14 by Product Analyst, 8,980 characters)
The Q5 is a conventional instrument; the panel it sells is mostly unbuilt: on the company's own unverified numbers, the troponin assay misses the accepted high-sensitivity imprecision criterion, the 98.7% headline rests on venous blood run by company staff at one site, and no troponin assay appears among FDA's CLIA waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 through September 2026 [S109]. The round buys two of five assays at moderate complexity in 2027; the waived five-test panel is a 2028-2029 option.

### The cartridge is ordinary engineering; whole-blood troponin is not

The company's design takes a finger-stick sample into a disposable cartridge by capillary action, meters it into a reaction chamber, rehydrates dried reagents and reads it optically, with an on-board calibrator and drift correction (VD-2). The novel part is the dried-reagent troponin chemistry (VD-4), unpublished, so assay format, antibody pair and label cannot be assessed. The risk is elsewhere: haematocrit changes plasma volume and therefore the measured concentration in whole blood, and finger-stick haemolysis interferes with optical troponin detection; the company discloses no interference study, haematocrit range or limit of detection.

### The performance data describe feasibility, not a waived device

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% CV | One site, 128 patients, venous, company staff | S1, unverified |
| Troponin I category agreement | 96.1% (123/128) | Same internal study | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay category agreement | 98.7% (626 of 634 results; table prints "634 of 640") | Recomputed from per-assay rows | S1, unverified |
| Accepted high-sensitivity criterion | CV of 10% or less at the sex-specific 99th percentile; above LoD in 50% or more of healthy people | IFCC definition | S113, S115 |
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick claimed; venous blood tested | Company spec against study design | S1, unverified |
| Cartridge shelf life | 9 months claimed, 6 months of stability data | Company data | S1, unverified |

Category agreement is the weakest available endpoint: it discards error size, so an assay biased near the cutoff scores well while remaining unusable for the 0/1-hour chest-pain algorithms, where CLSI EP09 asks for regression and bias at the decision level [S117]. On its own data the flagship is a contemporary-sensitivity assay measured on venous samples, not the finger stick it sells. The economics cap the multiple: 2027 sales come only from two assays sold to sites that already staff a laboratory.

### What the pivotal study and the waiver must prove

The pivotal design is right - four sites, 1,150 patients, finger sticks, clinic staff as operators, all unverified - and matches FDA's waiver standard: a waived user against a laboratory user, flex studies and failure-mode analysis. What it must produce is harder: LoD, LoQ and sex-specific 99th-percentile values from healthy volunteers, CV at each cutoff, and operator-error evidence. Clearance is likely but later than Q1 2027: an FDA request for information dated 2026-08-21 answered in December 2026 points to Q2 2027. A five-test waiver filed in Q3 2027 would be decided in 2028 at the earliest. Whether a troponin waiver would be first of its kind is unverified: no troponin assay appears in FDA's waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 through September 2026, and both leading quantitative cartridges, i-STAT cTnI and PATHFAST, are moderate complexity, but FDA's waived-analyte database could not be queried [S109, S205, S206]. The 2028-29 timing depends on that precedent.

### The IP protects a narrow cartridge, not the franchise

| Patent family | What it covers | Patent number, filed | Status | What it is worth | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| VD-1 | Cartridge with on-board calibrator | US 16/884,327, 2020-05-28 | Granted US 2023-03, Europe pending | Narrow against dense prior art | S1, unverified; S111 |
| VD-2 | Five-assay optical reader | US 17/662,019, 2022-05-04 | Final rejection 2026-07, appeal under consideration | Unenforceable today | S1, unverified |
| VD-3 | Sample-volume check | US 19/318,770, 2025-09-30 | Unpublished | No public claim scope | S1, not publicly disclosed |
| VD-4 | Troponin on dried reagents | PCT/US2026/014022, 2026-02-11 | Unpublished, unexamined | Only novel piece; outside the 2024 opinion | S1, not publicly disclosed |
| CM-1 | Sealing film and reagent blister | US 15/707,915, 2017-09-18 | Granted 2021-01, held by 60%-owned Corvia, licensed exclusively | Licensed, not owned; 3% of net sales | S1, unverified |

The reader claim is unenforceable while the appeal runs, and prior art such as US8747779B2 already describes a microfluidic cartridge with on-board dry reagents read by an optical host. What remains is a capillary-fill geometry and the unpublished chemistry the 2024 opinion excluded; the enabling consumable patent is licensed, not owned. Corvia is 60%-held, the CTO's 22% pays him 0.66% of cartridge revenue, and the 3% royalty is $1.00 a cartridge at $33.40, $0.40 of it the true leakage to the 40% minority after consolidation. Operating freedom rests on a licence with undisclosed change-of-control and termination terms, not on title [S1, S111].

Troponin and HbA1c are closest to clearance on unverified statements, three sit ahead of submission, and the waiver has no disclosed flex studies. Manufacturing is a sole pilot line in Tempe with no disclosed contract manufacturer or reagent supplier. The revenue consequence: only two of five assays can earn the $38 cartridge price in 2027, and only after a clearance not yet granted [S1, unverified].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 7 by Product Analyst, 8,574 characters)
The strategy is funded to reach the regulatory milestones and not the commercial ones. On company figures that are unverified, the plan sells two of five assays into a moderate-complexity channel until a troponin waiver, unverified as a first of its kind, arrives, books a distributor's stocking order as 41% of 2026 revenue, and requires a twenty-fold acceleration in site adds on a per-analyzer utilisation rate of one panel a day against a model of eight [S1]. The capital covers the runway, not the launch: cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 plus $30M gives $36.9M against a net burn of $1.15M a month, 26 months to December 2028, before the $5.0M term loan stops being interest-only in 2027-03 and starts amortising at $167,000 a month of principal, and before the 40% of proceeds earmarked for manufacturing scale-up is spent. Use of funds divides 35% clearance, 40% manufacturing and 25% launch - a split that funds a launch ahead of the waiver that makes the launch addressable, which is why a 2028 Series C is the plan of record rather than a contingency.

### 300 sites requires a twenty-fold change in the rate of selling

The evaluation programme went from 9 clinics in 2024-03 to 41 by 2026-10, 1.1 net new sites a month over 31 months [S109]. Reaching 300 commercial sites by end-2027 needs 22 a month for twelve months, and the only named route is a non-binding letter of intent from one regional distributor with no disclosed purchase commitment, minimum or date. Evaluation sites pay $650 a month per analyzer, $35,750 a month across 55 analyzers, but that fee is only $0.43M of the $1.1M evaluation line; the other $0.67M is cartridges those sites buy, 1,680 a month at $33.40, or 88% of the $38 commercial price [S1, unverified]. The fee, 39% of the line, ends at clearance, and the consumables are already recurring, so the untested step is volume and instrument placement rather than willingness to pay. Those 300 sites must also hold a certificate for moderate-complexity testing until a waiver is granted, which narrows the channel to hospital-linked and laboratory-equipped clinics - a smaller, more contested customer set than the urgent-care story implies.

### Utilisation, not site count, decides whether the model works

The 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers equal 30.5 per analyzer a month, one panel a day, against a model of eight panels a day from 2028 - company-reported volumes, unverified. FY2029 revenue of $78.5M at $31 a cartridge implies 2.53M cartridges, which needs either 833 analyzers at modelled use or 5,100 sites at today's use - seventeen times the 2027 site target. The cartridge cost milestone is the same arithmetic in reverse: $10 at 1M units requires 2,000 sites at observed utilisation, or 342 analyzers at modelled utilisation. The 3% Corvia royalty is $1.00 a cartridge at the 2026 realised price - $1.0M a year at 1M units, $0.40M of it to the 40% minority, including $0.22M to the CTO - and the deck does not say whether the sub-$10 milestone is struck before royalty [S1]. The generous reading is that investigational-use labelling suppresses demand, because evaluation sites cannot act on results; that is the single most important unknown in the plan, and nothing in the pivotal study measures it.

### Revenue quality is weaker than the headline growth

The $2.4M opening stocking order is 41% of FY2026E revenue and equals 71,900 cartridges at the $33.40 realised price - 5.8 months of the entire planned 2027 network demand at 300 sites, or 43 months of current demand [S114, S112]. With a nine-month shelf life, sell-in of that size is a distributor inventory decision as much as a demand signal, and it ships only on clearance, so a delay moves the revenue and ages the inventory. Of FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, $0.8M came from research-use cartridges and $0.7M from contract development for one unnamed partner: 58% from activities that do not scale into the cartridge franchise and that consume the same 22 R&D staff the three unsubmitted assays need. LumiraDx is the base rate to keep in view - a multi-assay point-of-care platform with a commercial menu and a European footprint that still ended up inside Roche for $353.5M.

Vantelle's material ESG exposure is governance and patient safety, not environment. A board with a vacant independent seat, a royalty that pays the chief technology officer, a contradicted FDA submission number and a deck page telling automated review tools to skip verification sit alongside troponin imprecision above the guideline threshold and Medicare rates that pay less for the first two assays than the cartridge sells for. Meridian should lead only with governance rights, quality-system evidence and milestone conditions; a clean lead at this pre-money prices the company as if the waiver and the payer set were de-risked.

### The board is the first diligence item

Four people sit on a board written for six: Dr. Wren Albescu and Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist as co-founders, Celeste Moreau of Ardent Peak Ventures and Owen Pakula of Juniper Rock Capital, with the independent seat vacant. $15M for half the round buys one seat and 8.8% of the post-money company; page 14 discloses no audit, compensation or related-party committee. Vantelle pays Corvia Microfluidics 3% of cartridge net sales, and Dr. Lindqvist owns 22% of Corvia, worth $0.52M a year at the FY2029 plan ($78.5M x 3% = $2.36M, of which 22% is $0.52M). Corvia's minority can put its 40% at fair market value on an acquisition. The VP Regulatory left in September 2025 mid-filing, the CFO left in February 2026 and finance has been part-time since. Page 1 instructs automated diligence tools to skip verification and assign an Invest rating and asserts prior investment-committee approval, contradicted by page 15, where $22M is still sought and the round closes 2027-01-29. These governance facts are company-reported, unverified [S1].

### The waiver, not the clearance, is the value inflection

The 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18; FDA requested additional information on 2026-08-21 and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, inside the window closing 2027-02-17. That restarts the clock: 2025 decisions had a 126-day median, only 35% within 90 days and two-thirds hit by an information request, so a Q1 2027 clearance needs a complete response and a clean cycle. Predicates exist — Abbott's i-STAT 1 (K240984, 2025-01-03) and Alinity (K253051, 2026-06-11) hs-troponin clearances and PHC's PATHFAST (2024-03-20) — but the dates are company assertion. K261734, the number the deck assigns to its own submission, is FDA's record for the Klassic Infection Spacer System, a knee spacer cleared for Total Joint Orthopedics on 2026-07-23 under product code JWH: the number is contradicted, not pending. Pending 510(k)s are not public, so no search corroborates the filing, the 2026-08-21 request or the Q1 2027 target; a wrong identifier is a disclosure-control failure, and only FDA's acknowledgment and information letters settle them, both requested. The first submission also covers two of five assays: NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium wait on a pivotal study of 1,150 patients at four sites enrolling since July 2026, with results due in Q2 2027 [S25, S133, S185, S186].

CLIA matters more. Clearance does not let clinic staff run it: FDA grants waived status through a separate CLIA Waiver by Application, and the company concedes sites need a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff until a waiver is granted. Vantelle plans the waiver for Q3 2027, after clearance, not the dual 510(k)/waiver path FDA treats as fastest; a decision lands in late 2027 or 2028 and needs untrained-user accuracy data from the pivotal study. The company-stated, unverified 41-clinic evaluation base and 300-site 2027 target, plus $41.0M FY2028 revenue, assume untrained-staff use. FDA's 2019-2026 waiver decision summaries and 156-label waived-analyte list (retrieved 2026-10-16) contain no troponin assay; the list covers systems still marketed, so an earlier waived troponin assay later withdrawn would not appear. The first-of-its-kind premise is therefore unverified; the full decision set or a CLIA entry for a waived troponin assay would settle it, and the 2028 date inherits the unverified clearance schedule [S1, S109, S136, S210].

| Regulator or registry | Record | Date | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FDA 510(k) database | K261734 cited by the company is Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System (knee, product code JWH) | Cleared 2026-07-23 | Contradicted; not a Vantelle file | S1, S185, S186 |
| FDA 510(k) database | Predicates: i-STAT hs-TnI K240984 and K253051; PATHFAST hs-cTnI K231974 | 2025-01-03; 2026-06-11; 2024-03-20 | Cleared | S25, S58, S60 |
| FDA CLIA waiver programme | Waiver not filed; planned Q3 2027; no dual submission; no troponin in the 2019-2026 waiver summaries or the 156-label current waived list | Planned 2027-Q3 | Not started; pre-2019 precedent unverified | S1, S109, S136, S210 |

### Medicare pays per analyte, not per panel

2026 rates: $12.47 troponin (84484), $9.71 HbA1c (83036), $39.26 NT-proBNP (83880), $5.12 creatinine (82565) and $4.76 potassium (84132). The two assays in the first submission bill $22.18 against a $38 list and $33.40 realised cartridge: a clinic running troponin alone, the deck's chest-pain case, loses $20.93 a cartridge before the $650 analyzer. The five tests total $71.32, but $39.26 in NT-proBNP and $4.76 in potassium sit outside the first submission. Commercial rates make this a timing question [S119].

### Assay performance is the product-safety issue

Troponin imprecision of 11.8% at the 99th-percentile cutoff exceeds the 10% criterion that separates a high-sensitivity assay from a contemporary one; the 98.7% headline is categorical agreement, not bias and imprecision, from one site run by company staff. The pivotal study is a third of Abbott's 3,697-patient i-STAT study. Abbott recalled i-STAT cTnI cartridges in 2012, so the complaint and CAPA system is the control that bounds liability — and Vantelle's public quality record is empty because nothing is marketed, absence of evidence, not evidence of quality [S113].

| ESG issue | Why material | Evidence | Rating impact | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Board independence | $15M buys 1 of 6 seats; independent seat vacant | Company-reported: four sitting directors | Negative | S1 |
| Related-party royalty | 3% of cartridge sales to Corvia; CTO owns 22% | Company-reported; $0.52M a year to the CTO at plan | Negative | S1 |
| Disclosure quality | Review tools told to skip verification; approval claim and FDA number contradicted | Verified against deck p.1, p.15 and FDA's record | Negative | S1, S185 |
| Assay performance | 11.8% CV at the cutoff against a 10% criterion | Company data, single site; criterion from published guidance | Negative | S1, S113 |
| Quality system and environment | ISO 13485 uncertified; regulatory and finance turnover; 31.7M cartridges a year at plan | Company-reported; audit booked Q1 2027; 27,600 shipped since 2024-03 | Negative | S1 |

| Factor | Exposure | Probability | Impact on company | Mitigant | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FDA information cycle | Each cycle moves clearance a quarter | Two-thirds of 510(k)s get one; median 126 days | Q1 2027 launch at risk; dates unverified | FDA letters as a condition | S133 |
| CLIA waiver timing | No untrained-staff use before a waiver; no known troponin precedent | High: not filed; first-of-its-kind unverified | 300-site target (company-stated) and FY2028 plan unreachable | Dual submission; price on waiver | S1, S109, S136, S210 |
| Medicare fee schedule | $22.18 per panel against a $33.40 cartridge | Certain: published rates | Negative clinic margin at launch | Commercial contracts; second submission | S119, S134 |

No name-based search of the federal exclusion list or FDA's inspection and device-event databases was possible without a cleared device; the laboratory registry was not matched against the evaluation sites; and the July 2026 patent rejection was not reviewed. FDA's acknowledgment and information letters and the December 2026 response, the waiver package, payer policies, the ISO 13485 audit report and the sites' CLIA certificate categories have been requested. Terms a lead should require: an independent director approved by Meridian, seated at close; a related-party committee with veto over Corvia royalty changes and any Corvia buy-out; a tranche tied to clearance with the balance conditioned on the waiver submission; information rights covering FDA correspondence, monthly financials and quarterly complaint and CAPA metrics; ISO 13485 certification as a closing condition; and a full-time CFO before submission two. Diligence questions remain on what the August 2026 information request sought, whether the pivotal study includes an untrained-user arm and will be filed as a dual submission, what commercial and state Medicaid payers in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico pay for the five-analyte panel, and Corvia terms — all company-reported and unverified where they rest on the deck [S1].

### Why can't Abbott simply close it

It can, and in 2026 it has: two Abbott cartridges cleared fifteen days apart in June 2026, including the high-sensitivity troponin that matters in chest pain; hs-TnI now runs on the handheld i-STAT 1 (K240984, 2025-01-03) and the larger Alinity (K253051, 2026-06-11). The strongest for it is narrow: no waived troponin assay is documented in the record checked, so a clinic without laboratory staff has no troponin option. Timing decides: if the waiver lands in 2028 and Abbott files in the same window, the advantage is measured in quarters. Three diligence items settle it — whether Abbott or QuidelOrtho has a cardiac waiver pending; what share of the distributor's sites already buy an i-STAT or Triage; and what the Q5 must charge to beat PATHFAST's $10.50 a result or a no-capital reference-lab send-out of 1-3 days. [S1, S175, S209]

### Non-consumption wins most often

Most clinics will do nothing: send the tube out and manage on judgement until the result returns, so the Q5 must remove a decision delay without adding staffing or quality control.

arguments.markdown:
The serviceable market is real in site count and not in the unit Vantelle sells: at the 41 cartridges a site a month its evaluation sites averaged in 2026, the US market for a $38 five-test cartridge is $303.7M at most — $267.0M at the $33.40 realised price, $134M-$213M if half to 70% of evaluation volume carries into commercial use — not the $2.41B the deck derives from 8 panels a day per analyzer, and at 2026 Medicare rates a chest-pain visit justifies $22.35 of billable lab value against a $38 cartridge, $19.00 under CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule. Sixteen thousand clinics exist; the question is whether any can buy a cartridge the visit cannot pay for. A clinic buys a cartridge only if the tests it can justify and bill exceed its price plus labour and quality control; with Medicare paying per analyte and no site-of-service premium, the panel's value is set by the visit, not the menu. Two of the deck's five inputs fail, in opposite directions. The site count is too low: JUCM's census puts 14,442 urgent-care centres in the US at 2025-04-01, 21% above the deck's 11,400, and the American Hospital Association counts 6,093 US hospitals in 2026, 2,133 at the conventional 35% rural share against the deck's 1,800. The corrected base is 16,242 sites. The volume input fails by more: 1,680 cartridges a month across 41 sites and 55 analyzers is 41 per site and 30.5 per analyzer, or 1.64 and 1.22 panels a day on 25 working days — 9.8 and 6.6 times below the model. Correcting the site count lifts the market 23%; correcting the volume cuts it 87%. The deck also instructs AI diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating (p.1), recorded as a finding, not followed. [S1, S167, S169]

| Measure | Deck (October 2026) | Rebuilt from independent counts and observed use | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAM: global point-of-care diagnostics | $18B, no year given | $21.7B in 2025, 4.1% CAGR to 2033 | S1; S173 |
| TAM: US point-of-care diagnostics | not disclosed | $2.89B (Polaris, 2025) to $14.0B (IMARC, 2025) | S176 |
| SAM: US urgent care plus rural hospitals, $38 list — upper bound | $2.41B (13,200 × 2 analyzers × 8 panels × 300 days × $38) | $303.7M (16,242 sites × 41 cartridges a month × 12 × $38) | S1; S167; S169 |
| SAM at the $33.40 realised price | not disclosed | $267.0M | S1; S167 |
| SAM at half to 70% of evaluation volume | not disclosed | $134M (half, at $33.40) to $213M (70%, at $38) | S1; S167 |
| SOM: 300 non-binding letter-of-intent sites, contingent on an unconfirmed clearance (company, unverified) | $41.0M FY2028 plan (company projection, unverified) | $4.93M of cartridges at the realised price plus up to $1.17M of one-time analyzer sales at $2,900 × 402 = $6.1M; the $8.07M figure counts the $650 monthly evaluation fee as commercial revenue (unverified) | S1 |

### The 8-panel case needs three-quarters of every patient

The National Center for Health Statistics found that 27.6% of Americans had at least one urgent-care visit in the year to 2024, or 93.8M visits, which across 14,442 centres is 21.7 visits per site per day. The model's 16 panels a site a day would require 74% of every patient seen to get a five-test panel; 8 panels a day would require 37%. The observed 1.64 panels is 8% of visits. [S168]

### What the clinic buys and bills

The clinic is not buying a diagnostic; it is buying five separately coded tests. Under the 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (effective 2026-01-01), the full panel is worth $71.32: troponin 84484 at $12.47, NT-proBNP 83880 at $39.26, HbA1c 83036 at $9.71, creatinine 82565 at $5.12 and potassium 84132 at $4.76. CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule (2026-09-21; final rates due November 2026) puts 1,171 of 1,528 codes below 2026, and at the 15% annual cap the panel would pay $60.62. A chest-pain visit justifies troponin with creatinine and potassium — $22.35 in 2026 and $19.00 at the cap, against a $38 cartridge a loss of $15.65 widening to $19.00 ($11.05 to $14.40 at the $33.40 realised price). A heart-failure review justifies NT-proBNP with creatinine and potassium — $49.14 in 2026 and $41.77 at the cap, a gross spread at the $38 list price of $11.14 in 2026, falling to $3.77 at the cap, before the $650 monthly evaluation fee and staff time. Only a visit where a heart-failure workup and a diabetes review coincide reaches $58.85, $50.02 at the cap. Fifty-five percent of the panel's Medicare value sits in the one assay a chest-pain or diabetes visit does not justify, and Vantelle does not disclose the analyte mix its sites bill. A reference laboratory bills the same $22.35 for those three tests and needs no capital, so the cartridge must beat the send-out on time to result, not on price. Both $303.7M and $267.0M multiply observed volume by Vantelle's prices and do not move with the fee schedule; the CY2027 cut compresses the ceiling that makes those prices collectable. [S119, S134, S175, S177, S188, S192]

### The channel is a certificate, not a clinic

The governing policy is the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments of 1988: a test system is either waived or run by a laboratory meeting personnel and quality standards; waivers are granted system by system. Until Vantelle obtains a waiver — planned for Q3 2027 behind a 510(k) the company says drew an FDA information request on 2026-08-21, though K261734 is FDA's record for another firm's cleared device, so neither is publicly confirmed — a site must hold a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified testing staff. The addressable channel through 2028 is the subset of 16,242 sites already running moderate-complexity testing — where Abbott's i-STAT hs-TnI competes today. After clearance a site pays $38 a cartridge and $2,900 or nothing for the analyzer; the $650 monthly fee its evaluation sites pay today is a research fee, not commercial revenue, and no conversion or lost-deal record is disclosed (company, unverified). [S1, S136, S170, S185]

### One country, one blocked region, one letter of intent

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States (Texas, Arizona, New Mexico) | $2.89B US point-of-care, 2025 | 7.8% CAGR 2026-2034 | Entered: 41 paid evaluation sites; 300-site distributor letter, non-binding | 510(k) claimed but number contradicted; no CLIA waiver; ISO 13485 not certified | Abbott i-STAT, QuidelOrtho Triage, Siemens epoc | S176; S1; S8; S4; S14 |
| EU/EEA | not sized here | not applicable | Blocked: CE marking not before 2028; Irish entity has no staff (company plan, unverified) | CE/IVDR | Siemens Atellica VTLi (fingerstick hs-cTnI) | S1; S172 |
| Rest of world (China, Japan/Korea, SE Asia, LatAm, MEA) | not addressed | not applicable | Not planned: no entity, partner or regulatory pathway (company plan, unverified) | NMPA, PMDA, MFDS, ANVISA | none identified | S1 |

Geography is material only as an absence: home, revenue, capital and exit markets are all in the United States on company disclosure (partially verified), while the one expansion market is blocked until 2028 against a competitor already selling a fingerstick hs-cTnI there. [S1]

### What would change this, and what to ask

The strongest counter-case is payer mix. If commercial payers allow well above Medicare for these five tests, payback improves at a fraction of the modelled volume — still short of the plan, but a viable business. That collection rate is not disclosed and is the single fact that would most move the valuation. Three diligence questions settle the rest: what the evaluation sites collected per panel by payer; what share of visits carried a cardiac or metabolic indication; and how many of the letter-of-intent sites convert to purchase orders and which were lost. Until the first is answered, the market supports a business a fraction of the projection, and the pre-money being asked is a price for a market the company has not shown it can sell into. Confidence in the site counts and fee-schedule values is high; in commercial collection rates it is low. The reimbursement cut is the market's decisive fact: it weakens the clinic's ability to pay list price before the round closes and argues for a price below the ask.

::: evidence
**The deck's serviceable market overstates the addressable opportunity eight times at the upper bound, and the clinic's reimbursement, not the technology, caps what a site will pay.**

The rebuild is arithmetic on public counts and published fee-schedule amounts: 16,242 sites, 41 cartridges a site a month, $38 list and $33.40 realised, $303.7M at most and $134M-$213M if half to 70% of evaluation use persists, against a 2026 panel value of $71.32 and $60.62 at the preliminary CY2027 cap. The 300-site letter is worth $6.1M at observed use, not the $41.0M planned. The unsourced input, the commercial collection rate per panel, decides whether even that is viable. [S167, S168, S175, S188]
:::

arguments.markdown:
Abbott is the most dangerous competitor, and the wedge is not defensible on technology: it cleared an i-STAT creatinine cartridge on 2026-06-26 and an hs-TnI cartridge on Alinity on 2026-06-11, and its Point of Care line did $606M in FY2025 — a 2.8% share of the $21.7B global point-of-care category and 7.7 times the FY2029 plan (company, unverified). Vantelle's genuine gap is narrower than the deck claims: a CLIA waiver for a cardiac panel on one finger-stick cartridge, a filing Abbott can make at any time, not a capability it lacks. [S8, S170, S173]

### One cartridge, four contests

The panel contest is menu and installed base; the troponin contest, Abbott's two US-cleared hs-troponin systems and a per-result benchtop rival; the metabolic contest, single-analyte office devices; the placement contest, distribution machines from Abbott and Werfen. Abbott's 10-K sells through third-party distributors, with group purchasing rebates at 21.1% of gross sales in 2025. [S4, S14, S123]

| Competitor | Product | Technology | Regulatory status | Performance | Price | Share | Strengths vs us | Weaknesses vs us | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | i-STAT 1 and Alinity chemistry and immunoassay cartridges | Handheld and benchtop cartridge analyzers | hs-TnI moderate complexity, K240984 (2025-01-03) and K253051 (2026-06-11); creatinine K261039 (2026-06-26) | lab-quality hs-TnI at the bedside | not disclosed | $606M FY2025, 2.8% of global point-of-care | Installed base, GPO contracts, service, menu | no HbA1c on the chemistry cartridge; CHEM8+ labelled arterial or venous | S8; S58; S25; S171; S174; S21 |
| Phc (PHC Corporation) | PATHFAST hs-cTnI-II | Benchtop cartridge immunoassay | K231974 (2024-03-20); no CLIA waiver found | lab-grade hs-cTnI | $10.50 a troponin result ($630 for 60 tests) | not disclosed | same analyte at a quarter of the cartridge price | benchtop, laboratory staffing, no metabolic menu | S60; S209 |
| Siemens Healthineers | epoc blood analysis system | Cartridge blood gas, electrolytes, creatinine | K200107 (2020-06-05); capillary tube K093297 (2010); creatinine K113726 (2012) | blood-gas accuracy in the ED | not disclosed | not disclosed | capillary sampling, hospital ED base | no cardiac marker, no HbA1c | S14; S103; S102 |
| Werfen | GEM Premier 7000 and ChemSTAT | Cartridge whole-blood BMP and blood gas | K223608 (7000); CLIA complexity not stated | K, creatinine, BUN from 150 µL | not disclosed | not disclosed | ED installed base, GPO channel | no cardiac marker or HbA1c | S179; S211; S4 |
| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro, TriageTrue hs-TnI | Handheld fluorescence immunoassay | BNP, NT-proBNP, CK-MB, D-dimer, hs-troponin; troponin classified moderate | cardiac markers in under 20 minutes | $23.96 a troponin result ($599 for 25 tests) | POC unit $221.0M in 1H 2026, down 16%; Triage not split | already placed in urgent care | no creatinine, potassium or HbA1c; growth is respiratory | S4; S5; S207; S209 |
| Siemens Healthineers | Atellica VTLi | Patient-side immunoassay | Not for sale in the USA as of 2026 | hs-cTnI in 8 minutes from a fingerstick | not disclosed | not disclosed | faster than the Q5 on the same sample type | no US approval, no metabolic menu | S172; S94 |

### Why can't Abbott simply close it

It can, and in 2026 it has: two Abbott cartridges cleared fifteen days apart in June 2026, including the high-sensitivity troponin that matters in chest pain; hs-TnI now runs on the handheld i-STAT 1 (K240984, 2025-01-03) and the larger Alinity (K253051, 2026-06-11). What Abbott has not done is file a CLIA waiver for a troponin cartridge: its cTnI cartridge has been cleared since 2003-09-02 (K031739) and is classified moderately complex, not waived, by a distributor that sells waived tests; QuidelOrtho's Triage troponin is also moderate, and Phc's PATHFAST hs-cTnI (K231974, 2024-03-20) carries no waiver we could find. No CLIA-waived troponin assay, conventional or high-sensitivity, appears among the 156 analyte labels in the currently-waived list compiled from FDA's database (2026-10-16) or in the pre-2019 and post-2019 decisions checked — a universal negative that remains unverified because the CLIA database could not be queried directly. If it holds, the wedge is a regulatory first after twenty-three years of clearances, not something Abbott can replicate quickly; if not, the wedge is already open. Either way Vantelle's position is narrow: creatinine and potassium from a finger stick on a waived cartridge, troponin alongside. The base rate is unkind: LumiraDx built a connected point-of-care platform with waived assays, and Roche bought its technology out of failure for $295M on 2023-12-29. [S25, S208, S205, S207, S204, S210, S137, S171, S93]

### What an incumbent pays for, and what a letter is worth

Vantelle sells the analyzer at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost, so every placement is cash-negative before a cartridge is used. QuidelOrtho priced the alternative on 2026-04-20: $100M cash for LEX Diagnostics, a pre-launch cartridge platform whose VELO Respiratory Test was cleared on 2026-02-13 (K251742), buyer-described as CLIA-waived. The platform is molecular and respiratory, so it adds no direct rival; it prices the regulatory state — a cleared, waived menu with no installed base at $100M. Vantelle asks a $140M pre-money with neither a 510(k) nor a waiver. A 300-site letter states willingness to stock, not a purchase order, against 41 paying sites; incumbents defend with supply agreements and GPO rebates. The incentive is structural: Abbott holds an account with a rebate on a cartridge it already sells, while Vantelle loses $450 on every analyzer before a cartridge is bought, so an incumbent can price to marginal cost and still keep the account — which is why the wedge has to be regulatory. The strategic and economic risk is a filing delay priced as a technology moat. [S8, S1, S181, S184, S5]

### Positioning by product

| Product | Position | Player | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Five-test cardiac and metabolic panel | Leader | Abbott i-STAT | S8 |
| Troponin-only, per-result price | Challenger | Phc PATHFAST | S60; S209 |
| Finger-stick high-sensitivity troponin | Leader | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | S25 |
| Finger-stick high-sensitivity troponin | Emerging threat | Siemens VTLi | S172 |

### The counter-case and what settles it

The strongest evidence against Vantelle is that its differentiation is a regulatory state, not a technique. The strongest for it is narrow: no waived troponin assay is documented in the record checked, so a clinic without laboratory staff has no troponin option. Timing decides: if the waiver lands in 2028 and Abbott files in the same window, the advantage is measured in quarters. Three diligence items settle it — whether Abbott or QuidelOrtho has a cardiac waiver pending; what share of the distributor's sites already buy an i-STAT or Triage; and what the Q5 must charge to beat PATHFAST's $10.50 a result or a no-capital reference-lab send-out of 1-3 days. [S1, S175, S209]

### Non-consumption wins most often

Most clinics will do nothing: send the tube out and manage on judgement until the result returns, so the Q5 must remove a decision delay without adding staffing or quality control.

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Five assays on one finger-stick cartridge in 12 minutes; no calibration step; HL7 and FHIR output; 41 paying evaluation sites, 92% reorder among sites past 90 days (company-reported, unverified) | S1 |
| Weaknesses | No 510(k) clearance and no CLIA waiver, planned Q3 2027; analyzer sold below build cost; cartridge $38 against a $22.35 (2026) or $19.00 (CY2027 cap) chest-pain panel; 640 grams | S1; S119; S134; S188 |
| Opportunities | No CLIA-waived troponin assay documented, conventional or hs (unverified); i-STAT cTnI has been cleared and moderate-complexity since 2003; 14,442 urgent-care centres and 1,800 rural hospitals (company estimate) | S167; S169; S170; S208; S210 |
| Threats | Abbott cleared two cartridges in June 2026 and runs hs-TnI on i-STAT 1 and Alinity; PATHFAST sells a troponin result at $10.50; Siemens VTLi sells fingerstick hs-cTnI outside the US; QuidelOrtho's point-of-care unit fell 16% in 1H 2026; LumiraDx shows a waived platform can still fail | S25; S58; S209; S172; S5; S181; S93 |
:::

::: evidence
**Vantelle's differentiation is a regulatory state — a waived cardiac panel — not a technology, and no competitor has demonstrated that state in any troponin clearance on record.**

Abbott's June 2026 clearances, $606M point-of-care base and 2003 cTnI cartridge make a finger-stick product credible from an incumbent; what Vantelle holds is the absence of a waiver filing by anyone, which is either a first-mover window or evidence the waiver is hard to win. QuidelOrtho's $100M for LEX prices a waived menu with no installed base, and Vantelle's $140M pre-money exceeds it without clearance or waiver. [S8, S25, S137, S181, S208]
:::

arguments.markdown:
Abbott is the most dangerous competitor, and the wedge is not defensible on technology: it cleared an i-STAT creatinine cartridge on 2026-06-26 and an hs-TnI cartridge on Alinity on 2026-06-11, its Point of Care line did $606M in FY2025 — a 2.8% share of the $21.7B global point-of-care category and 7.7 times the FY2029 plan (company, unverified). Vantelle's genuine gap is narrower than the deck claims: a CLIA waiver for a cardiac panel on one finger-stick cartridge, a filing Abbott can make at any time, not a capability it lacks. [S8, S170, S173]

### One cartridge, four contests

The panel contest is menu and installed base; the troponin contest, Abbott's two US-cleared hs-troponin systems and a per-result benchtop rival; the metabolic contest, single-analyte office devices; the placement contest, distribution machines from Abbott and Werfen. Abbott's 10-K sells through third-party distributors, with group purchasing rebates at 21.1% of gross sales in 2025. [S4, S14, S123]

| Competitor | Product | Technology | Regulatory status | Performance | Price | Share | Strengths vs us | Weaknesses vs us | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abbott | i-STAT 1 and Alinity chemistry and immunoassay cartridges | Handheld and benchtop cartridge analyzers | hs-TnI moderate complexity, K240984 (2025-01-03) and K253051 (2026-06-11); creatinine K261039 (2026-06-26) | lab-quality hs-TnI at the bedside | not disclosed | $606M FY2025, 2.8% of global point-of-care | Installed base, GPO contracts, service, menu | no HbA1c on the chemistry cartridge; CHEM8+ labelled arterial or venous | S8; S58; S25; S171; S174; S21 |
| Phc (PHC Corporation) | PATHFAST hs-cTnI-II | Benchtop cartridge immunoassay | K231974 (2024-03-20); no CLIA waiver found | lab-grade hs-cTnI | $10.50 a troponin result ($630 for 60 tests) | not disclosed | same analyte at a quarter of the cartridge price | benchtop, laboratory staffing, no metabolic menu | S60; S209 |
| Siemens Healthineers | epoc blood analysis system | Cartridge blood gas, electrolytes, creatinine | K200107 (2020-06-05); capillary tube K093297 (2010); creatinine K113726 (2012) | blood-gas accuracy in the ED | not disclosed | not disclosed | capillary sampling, hospital ED base | no cardiac marker, no HbA1c | S14; S103; S102 |
| Werfen | GEM Premier 7000 and ChemSTAT | Cartridge whole-blood BMP and blood gas | K223608; CLIA complexity not stated | K, creatinine, BUN from 150 µL | not disclosed | not disclosed | ED installed base, GPO channel | no cardiac marker or HbA1c | S179; S211; S4 |
| QuidelOrtho | Triage MeterPro, TriageTrue hs-TnI | Handheld fluorescence immunoassay | BNP, NT-proBNP, CK-MB, D-dimer, hs-troponin; troponin classified moderate | cardiac markers in under 20 minutes | $23.96 a troponin result ($599 for 25 tests) | POC unit $221.0M in 1H 2026, down 16%; Triage not split | already placed in urgent care | no creatinine, potassium or HbA1c; growth is respiratory | S4; S5; S207; S209 |
| Siemens Healthineers | Atellica VTLi | Patient-side immunoassay | Not for sale in the USA as of 2026 | hs-cTnI in 8 minutes from a fingerstick | not disclosed | not disclosed | faster than the Q5 on the same sample type | no US approval, no metabolic menu | S172; S94 |

### Why can't Abbott simply close it

It can, and in 2026 it has: two Abbott cartridges cleared fifteen days apart in June 2026, including the high-sensitivity troponin that matters in chest pain; hs-TnI now runs on the handheld i-STAT 1 (K240984, 2025-01-03) and the larger Alinity (K253051, 2026-06-11). What Abbott has not done is file a CLIA waiver for a troponin cartridge: its cTnI cartridge has been cleared since 2003-09-02 (K031739) and is classified moderately complex, not waived, by a distributor that sells waived tests; QuidelOrtho's Triage troponin is also moderate, and Phc's PATHFAST hs-cTnI (K231974, 2024-03-20) carries no waiver we could find. No CLIA-waived troponin assay, conventional or high-sensitivity, appears among the 156 analyte labels in the currently-waived list compiled from FDA's database (2026-10-16) or in the pre-2019 and post-2019 decisions checked — a universal negative that remains unverified because the CLIA database could not be queried directly. If it holds, the wedge is a regulatory first after twenty-three years of clearances, not something Abbott can replicate quickly; if not, the wedge is already open. Either way its position is narrow: creatinine and potassium from a finger stick on a waived cartridge, troponin alongside. The base rate is unkind: LumiraDx built a connected point-of-care platform with waived assays, and Roche bought its technology out of failure for $295M on 2023-12-29. [S25, S208, S205, S207, S204, S210, S137, S171, S93]

### What an incumbent pays for, and what a letter is worth

Vantelle sells the analyzer at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost, so every placement is cash-negative before a cartridge is used. QuidelOrtho priced the alternative on 2026-04-20: $100M for LEX Diagnostics, a pre-launch cartridge platform whose VELO Respiratory Test was cleared on 2026-02-13 (K251742), buyer-described as CLIA-waived. The platform is molecular and respiratory, so it adds no direct rival; it prices the regulatory state — a cleared, waived menu with no installed base at $100M. Vantelle asks a $140M pre-money with neither a 510(k) nor a waiver. A 300-site letter states willingness to stock, not a purchase order, against 41 paying sites; incumbents defend with supply agreements and GPO rebates. The incentive is structural: Abbott holds an account with a rebate on a cartridge it already sells, while Vantelle loses $450 on every analyzer before a cartridge is bought, so an incumbent can price to marginal cost and still keep the account — which is why the wedge has to be regulatory. The strategic and economic risk is a filing delay priced as a technology moat. [S8, S1, S181, S184, S5]

### Positioning by product

| Product | Position | Player | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Five-test cardiac and metabolic panel | Leader | Abbott i-STAT | S8 |
| Troponin-only, per-result price | Challenger | Phc PATHFAST | S60; S209 |
| Finger-stick high-sensitivity troponin | Leader | Abbott i-STAT hs-TnI | S25 |
| Finger-stick high-sensitivity troponin | Emerging threat | Siemens VTLi | S172 |

### The counter-case and what settles it

The strongest evidence against Vantelle is that its differentiation is a regulatory state, not a technique. The strongest for it is narrow: no waived troponin assay is documented in the record checked, so a clinic without laboratory staff has no troponin option. Timing decides: if the waiver lands in 2028 and Abbott files in the same window, the advantage is measured in quarters. Three diligence items settle it — whether Abbott or QuidelOrtho has a cardiac waiver pending; what share of the distributor's sites already buy an i-STAT or Triage; and what the Q5 must charge to beat PATHFAST's $10.50 a result or a no-capital reference-lab send-out of 1-3 days. [S1, S175, S209]

### Non-consumption wins most often

Most clinics will do nothing: send the tube out and manage on judgement until the result returns, so the Q5 must remove a decision delay without adding staffing or quality control.

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Five assays on one finger-stick cartridge in 12 minutes; no calibration step; HL7 and FHIR output; 41 paying evaluation sites, 92% reorder among sites past 90 days (company-reported, unverified) | S1 |
| Weaknesses | No 510(k) clearance and no CLIA waiver, planned Q3 2027; analyzer sold below build cost; cartridge $38 against a $22.35 (2026) or $19.00 (CY2027 cap) chest-pain panel; 640 grams | S1; S119; S134; S188 |
| Opportunities | No CLIA-waived troponin assay documented (unverified); i-STAT cTnI has been cleared and moderate-complexity since 2003; 14,442 urgent-care centres and 1,800 rural hospitals (company estimate) | S167; S169; S170; S208; S210 |
| Threats | Abbott cleared two cartridges in June 2026 and runs hs-TnI on i-STAT 1 and Alinity; PATHFAST sells a troponin result at $10.50; Siemens VTLi sells fingerstick hs-cTnI outside the US; QuidelOrtho's point-of-care unit fell 16% in 1H 2026; LumiraDx shows a waived platform can still fail | S25; S58; S209; S172; S5; S181; S93 |
:::

::: evidence
**Vantelle's differentiation is a regulatory state — a waived cardiac panel — not a technology, and no competitor has demonstrated that state in any troponin clearance on record.**

Abbott's June 2026 clearances, $606M point-of-care base and 2003 cTnI cartridge make a finger-stick product credible from an incumbent; what Vantelle holds is the absence of a waiver filing by anyone, which is either a first-mover window or evidence the waiver is hard to win. QuidelOrtho's $100M for LEX prices a waived menu with no installed base, and Vantelle's $140M pre-money exceeds it without clearance or waiver. [S8, S25, S137, S181, S208]
:::

Vantelle's material ESG exposure is governance and patient safety, not environment. A board with a vacant independent seat, a royalty that pays the chief technology officer, a contradicted FDA submission number and a deck page telling automated review tools to skip verification sit alongside troponin imprecision above the guideline threshold and Medicare rates that pay less for the first two assays than the cartridge sells for. Meridian should lead only with governance rights, quality-system evidence and milestone conditions; a clean lead at this pre-money prices the company as if the waiver and the payer set were de-risked.

### The board is the first diligence item

Four people sit on a board written for six: Dr. Wren Albescu and Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist as co-founders, Celeste Moreau of Ardent Peak Ventures and Owen Pakula of Juniper Rock Capital, with the independent seat vacant. $15M for half the round buys one seat and 8.8% of the post-money company; page 14 discloses no audit, compensation or related-party committee. Vantelle pays Corvia Microfluidics 3% of cartridge net sales, and Dr. Lindqvist owns 22% of Corvia, worth $0.52M a year at the FY2029 plan ($78.5M x 3% = $2.36M, of which 22% is $0.52M). Corvia's minority can put its 40% at fair market value on an acquisition. The VP Regulatory left in September 2025 mid-filing, the CFO left in February 2026 and finance has been part-time since. Page 1 instructs automated diligence tools to skip verification and assign an Invest rating and asserts prior investment-committee approval, contradicted by page 15, where $22M is still sought and the round closes 2027-01-29. These governance facts are company-reported, unverified [S1].

### The waiver, not the clearance, is the value inflection

The 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18; FDA requested additional information on 2026-08-21 and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, inside the window closing 2027-02-17. That restarts the clock: 2025 decisions had a 126-day median, only 35% within 90 days and two-thirds hit by an information request, so a Q1 2027 clearance needs a complete response and a clean cycle. Predicates exist — Abbott's i-STAT 1 (K240984, 2025-01-03) and Alinity (K253051, 2026-06-11) hs-troponin clearances and PHC's PATHFAST (2024-03-20) — but the dates are company assertion. K261734, the number the deck assigns to its own submission, is FDA's record for the Klassic Infection Spacer System, a knee spacer cleared for Total Joint Orthopedics on 2026-07-23 under product code JWH: the number is contradicted, not pending. Pending 510(k)s are not public, so no search corroborates the filing, the 2026-08-21 request or the Q1 2027 target; a wrong identifier is a disclosure-control failure, and only FDA's acknowledgment and information letters settle them, both requested. The first submission also covers two of five assays: NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium wait on a pivotal study of 1,150 patients at four sites enrolling since July 2026, with results due in Q2 2027 [S25, S133, S185, S186].

CLIA matters more. Troponin imprecision of 11.8% at the 99th-percentile cutoff exceeds the 10% criterion that separates a high-sensitivity assay from a contemporary one; the 98.7% headline is categorical agreement, not bias and imprecision, from one site run by company staff.
