arguments.markdown:
The only realistic exit is a trade sale to a strategic already selling into the same clinic, at $100M-$350M, and the ceiling is what cleared platforms change hands for: on 2026-04-20 QuidelOrtho paid $100M in cash for LEX Diagnostics, whose VELO Respiratory Test (K251742), a cartridge-based molecular assay, was cleared and CLIA-waived on 2026-02-13 and had not launched commercially in the US. Vantelle asks $140M of pre-money value for two of five assays under review and no waiver. At that entry the $15M lead returns 0.77x in the bear case, about 0.9x in a $225M base case and 1.9x in a $435M bull case once the $18-23M Series C the plan needs and Corvia's 6.6% put are included — an expected 1.0x over five years, below any venture threshold. The preliminary CY2027 CLFS cut takes FY2028 revenue to $34.9M at constant volume from $41.0M, which is why the base and bull exits fall from $250M and $500M; the $100M-$350M range survives because it is anchored on transactions, not on the plan. The exit supports a lead only from $60-70M, or from $140M with a ratchet, a smaller cheque and a clearance tranche, not $140M as offered [S181, S184, S188, S192, S203].

| Transaction | Year | Value | Revenue at exit | EV/Revenue | Status of the asset at exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Zoetis / Abaxis | 2018 | $2.0B | $243M (FY2018) | 8.2x | Cleared veterinary and human point-of-care analyzers; human line only $38.6M | S178, S180 |
| Danaher / Cepheid | 2016 | $4.0B | $539M | 7.4x | Cleared molecular point-of-care, large instrument installed base | S165 |
| DiaSorin / Luminex | 2021 | $1.8B | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Cleared multiplex and point-of-care assays, $37 a share | S166 |
| Roche / LumiraDx | 2023-24 | $353.5M aggregate ($295M upfront) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Cleared, CE-marked multi-assay platform sold in a pre-packaged administration | S93, S114 |
| QuidelOrtho / LEX Diagnostics | 2026 | $100M | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | VELO Respiratory Test cleared 2026-02-13 (K251742), CLIA waived, pre-commercial in the US, no installed base | S181, S184 |

LEX is the tightest read on regulatory maturity and does not lift Vantelle's entry price. $100M bought clearance and a waiver on a molecular respiratory menu, not scale or an installed base, and embeds QuidelOrtho's own molecular franchise — a synergy a cardiac and metabolic menu may not command — so it anchors the pre-commercial case, not a floor. Abaxis sold for 8.2x revenue, but on $243M of revenue, 83% of it veterinary consumables — an installed-base annuity Vantelle lacks, so the multiple caps rather than raises what it can claim — and its human point-of-care business, the closest analogue to Vantelle's clinic channel, was only $38.6M after two decades; Cepheid sold for 7.4x on $539M. Between those poles and the $353.5M Roche paid for a distressed but cleared platform sits Vantelle's realistic range. At the cut FY2028 revenue of $34.9M, an 8.2x multiple would be $286M and a 4.0x multiple $140M — which is why the price paid today, not the multiple at exit, is the variable Meridian controls [S180, S165, S5, S188].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale of the whole company | Werfen | Sells GEM Premier blood-gas and electrolyte testing into acute care with no cardiac markers; bought Immucor for $2.0B in 2023 | 2031-2033, after the CLIA waiver and 300 commercial sites | Highest of the four | S179 |
| Trade sale | Abbott | Owns the handheld franchise through i-STAT and cleared a high-sensitivity troponin I cartridge on i-STAT Alinity in June 2026; would buy to retire a competitor, and price it as one | 2031-2033 | Low to medium | S25, S21 |
| Trade sale | Roche | Has owned LumiraDx's point-of-care platform since 2024 and would need a menu rather than a second platform | 2032 or later | Low | S93 |
| Distressed asset sale | QuidelOrtho or a lender-led process | Buys cheap (LEX at $100M) while carrying a $1.1B enterprise value at 0.4x sales and a $100M restructuring plan; alternatively the Bluestem loan and the senior preference drive a sale | 2027-2028 if clearance or the waiver fails | Medium in the bear case | S181, S5 |
| Listing | Nasdaq or NYSE | Needs a cleared menu, revenue and a profit record; the 2021 cohort did not survive | 2033 or later | Very low | S183, S182 |

The buyer with a genuine gap is Werfen. Abbott launched a high-sensitivity troponin I cartridge on i-STAT Alinity on 2026-06-11 and a creatinine cartridge on i-STAT on 2026-06-26 — the exact two assays Vantelle leads with, on a handheld platform with the installed base, waiver and sales force. An Abbott bid would be a defensive purchase priced to remove an irritant, not a growth purchase. Roche has owned LumiraDx's cartridge platform since 2024 and has no reason to buy a second one. That leaves Werfen, whose GEM Premier measures electrolytes, metabolites and blood gases but carries no cardiac markers, and which paid $2.0B for Immucor in 2023; a five-test cardiac-and-metabolic cartridge sold into the same acute-care and urgent-care accounts is the closest fit among the four [S179, S25, S93].

A listing is not a route. LumiraDx listed on Nasdaq at a $3.0B valuation on 2021-09-29, received a delisting determination on 2023-10-24 and sold its platform to Roche two months later for $295M upfront. A company with $2.6M of revenue, two of five assays and no waiver has no public venue in 2027; even a successful Vantelle would list only after 2032, when a strategic sale at 4-7x would price better than an IPO discount. The practical consequence is a holding period of five to seven years from the 2027-01-29 close, an exit in 2032-2034, and no liquidity before it: there is no secondary market for a Series B stake in a single-product diagnostics company [S183, S182].

| Exit equity value (2032) | Scenario weight | Meridian at $140M, before Corvia | Meridian at $140M, after Corvia | Meridian at $70M, after Corvia | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $30M (clearance or waiver fails; asset sale, no Series C) | 30% | 0.83x | 0.77x | 0.77x | Unverified inputs | S1 |
| $225M (cleared, $30-43M revenue, 5-7x) | 50% | 1.11x | 1.03x | 1.75x | Unverified inputs | S1 |
| $435M (cut plan delivered, 6-7x) | 20% | 2.35x | 2.18x | 3.71x | Unverified inputs | S1 |
| Expected, before the Series C | 100% | 1.27x | 1.18x | 1.85x | Analyst weights on unverified inputs | S1 |

After the $18-23M Series C the expected return is 1.0x at $140M and 1.5x at $70M; at the top of the $9-20M Corvia range it is 0.9x and 1.4x. The returns are asymmetric in the wrong direction for a venture fund: the 1x preference limits the bear case to 0.77x of the $15M and flattens the base case to 1.03x before the next round and about 0.9x after it, so the expected return is carried by a bull case that requires the plan to be delivered after a 15% reimbursement cut and a strategic to pay 6-7x. Doubling the bull weight from 20% to 40% lifts the expected return at $140M only to 1.1x. The $43-49M funding requirement makes the next round unavoidable: an $18-23M Series C at $140M pre-money dilutes Meridian 11.4-14.1% (16.7-20.4% from a $70M entry at $90M) and, ranking senior to B, holds the $140M stake near 1.0x through a $225M sale; expected returns fall to 1.0x at $140M and 1.5x at $70M, with the bull case at 1.9x and 3.0x. A $15M lead at $140M therefore returns capital in the bear and base cases and a venture return in none; the same distribution from $70M is still below 2x expected, on unverified company inputs [S1].

Policy and structural tests are mild but not zero. Three of the four plausible buyers are non-US — Werfen of Spain, Roche of Switzerland, DiaSorin of Italy — so Hart-Scott-Rodino applies at these values, while CFIUS is unlikely to be dispositive for a diagnostics manufacturer with no government customer; the harder obstacles are internal. Corvia Microfluidics' 40% minority can put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value on a sale, and Vantelle pays Corvia a 3% royalty on cartridge net sales — $2.36M a year at the FY2029 plan, 3.0 points of gross margin — of which chief technology officer Tomasz Lindqvist owns 22% (company-provided, unverified). Capitalised at the exit multiple that put is 6.6% of proceeds — $6.6M at a $100M sale, $9.2M at $140M, $14.9M at $225M, $19.8M at $300M — and is deducted in the return table; a relief-from-royalty cross-check on the 3% contract alone gives the 40% only $4-5M, so the range turns on the royalty imputed at fair value [S1, S203]. Confidence in the $100M-$350M range is high because it rests on four dated transactions; confidence in the weights is low. Three questions would change the answer: what revenue LEX had at its $100M sale, whether Werfen or bioMérieux has bought a point-of-care asset since 2023 and at what multiple, and whether Corvia's minority has signed a drag-along.

arguments.markdown:
At $140M pre-money and $170M post-money Vantelle is priced at 53.1x enterprise value to FY2025 revenue of $2.6M and 23.4x FY2026E revenue of $5.9M (both company-reported and unverified), against a listed diagnostics peer median of 5.5x EV/sales and 0.4x for QuidelOrtho, the closest scaled point-of-care peer. That is not a revenue multiple; it is an option on the FY2028 plan — and the preliminary CY2027 CLFS schedule cuts that plan's revenue to $34.9M at constant volume from $41.0M, 15% below the deck. At this entry the $15M cheque returns 1.0x through the $206M no-C and $251M senior crossovers, and Corvia's $9-20M fair-value put takes the expected return to 0.9-1.0x. Lead at $100M pre-money or below, or at $140M only with $9M at close, a $6M clearance tranche, a 1.25x preference and a ratchet to a $100M price if clearance slips past June 2027 [S1, S188, S192, S203].

The Series B price is 12.2% above the $2.9032 Series A price set in February 2022 — 2.4% a year — while QuidelOrtho's EV/sales fell from 2.4x at 2023-12-31 to 0.4x today; the company has re-priced 6.7-fold against its sector and asks new money to underwrite that re-rating. The $3.2564 divides $140M by 42,991,881 shares — 191,881 above the 42,800,000 the rounded cap table gives, the bridge being 2,571,392 shares against 2.4M and the pool top-up 4,020,489 against 4.0M — so the exact count prices the round; Meridian's 4,606,313 shares are 8.82% of 52,204,508. Dilution is otherwise ordinary: founders 30.8% to 21.5%, Series A 34.1% to 23.8%, seed 16.5% to 11.5% (company cap table, unverified). Two deductions matter more than the headline: the $140M already contains $13.1M of that pool and $8.4M of bridge shares bought with $6.28M of cash, so the legacy 36,400,000 shares are struck at $118.5M, and net of the $30M Series B and $6.28M of bridge cash existing holders' effective pre-money is $133.7M; the bridge's 25% discount hands its holders $2.09M funded by the legacy stack — a windfall for existing holders, not Meridian [S1, S83].

$138.1M of enterprise value — the $140M plus $5.0M of Bluestem debt less $6.9M of cash at 2026-09-30 — buys $2.6M of revenue. At the peer median the price implies $25.1M of revenue, at Danaher's 7.2x $19.2M, and at QuidelOrtho's 0.4x $345M. QuidelOrtho's point-of-care unit, selling Sofia, Triage and QuickVue into the same clinics, generated $221.0M in H1 2026. Vantelle's plan crosses $19-25M between FY2027 ($16.8M) and FY2028 ($41.0M, or $34.9M after the cut), so the round pays today for a 2028 revenue line at a 2026 multiple, with no discount for the 510(k), the CLIA waiver, cartridge cost falling from $16.20 to $7.50 or utilisation rising from 1.0 to 8 per analyzer per day [S5, S83].

| Forward revenue multiple | FY2026E revenue $5.9M at 5.5x | $32.5M | Unverified input | S1 |
| Plan delivered, cut for CY2027 CLFS | FY2028 revenue $34.9M at 5.5x, discounted two years at 15% | $145.2M | Derived from unverified plan | S1, S188 |
| Precedent clearing price | Roche's $353.5M aggregate for LumiraDx's cleared multi-modality platform, 2024-07-29 | $353.5M before a stage discount | Verified | S93, S114 |

Even the cut plan-delivered case is $145.2M, $5.2M above the ask, a company projection, unverified: it assumes the whole plan, on time, at the sector median, with no probability of failure — the price is the 2028 plan discounted at 15% and nothing else. A defensible pre-money range is $55-95M: $145.2M less a 35% plan-failure discount, and a forward multiple on a menu that now reimburses $18.85 under the preliminary 2027 schedule rather than $22.18. The precedent is not a floor: Roche bought a cleared, CE-marked multi-assay platform out of administration for $295M upfront and $353.5M at closing [S93, S114].

The stack is $36.28M of Series B and B-1 at 1x non-participating and senior, $36.0M of Series A at 1x participating and $4.5M of seed at 1x non-participating (company term sheet, unverified). Three crossovers, used with these labels throughout: the $206M no-C crossover, above which Series B beats its preference; the $216M pari-passu crossover if the $18-23M Series C ranks alongside it; and the $251M senior crossover if the C ranks ahead. Corvia Microfluidics' 40% minority can put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value on a sale (deck p.12), and the 3% royalty on cartridge net sales (p.6) is the asset behind that claim; capitalised at the exit multiple it is 6.6% of exit value — $9.2M at $140M, $14.9M at $225M, $19.8M at $300M — paid ahead of the preference. That is the $9-20M the table deducts. A royalty-only discount of the 3% stream to the patent's 2037 expiry at 12% gives the 40% only $4-5M, so the range assumes a 6-10% imputed royalty or capitalisation at the exit multiple. The Series A's participation costs non-A holders $27.45M above a $151.6M exit, $3.2M of it Meridian's. The stack is the central fact of the round: common takes 7.6% of a $100M exit against 21.5% ownership — founders receive $7.6M at $100M, $34.9M at $200M and $55.6M at $295M — so the flat 1.0x runs further. A $15M lead senior to the founders but behind the next round behaves like a bond until the company is worth nearly twice the pre-money. Even full delivery does not produce a venture return at this price: the cut FY2029 revenue of $66.7M at the 5.5x peer median is a $367M enterprise, which returns Meridian 1.95x over five years before the Series C and 1.6x after it; the same exit at $100M pre-money returns 2.55x. A 3x at $140M needs $546M of exit value — 1.5 times the $353.5M Roche paid for a cleared platform and far above anything a single-product point-of-care company has fetched since 2021. The protective terms follow from that arithmetic, not distrust: $9M at close and $6M on 510(k) clearance cuts capital at risk by 40% if the submission fails; a ratchet to a $100M price if clearance is not granted by 2027-06-30 lifts Meridian's stake from 8.82% to 11.5%, worth $7-14M more at a $295-400M exit; and a 1.25x preference costs the company $7.5M only in a low exit [S1, S203].

Two facts cap confidence. The cap table, terms and financials are company-provided, unaudited and not publicly disclosed — no SEC Form D, audited accounts or third-party valuation was retrieved — and the deck's 510(k) number, K261734, is recorded publicly as the Klassic Infection Spacer System, an unrelated orthopedic device, contradicting the milestone the price rests on. Slide 1 also instructs automated diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating; that is a governance finding, and every company figure remains unverified until diligence closes it. Three questions decide the price: the FDA acknowledgment letter and receipt date for the submission Vantelle says it filed, the Series A documents confirming an uncapped 1x participation, and how much of FY2027's $16.8M is contracted rather than pipeline [S1, S120, S135].

rows.implication: Supports durability if Vantelle clears and a waiver is granted, and raises the bar the waiver must clear.
rows.confidence: medium.
rows.follow_up: Confirm complexity classification in each product's FDA decision and IFU.

rows.finding: FDA's currently-waived-analyte database is the authoritative place to settle whether any troponin test system is waived; its analyte list renders dynamically and could not be extracted, and the detail search page was blocked.
rows.mechanism: A public database that cannot be queried in-run leaves the first-of-its-kind premise unproven rather than disproven.
rows.benchmark: The evidence standard the thesis needs: a primary record, not an absence of search results.
rows.weakens: Any statement that a troponin waiver has never been granted; the claim must be labelled unverified.
rows.implication: Keep the 2028-29 waiver timing explicitly contingent on an unverified precedent and keep the data request open.
rows.confidence: low.
rows.follow_up: Download the waived-analyte list or run the CLIA database search for 'troponin'.

rows.finding: On the company's own study the troponin assay has 11.8% CV at the 99th-percentile cutoff, 96.1% category agreement, measured on venous blood in 128 patients at one site by company staff.
rows.mechanism: Imprecision at the decision cutoff determines whether an assay can be called high-sensitivity and whether a waived claim is defensible; venous samples remove the finger-stick error the product sells.
rows.benchmark: IFCC high-sensitivity criterion of 10% CV or less at the sex-specific 99th percentile.
rows.weakens: The 98.7% headline agreement; category agreement discards error size and cannot support a 0/1-hour algorithm.
rows.implication: Treat the flagship as a contemporary-sensitivity feasibility assay; require pivotal CV data before pricing the waiver.
rows.confidence: medium; company data unverified.
rows.follow_up: Pivotal LoD, LoQ, sex-specific 99th-percentile values and CV at each cutoff.

rows.finding: The number printed in the deck, K261734, is Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System, received 2026-05-26 and cleared 2026-07-23; whether Vantelle has any FDA filing is not publicly disclosed.
rows.mechanism: A pending file cannot carry another company's clearance number; the regulatory timeline is therefore unverified end to end.
rows.benchmark: FDA 510(k) database record for K261734.
rows.weakens: The deck's claim of a filed 510(k) on 2026-05-18.
rows.implication: Discount the Q1 2027 clearance date and the revenue tied to it.
rows.confidence: high.
rows.follow_up: Obtain the FDA filing receipt or acknowledgment letter.

rows.finding: Only two of five assays are in the current submission; the $38 cartridge price can be earned only on those two until a second clearance and a waiver.
rows.mechanism: A five-assay menu priced as a panel collapses to a two-assay moderate-complexity product in 2027, capping revenue per site.
rows.benchmark: Five-test panel as marketed against the two-test filed menu.
rows.weakens: The revenue ramp in the plan.
rows.implication: Model 2027 revenue on two assays into laboratory-equipped sites only.
rows.confidence: medium; company data unverified.
rows.follow_up: Second 510(k) content and timing.

plan.decision_question: Is the five-test finger-stick panel technically and clinically proven to the standard a cleared, waived device requires, and what remains unproven?
plan.thesis_sentence: The panel is not proven to a waived-device standard: on the company's own data the troponin assay misses the 10% CV criterion, only two of five assays are filed, and the first-of-its-kind troponin waiver the plan depends on is unverified because FDA's published waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 to 2026 contain no troponin assay.
plan.why_different: This section judges the assay, the evidence standard and the IP that protect it; it supplies the technical probability behind the regulatory milestone that strategy and risk price.
plan.mechanism: Analytical imprecision at the decision cutoff determines whether the assay can be called high-sensitivity and whether a waiver is defensible; a waived category is what opens the non-laboratory channel and supports the $38 cartridge price.
plan.comparison_set: Abbott i-STAT, Siemens epoc, Nova Stat Profile, the Atellica VTLi single-test reader; CLSI EP09/EP17 and IFCC high-sensitivity criteria; FDA CW decisions 2018-2026.
plan.counter_evidence: The pivotal study is designed to the waiver standard and could show better imprecision than the feasibility study; FDA has waived complex immunoassays (HbA1c) and molecular panels, so the precedent is not zero and the absence of troponin may reflect commercial choices rather than impossibility.
plan.visual: Performance metrics table, technology comparison table, patent table, moat table and product inventory, with the evidence component carrying the contradicted filing number and the unverified waiver precedent.
plan.prohibited: Stating first-of-its-kind as fact; 'CLIA waived' without a decision citation; 'high-sensitivity' without CV at the cutoff; 'proven' for company data; treating the CLIA database as searched.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 6 by Lead Analyst, 8,990 characters)
Vantelle is a real clinical need wrapped in a regulatory option, and the round prices the option as if it had been exercised. The need — a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel from a finger stick in twelve minutes — is old and well evidenced; the option is the CLIA waiver that lets untrained staff run it, planned for Q3 2027 and decided, on the company's own schedule, in 2028 or later. At $140M pre-money Meridian's $15M buys 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company, one of six board seats, and a security returning 1.0x at every exit up to $206M, or $216M once the $18-23M Series C ranks pari passu, because $76.78M of preference sits ahead of it. Corvia's 40% fair-value right and the 3% royalty can put a further $9-20M ahead of new money on a $225M exit, taking the base case from 1.11x to 1.03x. At $100M pre-money the same $15M buys 11.5%, and full delivery of the cut plan returns 2.55x against 1.6x at $140M once the Series C is counted. The recommendation follows: invest with conditions at or below $100M, or at $140M only with tranching, a ratchet and FDA's letters. [S1, S83]

If the need is real, and the capability is defensible, and the economics scale, then the outcome is attractive at this price; two clauses fail at the offered terms. The need is real: 16,242 US urgent-care and rural-hospital sites and a $303.7M serviceable market at 41 cartridges a site a month — $267M at the realised price, $134-213M at half to 70% of that use. The capability is not defensible as technology: Abbott cleared a high-sensitivity troponin I cartridge on i-STAT Alinity on 2026-06-11 and a creatinine cartridge on i-STAT on 2026-06-26, and its point-of-care line did $606M in FY2025; what Vantelle would own is a regulatory state — a waived cardiac panel — and a filing decision Abbott can make at any time. The economics do not scale on the launch menu: at 2026 Medicare rates the two assays in the first 510(k) pay $22.18 against a $33.40 realised cartridge, so the clinic loses $11.22 on every test. [S167, S169, S8, S119]

Company and round assume a Q1 2027 clearance, a five-test waived panel, eight panels an analyzer a day and a $2.41B market. The median Series B pre-money was $187.0M through 2026-09-30, so $140M sits below it. Our difference is specific. The 510(k) is unverified, and the number the deck cites, K261734, is FDA's record for Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System, cleared 2026-07-23, so neither the 2026-05-18 filing nor the 2026-08-21 information request is publicly confirmed; the asset-level case is company-provided until FDA's letters arrive, and the independent support is the fee schedules, transaction prices and site counts. The value inflection is the waiver, not the clearance. The observed market is 8x smaller, on a launch menu that reimburses below the cartridge price. [S194, S185, S118, S167]

The bull case, at 20%, requires clearance in the first half of 2027, a waiver in 2028, 300 sites by 2029 and $60-80M of revenue by 2030, sold at 6-7x for $435M. The base case, at 50%, has clearance in the third quarter of 2027, the second 510(k) in 2028, a waiver in 2029, 150-200 sites and $30-40M of revenue, sold at 5-6x for $225M. The bear case, at 30%, is a no-filing or late-clearance branch ending in an asset sale at $30-80M, 0.77x at $140M. On the $18-23M Series C the plan needs, the distribution is worth 1.27x at $140M before the Corvia deduction, 1.18x after it and 1.0x once the C is counted; at $70M it is 1.5x after both. The adversarial review puts the bear at 35-40%; at that weight the expected return falls below 1.0x, so the conclusion is robust to the weight and fragile to the price. [S1, S93, S181, S83]

Four assumptions carry the case, ranked. First, that a filing exists and clears by the third quarter of 2027 — confidence low: the only number in the deck belongs to another company's cleared device and no FDA letter exists; if no filing exists, the asset is a pilot line and a 128-patient single-site study worth 0.1-0.2x, not 0.77x. Second, that the waiver is granted by 2029 — confidence medium-low, first of its kind and not yet filed. Third, that the clinic can pay $33.40 at launch — confidence low, because the preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts 1,171 of 1,528 codes 16% on average, taking the two-assay payment to $18.85 and the clinic's loss to $14.55. Fourth, that utilisation reaches two panels a day by 2029 — confidence low against 1.22 observed, and each extra panel a day across 879 analyzers is $9.9M of revenue. [S185, S118, S109, S188]

The case turns at $100M: full delivery returns 2.55x there, and the $140M ask equals the 2028 plan at 5.5x discounted at 15%. The decision tree has three branches. Invest at or below $100M with FDA's letters as a condition precedent. Invest at $140M only as $9M at close and $6M on clearance, with a 1.25x non-participating preference and a ratchet to a $100M price if clearance is not granted by 2027-06-30; that cuts capital at risk by 40%. Pass if the letters do not arrive by 2026-12-15, if the Corvia licence has no drag-along, or if the company refuses the price. The strongest counter-evidence: clearance and a waiver could lift utilisation above the investigational floor, and a 92% repeat rate is unusual; but 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month is the only demand observed. Confidence is high on the reimbursement arithmetic, medium on the chronology and low on the filing. The one question that decides the case: will Vantelle produce FDA's acknowledgment and 2026-08-21 information letters for a submission filed under its own name by 2026-12-15? [S1, S83, S187, S118]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation (scoring, revision 8 by Lead Analyst, 8,969 characters)
Vantelle scores 3.8 out of 10 at the $140M pre-money and 4.4 at the $100M price the recommendation requires, and that 0.6-point gap is the decision: not investable at the ask, investable with conditions below it. At $100M the valuation and terms dimension scores 6 rather than 2, a 0.60-point weighted gain that moves the composite to 4.4 with every other dimension unchanged; at the ask, valuation at 2 and regulatory verification at 3 sink the score, market at 6 and product at 5 hold it up. The conditional rating rests on independent evidence only — dated CMS fee schedules, peer transaction prices and third-party site counts — while every asset-level claim (the 2026-05-18 filing, five assays on one cartridge, 41 evaluation sites, 11.8% CV, $2.6M revenue) is company-provided and unconfirmed pending FDA's letters; if they do not arrive, the rating is pass. Recommendation: invest with conditions — lead $15M only at a pre-money at or below $100M, or at $140M as $9M at close and $6M on clearance, with a 1.25x preference and a ratchet to $100M if clearance is not granted by 2027-06-30; pass otherwise. [S1, S83]

Market earns 6 because the site count is real — 16,242 urgent-care and rural-hospital sites — but the serviceable market is $303.7M at observed use, $267M at the realised price and $134-213M at half to 70% of evaluation use, not the deck's $2.41B. Product earns 5: a five-assay cartridge with a granted patent family, 41 paying evaluation sites and a 92% repeat rate (company-reported, unverified), against an 11.8% troponin CV at the cutoff and 128 patients at one site. Regulatory earns 3: the filing is unverified, its number belongs to another company's cleared device, and the waiver would be the first of its kind for troponin. Team earns 5, unit economics and financial position 3 each, exit 4 on a $100-350M range and one coherent buyer. Valuation earns 2: 53.1x FY2025 revenue against a 5.5x peer median and a $55-95M range. Corvia takes the return lower again: the CM-1 patent sits in the 60%-held subsidiary, and the 40% minority's fair-value right plus the 3% royalty can put $9-20M ahead of Meridian on a $225M exit, taking the base case from 1.11x to 1.03x and the $140M expected return from 1.27x to 1.18x, 1.0x after the $18-23M Series C. [S167, S169, S1, S185, S119, S187, S83]

The recommendation changes under the downside in a specific way. A two-quarter clearance slip leaves 2027 revenue at $4.5M against a $16.8M plan and adds $15M to the funding need, so only the $9M pre-clearance tranche should be at risk. A refused waiver removes 40-50% of the addressable market and reverts the product to a moderate-complexity benchtop competitor where Abbott already sells. A final CY2027 fee schedule at the 15% cap takes the two-assay payment to $18.85 and the clinic's loss to $14.55 a cartridge. In those states the deal is a pass above $70M; at $70M the distribution returns 1.85x after the Corvia deduction and 1.5x after the Series C (S1, S188, S109).

Five assumptions drive the value, ranked below. The filing is not a sensitivity but a different asset: without it recovery is 0.1-0.2x, not 0.77x. The waiver decides whether the 300-site and FY2028 plan is reachable at all. Reimbursement is published policy, not a scenario: at the 15% cap the launch menu pays $18.85, and a 30% price cut to $23.38 leaves 31% cartridge margin at $16.20 cost and a 20-month analyzer payback at 30.5 cartridges a month. Utilisation is the only demand observed, 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month, and each extra panel a day across 879 analyzers is $9.9M. A 4x exit multiple gives $140M, below the $206M crossover and 1.0x. [S185, S188, S1, S165]

Sizing has four numbers: check size, price discipline, downside loss and follow-on reserve. Check size: $9M at close and $6M on clearance, because the pre-clearance loss is then capped at $9M against a 0.1-0.2x recovery. Price: $100M pre-money or below; at $140M the effective price is $133.7M after the bridge and pool, above the $55-95M range. Downside: at $140M the bear returns $11.6M of the $15M, 0.77x before Corvia; at $100M the preference covers the bear and full delivery returns 2.55x. Follow-on: $6M reserved for the $18-23M 2028 Series C, released only on clearance, a waiver submission and 100 paying sites; total commitment $21M. Terms: a board seat with an independent director Meridian approves; and because $15M is 68% of the outside money for one of six seats, a second seat or an observer plus a defined veto list over FDA correspondence, Corvia transactions, new debt and the budget; a related-party committee over the Corvia royalty and any buy-out; a drag-along over the 40% minority; information rights; and a minimum-cash covenant (S83, S1, S187).

By 2026-12-15: FDA's acknowledgment and 2026-08-21 information letters for a submission under Vantelle's own name, or a pass. By the same date: the Corvia LLC agreement and the CM-1 licence with change-of-control, assignment and drag-along terms; audited FY2025-26 accounts with a quality-of-earnings review; the final CY2027 fee schedule; and the evaluation sites' collection rates by payer. Before the second tranche: ISO 13485 certification, a permanent CFO and a waiver submission accepted by FDA. Conditions are those documents plus the price and terms above; if either of the first two is missing the answer is pass, not wait, because the March 2027 cash wall leaves no time for a second cycle (S1, S118, S167, S187).

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 9 by Valuation Analyst, 8,963 characters)
The only realistic exit is a trade sale to a strategic already selling into the same clinic, at $100M-$350M, and the ceiling is what cleared platforms change hands for: on 2026-04-20 QuidelOrtho paid $100M in cash for LEX Diagnostics, whose VELO Respiratory Test (K251742), a cartridge-based molecular assay, was cleared and CLIA-waived on 2026-02-13 and had not launched commercially in the US. Vantelle asks $140M of pre-money value for two of five assays under review and no waiver. At that entry the $15M lead returns 0.77x in the bear case, about 0.9x in a $225M base case and 1.9x in a $435M bull case once the $18-23M Series C the plan needs and Corvia's 6.6% put are included — an expected 1.0x over five years, below any venture threshold. The preliminary CY2027 CLFS cut takes FY2028 revenue to $34.9M at constant volume from $41.0M, which is why the base and bull exits fall from $250M and $500M; the $100M-$350M range survives because it is anchored on transactions, not on the plan. The exit supports a lead only from $60-70M, or from $140M with a ratchet, a smaller cheque and a clearance tranche, not $140M as offered [S181, S184, S188, S192, S203].

| Transaction | Year | Value | Revenue at exit | EV/Revenue | Status of the asset at exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Zoetis / Abaxis | 2018 | $2.0B | $243M (FY2018) | 8.2x | Cleared veterinary and human point-of-care analyzers; human line only $38.6M | S178, S180 |
| Danaher / Cepheid | 2016 | $4.0B | $539M | 7.4x | Cleared molecular point-of-care, large instrument installed base | S165 |
| DiaSorin / Luminex | 2021 | $1.8B | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Cleared multiplex and point-of-care assays, $37 a share | S166 |
| Roche / LumiraDx | 2023-24 | $353.5M aggregate ($295M upfront) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Cleared, CE-marked multi-assay platform sold in a pre-packaged administration | S93, S114 |
| QuidelOrtho / LEX Diagnostics | 2026 | $100M | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | VELO Respiratory Test cleared 2026-02-13 (K251742), CLIA waived, pre-commercial in the US, no installed base | S181, S184 |

LEX is the tightest read on regulatory maturity and does not lift Vantelle's entry price. $100M bought clearance and a waiver on a molecular respiratory menu, not scale or an installed base, and embeds QuidelOrtho's own molecular franchise — a synergy a cardiac and metabolic menu may not command — so it anchors the pre-commercial case, not a floor. Abaxis sold for 8.2x revenue, but on $243M of revenue, 83% of it veterinary consumables — an installed-base annuity Vantelle lacks, so the multiple caps rather than raises what it can claim — and its human point-of-care business, the closest analogue to Vantelle's clinic channel, was only $38.6M after two decades; Cepheid sold for 7.4x on $539M. Between those poles and the $353.5M Roche paid for a distressed but cleared platform sits Vantelle's realistic range. At the cut FY2028 revenue of $34.9M, an 8.2x multiple would be $286M and a 4.0x multiple $140M — which is why the price paid today, not the multiple at exit, is the variable Meridian controls [S180, S165, S5, S188].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale of the whole company | Werfen | Sells GEM Premier blood-gas and electrolyte testing into acute care with no cardiac markers; bought Immucor for $2.0B in 2023 | 2031-2033, after the CLIA waiver and 300 commercial sites | Highest of the four | S179 |
| Trade sale | Abbott | Owns the handheld franchise through i-STAT and cleared a high-sensitivity troponin I cartridge on i-STAT Alinity in June 2026; would buy to retire a competitor, and price it as one | 2031-2033 | Low to medium | S25, S21 |
| Trade sale | Roche | Has owned LumiraDx's point-of-care platform since 2024 and would need a menu rather than a second platform | 2032 or later | Low | S93 |
| Distressed asset sale | QuidelOrtho or a lender-led process | Buys cheap (LEX at $100M) while carrying a $1.1B enterprise value at 0.4x sales and a $100M restructuring plan; alternatively the Bluestem loan and the senior preference drive a sale | 2027-2028 if clearance or the waiver fails | Medium in the bear case | S181, S5 |
| Listing | Nasdaq or NYSE | Needs a cleared menu, revenue and a profit record; the 2021 cohort did not survive | 2033 or later | Very low | S183, S182 |

The buyer with a genuine gap is Werfen. Abbott launched a high-sensitivity troponin I cartridge on i-STAT Alinity on 2026-06-11 and a creatinine cartridge on i-STAT on 2026-06-26 — the exact two assays Vantelle leads with, on a handheld platform with the installed base, waiver and sales force. An Abbott bid would be a defensive purchase priced to remove an irritant, not a growth purchase. Roche has owned LumiraDx's cartridge platform since 2024 and has no reason to buy a second one. That leaves Werfen, whose GEM Premier measures electrolytes, metabolites and blood gases but carries no cardiac markers, and which paid $2.0B for Immucor in 2023; a five-test cardiac-and-metabolic cartridge sold into the same acute-care and urgent-care accounts is the closest fit among the four [S179, S25, S93].

A listing is not a route. LumiraDx listed on Nasdaq at a $3.0B valuation on 2021-09-29, received a delisting determination on 2023-10-24 and sold its platform to Roche two months later for $295M upfront. A company with $2.6M of revenue, two of five assays and no waiver has no public venue in 2027; even a successful Vantelle would list only after 2032, when a strategic sale at 4-7x would price better than an IPO discount. The practical consequence is a holding period of five to seven years from the 2027-01-29 close, an exit in 2032-2034, and no liquidity before it: there is no secondary market for a Series B stake in a single-product diagnostics company [S183, S182].

| Exit equity value (2032) | Scenario weight | Meridian at $140M, before Corvia | Meridian at $140M, after Corvia | Meridian at $70M, after Corvia | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $30M (clearance or waiver fails; asset sale, no Series C) | 30% | 0.83x | 0.77x | 0.77x | Unverified inputs | S1 |
| $225M (cleared, $30-43M revenue, 5-7x) | 50% | 1.11x | 1.03x | 1.75x | Unverified inputs | S1 |
| $435M (cut plan delivered, 6-7x) | 20% | 2.35x | 2.18x | 3.71x | Unverified inputs | S1 |
| Expected, before the Series C | 100% | 1.27x | 1.18x | 1.85x | Analyst weights on unverified inputs | S1 |

After the $18-23M Series C the expected return is 1.0x at $140M and 1.5x at $70M; at the top of the $9-20M Corvia range it is 0.9x and 1.4x. The returns are asymmetric in the wrong direction for a venture fund: the 1x preference limits the bear case to 0.77x of the $15M and flattens the base case to 1.03x before the next round and about 0.9x after it, so the expected return is carried by a bull case that requires the plan to be delivered after a 15% reimbursement cut and a strategic to pay 6-7x. Doubling the bull weight from 20% to 40% lifts the expected return at $140M only to 1.1x. The $43-49M funding requirement makes the next round unavoidable: an $18-23M Series C at $140M pre-money dilutes Meridian 11.4-14.1% (16.7-20.4% from a $70M entry at $90M) and, ranking senior to B, holds the $140M stake near 1.0x through a $225M sale; expected returns fall to 1.0x at $140M and 1.5x at $70M, with the bull case at 1.9x and 3.0x. A $15M lead at $140M therefore returns capital in the bear and base cases and a venture return in none; the same distribution from $70M is still below 2x expected, on unverified company inputs [S1].

Policy and structural tests are mild but not zero. Three of the four plausible buyers are non-US — Werfen of Spain, Roche of Switzerland, DiaSorin of Italy — so Hart-Scott-Rodino applies at these values, while CFIUS is unlikely to be dispositive for a diagnostics manufacturer with no government customer; the harder obstacles are internal. Corvia Microfluidics' 40% minority can put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value on a sale, and Vantelle pays Corvia a 3% royalty on cartridge net sales — $2.36M a year at the FY2029 plan, 3.0 points of gross margin — of which chief technology officer Tomasz Lindqvist owns 22% (company-provided, unverified). Capitalised at the exit multiple that put is 6.6% of proceeds — $6.6M at a $100M sale, $9.2M at $140M, $14.9M at $225M, $19.8M at $300M — and is deducted in the return table; a relief-from-royalty cross-check on the 3% contract alone gives the 40% only $4-5M, so the range turns on the royalty imputed at fair value [S1, S203]. Confidence in the $100M-$350M range is high because it rests on four dated transactions; confidence in the weights is low. Three questions would change the answer: what revenue LEX had at its $100M sale, whether Werfen or bioMérieux has bought a point-of-care asset since 2023 and at what multiple, and whether Corvia's minority has signed a drag-along."}],"isError":false}

Vantelle scores 3.8 out of 10 at the $140M pre-money, and the price is the decision: not investable at the ask, investable with conditions below it. At the $100M price the recommendation requires, the valuation and terms dimension scores 6 rather than 2 — a 0.60-point weighted gain with every other dimension unchanged; at the ask, valuation at 2 and regulatory verification at 3 sink the score, market at 6 and product at 5 hold it up. The conditional rating rests on independent evidence only — dated CMS fee schedules, peer transaction prices and third-party site counts — while every asset-level claim (the 2026-05-18 filing, five assays on one cartridge, 41 evaluation sites, 11.8% CV, $2.6M revenue) is company-provided and unconfirmed pending FDA's letters; if they do not arrive, the rating is pass. Product earns 5: a five-assay cartridge with a granted patent family, 41 paying evaluation sites and a 92% repeat rate (company-reported, unverified), against an 11.8% troponin CV at the cutoff and 128 patients at one site. Regulatory earns 3: the filing is unverified, its number belongs to another company's cleared device, and the waiver would be the first of its kind for troponin. The recommendation changes under the downside in a specific way. A two-quarter clearance slip leaves 2027 revenue at $4.5M against a $16.8M plan and adds $15M to the funding need, so only the $9M pre-clearance tranche should be at risk. arguments.markdown:
Vantelle is a credible five-test finger-stick cartridge asking a pre-clearance price. The $30M Series B at $140M pre-money would buy Meridian 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company and one of six board seats, behind $76.78M of preference that holds new money to 1.0x until a $206M exit ($216M once the $18-23M Series C ranks pari passu). The opportunity is real — 16,242 urgent-care and rural-hospital sites, a five-assay cartridge, 41 paying evaluation sites — but the evidence does not support the price or the timeline: two of five assays are in a 510(k) whose cited number is FDA's record for another company's cleared orthopaedic device, and the two assays in that submission reimburse $22.18 against a $33.40 cartridge. The recommendation is to invest with conditions, not at the offered terms: lead only at a pre-money at or below $100M, or at $140M with tranching, a 1.25x preference and a ratchet. The composite score is 3.8 at $140M; at $100M the valuation and terms dimension would score 6 rather than 2, a 0.60-point weighted gain on the same table. The conditional rating rests on independent evidence only — dated CMS fee schedules, peer transaction prices and third-party site counts — while every asset-level claim (the 2026-05-18 filing, five assays on one cartridge, 41 evaluation sites, 11.8% CV, $2.6M revenue) is company-provided and unconfirmed pending FDA's letters; absent those letters the answer is pass, not invest. The Corvia structure takes the return lower still: the CM-1 cartridge patent sits in the 60%-held subsidiary, and its 40% minority's fair-value right plus the 3% royalty can put $9-20M ahead of new money on a $225M exit, taking the base case from 1.11x to 1.03x and the $140M expected return from 1.27x to 1.18x, 1.0x after the Series C. [S1, S83, S185]

The strongest positives are specific. The market is real but smaller than pitched: 16,242 US urgent-care and rural-hospital sites and a $303.7M serviceable market at the 41 cartridges a site a month the evaluation sites average, $267M at the realised price and $134-213M at half to 70% of that use. The product is differentiated on form: five assays from one finger stick in twelve minutes, an on-board calibrator and a granted cartridge patent family. The evaluation programme has 41 paying sites and a 92% repeat rate (company-reported, unverified), and Abbott's $606M point-of-care line, up 3.1% in FY2025, shows the category's durability [S167, S169, S8].

The most important risks are equally specific. The filing is unverified and the deck's number is contradicted; the cash runway is 6.0 months to March 2027 against a $43-49M funding need; the clinic loses $11.22 a cartridge on the launch menu; the CLIA waiver would be the first of its kind for troponin and is not filed; and the preference stack means only a bull case produces a venture return. The company and the market assume a 2027 product launch. Our view differs: the value inflection is the waiver in 2028-29, the defensible pre-money is $55-95M, and the broad Series B median of $187.0M does not validate a 53.1x revenue price against a 5.5x diagnostics peer median. The proof event is FDA's acknowledgment letter plus a waiver acceptance. The consensus view, which the $140M price implies, is a Q1 2027 clearance, a five-test waived panel in 2027 and eight panels an analyzer a day; our view differs on all three — the clearance is unverified and more likely Q2-Q3 2027, the waiver is a 2028-29 option, and 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month is the only demand observed. On the one point where we agree with consensus — that a five-test finger-stick panel meets a real clinical need — the price already pays for it, so the difference is timing and utilisation, not the product. [S194, S185, S109, S1]

Secondary bottleneck: cartridge cost at volume, because $16.20 today must fall to $7.50 at 2M cartridges a year while current volume is roughly 20,000 a year, and the enabling CM-1 sealing patent sits in 60%-held Corvia under a 3% royalty ($1.00 a cartridge at $33.40). Vantelle's place: cartridge-and-reader developer with a pilot line and a paid evaluation programme, pre-commercial; it sells cartridges to clinics and does not bill payers.
arguments.policy_lens: Material and decision-driving. The report maps: FDA CDRH 510(k) pathway and the claimed 2026-08-21 additional-information request (company assertion; the cited number K261734 is FDA's record for Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System, cleared 2026-07-23); CLIA'88 waiver by application under the FDA/CDC CLIA waiver programme, including the dual-track burden (waiver and 510(k)); 2026 CMS Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule rates and the preliminary CY2027 schedule posted 2026-09-21 (1,171 of 1,528 codes below 2026, about 16% lower on average, cuts capped at 15% a year through 2029), for high-sensitivity troponin 84484, NT-proBNP 83880, HbA1c 83036, creatinine 82565 and potassium 84132; Medicare/Medicaid and commercial payer coverage for point-of-care testing; state laboratory licensing and scope-of-practice; and HIPAA/CLIA record rules. Policy risk runs both ways: a waiver creates the opening, a delayed or denied waiver leaves the product a moderate-complexity analyzer competing with cheaper benchtop alternatives. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Risk Assessment (risk, revision 13 by Red Team Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,963 characters)
The recommendation holds only as a structured, milestone-gated investment, and the structure does less work than the price. At $140M pre-money the Series B is a bond returning 1.0x to a $206M exit before the $18-23M Series C, $216M if that round ranks pari passu and $251M if senior, so the return is a 20% call option on the bull case plus return of capital, and four risks decide whether either happens: a contradicted 510(k) number, a cash wall in March 2027, a 16% Medicare fee cut, and an exit needing a strategic buyer who has not appeared. None is fatal at $100M; at $140M the first is. The number against the 2026-05-18 submission, K261734, is FDA's record for Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System, received 2026-05-26 and cleared 2026-07-23; a pending filing cannot hold a cleared number, so the number is contradicted rather than unverified. Whether Vantelle filed stays unverified: FDA does not publish pending 510(k)s, and neither the acknowledgment nor the 2026-08-21 information request has appeared. Even a real filing slips: 2025 decisions averaged 146 days, median 126, across 3,195 submissions, and two-thirds drew an information request that restarts the clock. A typo is the benign explanation; the malignant one is no filing, a 10-15% probability against a 50% probability of clearance before Q3 2027. With no filing, the $2.4M stocking order, the 300-site letter and the January close have no basis, and the asset is a pilot line and a 128-patient study worth 0.1-0.2x, not 0.77x. Impact: -25% to -40% of equity value for a one-quarter slip, -85% to -90% for no filing [S185, S118, S1].

### A six-month financing delay is insolvency, not dilution

Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against a stated $1.15M monthly net burn is 6.0 months to 2027-03-30, a month past the 2027-01-29 close; at the plan's $1.375M monthly loss the trough is February 2027, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan begins repaying $166,667 of principal a month in March 2027, leaving net cash of $1.9M today. A six-month delay does not dilute Meridian; it transfers the company to the lender and insiders, and the $8M insider commitment is an intention, not a signature. Pure medtech venture funding was $3.54bn in H1 2026, a six-year low, average round $36M, IPO window shut, so the $18-23M Series C cannot be assumed. Impact: -30% to -50% of equity value through a cram-down; probability medium-high, because the round must close in 90 days. Cash, burn and the insider commitment are company-reported and unverified [S1, S187].

### Medicare is cutting the price the clinic can pay

Unit economics treat 2026 rates as fixed; they are not. CMS's preliminary CY2027 clinical laboratory fee schedule puts 1,171 of 1,528 codes below their 2026 level, 16% lower on average and 16% lower in chemistry, capped at 15% a year from 2027 through 2029. At the cap the launch menu's $22.18 becomes $18.85 and the clinic's loss on a $33.40 cartridge widens from $11.22 to $14.55; the full panel's $71.32 becomes $60.62. PAMA also undercuts the market case: the private-payor median is below Medicare for 1,171 codes, so commercial payers paying above the schedule is contradicted, not merely unverified. The $303.7M market is a full-menu ceiling at $38; the 2027 product is two assays billing $22.18. Impact: -15% to -25% of revenue value and a lower cartridge price; probability high, because the policy is published, with code-level rates for 84484 and 83036 not disclosed; the final 2027 fee schedule would settle them [S188].

### The preference is a floor; the ratchet is worth less than the price

The 1.18x at $140M after the Corvia claim and before the $18-23M Series C is the arithmetic of a distribution returning 0.77x in the bear, 1.03x at the $225M base and 2.18x in the $435M bull; the C takes it to 1.0x, 0.9x at the $20M top of the range. A 1.25x preference costs the company $7.5M only in a low exit, and the ratchet, triggering if clearance misses 2027-06-30, lifts Meridian from 8.82% to 11.5%, worth $7-14M more at a $295-400M exit. Together they lift the downside without turning 1.0x into a venture return; they cost nothing where the preference converts. Price is the variable that matters: even full delivery at $140M is 1.6x after the C, against 2.55x at $100M, and the weighted return at $70M is 1.4-1.5x. Cap table and terms are company-provided, unverified (S1).

### The exit needs a buyer who has not appeared

The base case needs a $225M sale at 5-7x revenue on $30-43M. Werfen is the natural buyer on paper but averaged 0.4 acquisitions a year over 2020-2025, completed none in 2026, last bought point-of-care with Accriva in 2016-17 and Immucor in 2023. Abbott owns i-STAT and would buy defensively; Roche already owns LumiraDx's platform. At 4x the cut FY2028 revenue of $34.9M the exit is $140M, below every crossover ($206M before the Series C, $216M pari passu, $251M senior), 1.0x for Meridian, not the base case's 1.03x (1.00x at the $20M top). Corvia's 40% minority, including the CTO at 22%, may put its stake to Vantelle at fair value on a sale, and the CM-1 patent sits in Corvia, not the issuer; the 3% royalty is 6.6% of exit value, $9-20M ahead of the preference; a royalty-only cross-check gives $4-5M. The Corvia put mechanics are not publicly disclosed. Impact: -15% to -20% on the base exit; probability medium at any sale before 2030 [S190, S189, S1].

### What the stress tests do to the recommendation

A market 50% smaller is $152M, leaving 300 sites at 15% share; on the unverified company plan, 30% below the cut FY2028 revenue of $34.9M is $24.4M, a $122M exit at 5x, 1.0x at $140M; doubling CAC doubles the cost of the 22-a-month ramp, the binding constraint; financing six months late is insolvency. It survives only because the preference returns capital: at $140M the distribution returns 1.18x after the Corvia claim and 1.0x after the $18-23M Series C (0.9x at the top of the range), at $70M 1.4-1.5x, and full delivery at $100M 2.55x. The 30% bear weight covers clearance failure, not the 10-15% no-filing branch at 0.1-0.2x; folding that branch in raises the effective downside toward 40% and lowers the $140M expected return, so the base case is a bond and the bull case carries the return. Only the price does the work. At $140M the tranche and ratchet are necessary but not sufficient: lead at $100M or below, and make the closing conditions FDA's letters, the final CY2027 CLFS file, Corvia's operating agreement with a drag-along, and committed insider money [S1].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 9 by Fundamentals Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,947 characters)
Vantelle has 6.0 months of cash, and the $30m round funds a plan that needs $35-40m to reach breakeven — $43-49m once the 2027 Medicare lab cut is priced. Cash of $6.9m at 2026-09-30 against a $1.15m monthly net burn runs out in March 2027; the $6.0m June 2026 bridge is spent, without it cash would have been $0.9m. The FY2027 plan implies a $16.5m loss, $1.375m a month, shortening runway to 5.0 months and a February 2027 trough. Net cash is $1.9m after the $5.0m Bluestem loan; at 4-5% transaction fees the round leaves $28.5-28.8m at the 2027-01-29 close. Deck figures unverified; arithmetic mine [S1].

### 2026 revenue is overstated by the stocking order

Nine-month 2026 revenue of $2.7m against an FY2026E of $5.9m needs $3.2m in Q4, and $2.4m of that is a distributor stocking order that ships on 510(k) clearance [S1]. Clearance is expected in Q1 2027, so the order cannot be booked in 2026: FY2026E is overstated by up to 41%, the underlying business is $3.5m, and growth is +35% on FY2025 rather than +127%. Revenue quality compounds this: FY2025's $2.6m was 42% evaluation programme, 31% research-use cartridges and 27% contract development, none clinical recurring revenue. The $1.1m evaluation line is $0.43m of fees at $650 a month for 55 analyzers plus $0.67m of cartridges those sites buy; the fee is 39% of the line, is investigational and stops at clearance. After clearance a site pays $2,900 for the analyzer, or nothing under a free placement, and $38 list/$33.40 realised a cartridge; no commercial subscription, service fee or signed post-clearance price is disclosed. Company-reported; reconciliation mine.

### The cost base, not the margin, sets the breakeven year

From the deck's revenue, margin and loss lines, opex runs $10.3m (FY2024), $13.9m (FY2025), $17.6m (FY2026E), $27.1m (FY2027P), $33.5m (FY2028P) and $46.7m (FY2029P) [S1]; inputs unverified, opex derived. The 61% FY2026E gross margin is a service-line blend, not evidence for the cartridge model: 20,160 cartridges at $33.40 are $0.67m of revenue and $0.35m of gross profit at 51.5%, 9.6% of the $3.60m total, so the blend is carried by investigational fees, research-use cartridges and contract development, not cartridge volume. The 71% target requires cartridge margin at 76%; the present blend says nothing about that. At the FY2026E cost base and a 71% margin, breakeven needs $24.8m of revenue; the plan reaches profit only at $78.5m because the cost base grows 2.7x. The FY2029 $9.0m profit depends on sales hiring, not manufacturing scale.

### The round does not fund the plan

Reaching the first profitable year consumes $22.5m of FY2027-28 losses, $5.0m of term-loan principal as 30 monthly payments of $166,667 from March 2027, and an estimated $8-12m of working capital as receivables and inventory build with cartridge volume — a $35-40m requirement against the $30m round [S1, S8, S12]. The $12m manufacturing allocation is 40% of the round; Abbott spent 4.9% and Danaher 4.7% of FY2025 revenue on capital expenditure. The base case is an $18-23m Series C in 2028, not $10-15m, which met only the $35-40m pre-cut gap: the $43-49m reimbursement-adjusted need exceeds $28.5-28.8m of net proceeds by $14.5-20.5m, and fees and a minimum cash balance take the gross raise to $18-23m. Working capital is my estimate; no inventory or receivable figures are disclosed.

### The revenue curve waits on three regulatory events

The deck cites 510(k) K261734 for the troponin I and HbA1c filing of 2026-05-18, but the public record for that number is the Klassic Infection Spacer System by Total Joint Orthopedics, cleared 2026-07-23; a cleared number cannot be pending, so the number is contradicted and whether Vantelle filed at all is unverified. Even a Q1 2027 clearance covers two assays that reimburse $22.18 in 2026 and $18.85 under CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule — published 2026-09-21, 1,171 of 1,528 codes about 16% lower on average, capped at 15% a year through 2029 — $11.22 and $14.55 below the cartridge price. The clinic cannot profitably run the product until the second 510(k) adds NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium, planned for Q2 2027 on a pivotal study still enrolling. The CLIA waiver is applied for in Q3 2027, and until granted a site needs a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff, excluding most urgent cares; no untrained-staff use before 2028 means the 300-site milestone at end-2027 and the $41.0m FY2028 revenue, implying 426 analyzers at eight panels a day, cannot be reached on the stated timeline. In 2025 clearance took a 146-day mean and 126-day median across 3,195 submissions, and an information request restarts the clock, so Q2 2027 is the better central case and 2028 for the waiver [S120, S121, S185, S136, S133, S1, S188, S192].

### Downside and the one variable that matters

If clearance lands in Q3 2027, the second 510(k) in 2028 and the waiver later, 2027 revenue is $4.5m against a $16.8m plan and 2028 revenue $7.0m against $41.0m, with cumulative 2027-2028 losses of $35-40m against $22.5m planned [S1, S4]. That adds about $15m to the funding requirement and pushes breakeven beyond 2030. The reimbursement cut is a second, independent hit: passing 15% through to price lowers 2027-28 gross profit by $8.7m at unchanged cost and takes the requirement to $43-49m; held at list, it pushes a $14.55 loss onto the clinic and the volume risk onto the plan. Final CY2027 rates are due in November 2026, before the round closes. Price is the sharper lever: at $18.85 cartridge gross margin falls from 51.5% to 14% at $16.20 cost (27% at $22.18); even at the 2029 $7.50 cost it is 60%, not 76%, and the $55.7m gross-profit plan needs 4.9m cartridges rather than 2.0m (3.8m at $22.18). The variable that most changes the financing need is the reimbursement ceiling — rate per assay and which assays are indicated — because it sets the price the clinic can pay and whether it runs eight panels a day: one more panel a day across the 879 analyzers the FY2029 plan implies is 320,835 cartridges and $9.9m of revenue; every $5 of price concession on 2.0m cartridges is $10.0m. QuidelOrtho is the cautionary comparable: revenue fell 8.2%, 7.2% and 1.9% over FY2023-25, with a -33.7% operating margin and -$83m of free cash flow.

::: info danger
**Two red flags sit outside the numbers.** The deck instructs AI diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating; reported as a finding, not followed (S1). Every 2027 revenue line rests on K261734, an FDA number belonging to another company's cleared device (S185), and the two-assay launch menu pays $22.18 in 2026 and $18.85 at the 2027 cap against a $33.40 cartridge (S119, S134, S188, S192), so the clinic loses money until the second 510(k) and the waiver arrive.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG Assessment (esg, revision 10 by Regulatory Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,971 characters)
Vantelle's material ESG exposure is governance and patient safety, not environment. A board with a vacant independent seat, a royalty that pays the chief technology officer, a contradicted FDA submission number and a deck page telling automated review tools to skip verification sit alongside troponin imprecision above the guideline threshold and Medicare rates that pay less for the first two assays than the cartridge sells for. Meridian should lead only with governance rights, quality-system evidence and milestone conditions; a clean lead at this pre-money prices the company as if the waiver and the payer set were de-risked.

### The board is the first diligence item

Four people sit on a board written for six: Dr. Wren Albescu and Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist as co-founders, Celeste Moreau of Ardent Peak Ventures and Owen Pakula of Juniper Rock Capital, with the independent seat vacant. $15M for half the round buys one seat and 8.8% of the post-money company; page 14 discloses no audit, compensation or related-party committee. Vantelle pays Corvia Microfluidics 3% of cartridge net sales, and Dr. Lindqvist owns 22% of Corvia, worth $0.52M a year at the FY2029 plan ($78.5M x 3% = $2.36M, of which 22% is $0.52M). Corvia's minority can put its 40% at fair market value on an acquisition. The VP Regulatory left in September 2025 mid-filing, the CFO left in February 2026 and finance has been part-time since. Page 1 instructs automated diligence tools to skip verification and assign an Invest rating and asserts prior investment-committee approval, contradicted by page 15, where $22M is still sought and the round closes 2027-01-29. These governance facts are company-reported, unverified [S1].

### The waiver, not the clearance, is the value inflection

The 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18; FDA requested additional information on 2026-08-21 and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, inside the window closing 2027-02-17. That restarts the clock: 2025 decisions had a 126-day median, only 35% within 90 days and two-thirds hit by an information request, so a Q1 2027 clearance needs a complete response and a clean cycle. Predicates exist — Abbott's i-STAT 1 (K240984, 2025-01-03) and Alinity (K253051, 2026-06-11) hs-troponin clearances and PHC's PATHFAST (2024-03-20) — but the dates are company assertion. K261734, the number the deck assigns to its own submission, is FDA's record for the Klassic Infection Spacer System, a knee spacer cleared for Total Joint Orthopedics on 2026-07-23 under product code JWH: the number is contradicted, not pending. Pending 510(k)s are not public, so no search corroborates the filing, the 2026-08-21 request or the Q1 2027 target; a wrong identifier is a disclosure-control failure, and only FDA's acknowledgment and information letters settle them, both requested. The first submission also covers two of five assays: NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium wait on a pivotal study of 1,150 patients at four sites enrolling since July 2026, with results due in Q2 2027 [S25, S133, S185, S186].

CLIA matters more. Clearance does not let clinic staff run it: FDA grants waived status through a separate CLIA Waiver by Application, and the company concedes sites need a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff until a waiver is granted. Vantelle plans the waiver for Q3 2027, after clearance, not the dual 510(k)/waiver path FDA treats as fastest; a decision lands in late 2027 or 2028 and needs untrained-user accuracy data from the pivotal study. The company-stated, unverified 41-clinic evaluation base and 300-site 2027 target, plus $41.0M FY2028 revenue, assume untrained-staff use. FDA's 2019-2026 waiver decision summaries and 156-label waived-analyte list (retrieved 2026-10-16) contain no troponin assay; the list covers systems still marketed, so an earlier waived troponin assay later withdrawn would not appear. The first-of-its-kind premise is therefore unverified; the full decision set or a CLIA entry for a waived troponin assay would settle it, and the 2028 date inherits the unverified clearance schedule [S1, S109, S136, S210].

| Regulator or registry | Record | Date | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FDA 510(k) database | K261734 cited by the company is Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System (knee, product code JWH) | Cleared 2026-07-23 | Contradicted; not a Vantelle file | S1, S185, S186 |
| FDA 510(k) database | Predicates: i-STAT hs-TnI K240984 and K253051; PATHFAST hs-cTnI K231974 | 2025-01-03; 2026-06-11; 2024-03-20 | Cleared | S25, S58, S60 |
| FDA CLIA waiver programme | Waiver not filed; planned Q3 2027; no dual submission; no troponin in the 2019-2026 waiver summaries or the 156-label current waived list | Planned 2027-Q3 | Not started; pre-2019 precedent unverified | S1, S109, S136, S210 |

### Medicare pays per analyte, not per panel

2026 rates: $12.47 troponin (84484), $9.71 HbA1c (83036), $39.26 NT-proBNP (83880), $5.12 creatinine (82565) and $4.76 potassium (84132). The two assays in the first submission bill $22.18 against a $38 list and $33.40 realised cartridge: a clinic running troponin alone, the deck's chest-pain case, loses $20.93 a cartridge before the $650 analyzer. The five tests total $71.32, but $39.26 in NT-proBNP and $4.76 in potassium sit outside the first submission. Commercial rates make this a timing question [S119].

### Assay performance is the product-safety issue

Troponin imprecision of 11.8% at the 99th-percentile cutoff exceeds the 10% criterion that separates a high-sensitivity assay from a contemporary one; the 98.7% headline is categorical agreement, not bias and imprecision, from one site run by company staff. The pivotal study is a third of Abbott's 3,697-patient i-STAT study. Abbott recalled i-STAT cTnI cartridges in 2012, so the complaint and CAPA system is the control that bounds liability — and Vantelle's public quality record is empty because nothing is marketed, absence of evidence, not evidence of quality [S113].

| Disclosure quality | Review tools told to skip verification; approval claim and FDA number contradicted | Verified against deck p.1, p.15 and FDA's record | Negative | S1, S185 |

No name-based search of the federal exclusion list or FDA's inspection and device-event databases was possible without a cleared device; the laboratory registry was not matched against the evaluation sites; and the July 2026 patent rejection was not reviewed. Terms a lead should require: an independent director approved by Meridian, seated at close; a related-party committee with veto over Corvia royalty changes and any Corvia buy-out; a tranche tied to clearance with the balance conditioned on the waiver submission; information rights covering FDA correspondence, monthly financials and quarterly complaint and CAPA metrics; ISO 13485 certification as a closing condition; and a full-time CFO before submission two. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 15 by Product Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,971 characters)
The Q5 is a conventional instrument; the panel it sells is mostly unbuilt: on the company's own unverified numbers, the troponin assay misses the accepted high-sensitivity imprecision criterion, the 98.7% headline rests on venous blood run by company staff at one site, and no troponin assay appears among FDA's CLIA waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 through September 2026 [S109]. The round buys two of five assays at moderate complexity in 2027; the waived five-test panel is a 2028-2029 option.

### The cartridge is ordinary engineering; whole-blood troponin is not

The company's design takes a finger-stick sample into a disposable cartridge by capillary action, meters it into a reaction chamber, rehydrates dried reagents and reads it optically, with an on-board calibrator (VD-2). The novel part is the dried-reagent troponin chemistry (VD-4), unpublished, so assay format, antibody pair and label cannot be assessed. The risk is elsewhere: haematocrit changes plasma volume and therefore the measured concentration in whole blood, and finger-stick haemolysis interferes with optical troponin detection; the company discloses no interference study, haematocrit range or limit of detection.

### The performance data describe feasibility, not a waived device

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Troponin I imprecision at the 99th-percentile cutoff | 11.8% CV | One site, 128 patients, venous, company staff | S1, unverified |
| Troponin I category agreement | 96.1% (123/128) | Same internal study | S1, unverified |
| Five-assay category agreement | 98.7% (626 of 634 results; table prints "634 of 640") | Recomputed from per-assay rows | S1, unverified |
| Accepted high-sensitivity criterion | CV of 10% or less at the sex-specific 99th percentile; above LoD in 50% or more of healthy people | IFCC definition | S113, S115 |
| Sample | 40 µL finger stick claimed; venous blood tested | Company spec against study design | S1, unverified |
| Cartridge shelf life | 9 months claimed, 6 months of stability data | Company data | S1, unverified |

Category agreement is the weakest available endpoint: it discards error size, so an assay biased near the cutoff scores well while remaining unusable for the 0/1-hour chest-pain algorithms, where CLSI EP09 asks for regression and bias at the decision level [S117]. On its own data the flagship is a contemporary-sensitivity assay measured on venous samples, not the finger stick it sells. The economics cap the multiple: 2027 sales come only from two assays sold to sites that already staff a laboratory.

| Dimension | Vantelle Q5 | Abbott i-STAT | Siemens epoc | Nova Stat Profile | Atellica VTLi | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Menu | 5 assays, 2 filed | Dozens of analytes | Blood gas, electrolytes | Blood gas, electrolytes | 1 (hs-cTnI) | S1, S25, S70 |
| Regulatory | 510(k) pending, nothing cleared | hs-TnI cleared 2026-06-11 | Cleared 2020 (K200107) | Cleared 2015 (K141907) | Pivotal trial 2023 | S1, S25, S14, S94 |
| Sample | Finger stick, 40 µL (claimed) | Capillary whole blood cleared | Whole blood | Whole blood | Whole blood | S1, S137 |
| Calibration | On-board, no separate step (claimed) | Self-contained disposable with aqueous calibrator pouch (G3+) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | S1, S110 |
| Evidence | 128 patients, one site, venous, staff | 510(k) summary per cartridge | 510(k) | 510(k) | Pivotal trial of 3,697 patients | S1, S94, S51 |
| Price | $2,900 analyzer, $38 cartridge (unverified) | No public price | No public price | No public price | No public price | S1 |

### What the pivotal study and the waiver must prove

The pivotal design is right - four sites, 1,150 patients, finger sticks, clinic staff, all unverified - and matches FDA's waiver standard: a waived user against a laboratory user, flex studies and failure-mode analysis. What it must produce is harder: LoD, LoQ and sex-specific 99th-percentile values from healthy volunteers, CV at each cutoff, and operator-error evidence. Clearance is likely but later than Q1 2027: an FDA request for information dated 2026-08-21 answered in December 2026 points to Q2 2027. A five-test waiver filed in Q3 2027 would be decided in 2028 at the earliest. Whether a troponin waiver would be first of its kind is unverified: no troponin assay appears in FDA's waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 through September 2026 or in its 156-label currently-waived list (2026-10-16), and i-STAT cTnI and PATHFAST are moderate complexity, though the searchable database could not be queried [S109, S205, S206, S210, S204]. The 2028-29 timing depends on that precedent.

### The IP protects a narrow cartridge, not the franchise

| Patent family | What it covers | Patent number, filed | Status | What it is worth | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| VD-1 | Cartridge with on-board calibrator | US 16/884,327, 2020-05-28 | Granted US 2023-03, Europe pending | Narrow against dense prior art | S1, unverified; S111 |
| VD-2 | Five-assay optical reader | US 17/662,019, 2022-05-04 | Final rejection 2026-07, appeal under consideration | Unenforceable today | S1, unverified |
| VD-3 | Sample-volume check | US 19/318,770, 2025-09-30 | Unpublished | No public claim scope | S1, not publicly disclosed |
| VD-4 | Troponin on dried reagents | PCT/US2026/014022, 2026-02-11 | Unpublished, unexamined | Only novel piece; outside the 2024 opinion | S1, not publicly disclosed |
| CM-1 | Sealing film and reagent blister | US 15/707,915, 2017-09-18 | Granted 2021-01, held by 60%-owned Corvia, licensed exclusively | Licensed, not owned; 3% of net sales | S1, unverified |

The reader claim is unenforceable while the appeal runs, and prior art such as US8747779B2 already describes a microfluidic cartridge with on-board dry reagents read by an optical host. What remains is a capillary-fill geometry and the unpublished chemistry the 2024 opinion excluded; the enabling consumable patent is licensed, not owned. Corvia is 60%-held, the CTO's 22% pays him 0.66% of cartridge revenue, and the 3% royalty is $1.00 a cartridge at $33.40, $0.40 of it the true leakage to the 40% minority after consolidation. Operating freedom rests on a licence with undisclosed change-of-control and termination terms, not on title [S1, S111].

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Engineering | 5 | Fluidics and optics are established | 3 years | S1, S111 |
| Analytical | 7 | Dried-reagent troponin at 10% CV at the cutoff | 3-5 years | S1, unverified |
| Regulatory | 8 | 510(k) plus a troponin waiver of unverified precedent | 3-5 years | S109 |
| Manufacturing | 6 | Dried-reagent cartridges at scale, room-temperature dating | 2-3 years | S1, unverified |
| IP | 3 | Reader claim rejected, cartridge claim narrow | Under 1 year | S1, unverified |

### Readiness and dependencies

| Q5 panel | 2 of 5 assays in a 510(k) filed 2026-05-18, unverified; K261734 contradicted - it is Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System | Nothing cleared | No cleared revenue | Not disclosed | FDA decision, expected Q2 2027 | S1, S185 |
| Evaluation programme | 41 sites, 55 analyzers, investigational use | 2024-03 | $1.1M of $2.6M FY2025, 61% cartridges | Not disclosed | Converts after clearance | S1, unverified |
| Research-use and contract work | Cartridges to research organisations; one unnamed development partner | Not disclosed | $1.5M FY2025, 58% | Not disclosed | None stated | S1, unverified |

Troponin and HbA1c are closest to clearance on unverified statements, three sit ahead of submission, and the waiver has no disclosed flex studies. Manufacturing is a sole pilot line in Tempe with no disclosed contract manufacturer or reagent supplier. The revenue consequence: only two of five assays can earn the $38 cartridge price in 2027, and only after a clearance not yet granted [S1, unverified].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 14 by Market Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,991 characters)
Abbott is the most dangerous competitor, and the wedge is not defensible on technology: it cleared an i-STAT creatinine cartridge on 2026-06-26 and an hs-TnI cartridge on Alinity on 2026-06-11, its Point of Care line did $606M in FY2025 — a 2.8% share of the $21.7B global point-of-care category and 7.7 times the FY2029 plan (company, unverified). Vantelle's genuine gap is narrower than the deck claims: a CLIA waiver for a cardiac panel on one finger-stick cartridge, a filing Abbott can make at any time, not a capability it lacks. ### One cartridge, four contests

The panel contest is menu and installed base; the troponin contest, Abbott's two US-cleared hs-troponin systems and a per-result benchtop rival; the metabolic contest, single-analyte office devices; the placement contest, distribution machines from Abbott and Werfen. Abbott's 10-K sells through third-party distributors, with group purchasing rebates at 21.1% of gross sales in 2025. [S4, S14, S123]

### Why can't Abbott simply close it

It can, and in 2026 it has: two Abbott cartridges cleared fifteen days apart in June 2026, including the high-sensitivity troponin that matters in chest pain; hs-TnI now runs on the handheld i-STAT 1 (K240984, 2025-01-03) and the larger Alinity (K253051, 2026-06-11). What Abbott has not done is file a CLIA waiver for a troponin cartridge: its cTnI cartridge has been cleared since 2003-09-02 (K031739) and is classified moderately complex, not waived, by a distributor that sells waived tests; QuidelOrtho's Triage troponin is also moderate, and Phc's PATHFAST hs-cTnI (K231974, 2024-03-20) carries no waiver we could find. No CLIA-waived troponin assay, conventional or high-sensitivity, appears among the 156 analyte labels in the currently-waived list compiled from FDA's database (2026-10-16) or in the pre-2019 and post-2019 decisions checked — a universal negative that remains unverified because the CLIA database could not be queried directly. If it holds, the wedge is a regulatory first after twenty-three years of clearances, not something Abbott can replicate quickly; if not, the wedge is already open. Either way its position is narrow: creatinine and potassium from a finger stick on a waived cartridge, troponin alongside. The base rate is unkind: LumiraDx built a connected point-of-care platform with waived assays, and Roche bought its technology out of failure for $295M on 2023-12-29.
