plan.decision_question: Should Meridian lead Vantelle's $30M Series B with $15M, and at what price and terms?
plan.thesis_sentence: The need is real and the cartridge platform is credible, but at $140M pre-money Meridian would own a bond-like 1.0x claim on a clearance the company cannot yet evidence; only a price at or below $100M, or a tranched $140M with a 1.25x preference and ratchet, earns the risk.
plan.why_different: It separates the 510(k) from the CLIA waiver and prices the clinic's reimbursement arithmetic, not the technology narrative.
plan.mechanism: Value accrues at the CLIA waiver, not the 510(k): until untrained clinic staff can run the panel the buyer is a laboratory-equipped site and the launch menu reimburses $22.18 against a $33.40 cartridge, so the entry price must discount an unverified filing and a 2028-29 waiver.
plan.comparison_set: Point-of-care precedents: i-STAT/Abbott 2004 $392M; Abaxis/Zoetis 2018 $2.0B at 8.2x; Cepheid/Danaher 2016 $4.0B at 7.4x; LumiraDx/Roche 2023-24 $353.5M; QuidelOrtho/LEX 2026 $100M; listed diagnostics median 5.5x EV/sales; Series B median pre-money $187M.
plan.counter_evidence: Clearance and a waiver could lift utilisation above the investigational floor; a 92% repeat rate is unusual for a first instrument; contract development shows platform capability; a strategic buyer could emerge earlier than modelled.
plan.visual: scenarios component and the key assumptions table
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned

user_data_requests.database: FDA CDRH 510(k) file K261734 and CLIA waiver file (pending submissions are not in the public 510(k) database)
user_data_requests.query: The FDA 510(k) acknowledgment letter for K261734; the 2026-08-21 additional-information request and Vantelle's December 2026 response; the cleared indications and any high-sensitivity claim; the CLIA waiver submission package (risk analysis, flex studies, untrained-user reproducibility study) once filed.
user_data_requests.why: Settles whether clearance arrives in Q2 2027 or slips to Q4 2027, whether the troponin claim will carry a high-sensitivity rule-out indication, and whether the CLIA waiver can be granted on the pivotal study already enrolling. It moves the value inflection by two to three quarters and is the largest single uncertainty in the $140M pre-money.
user_data_requests.how: Ask Vantelle management for redacted copies under the diligence data room; the company receives these letters directly from FDA and they are not published while a submission is pending.

user_data_requests.database: Commercial and Medicaid payer medical policies (Aetna, Cigna, UnitedHealthcare, Blue Cross plans in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico, plus state Medicaid fee schedules)
user_data_requests.query: Coverage and payment for CPT 84484, 83880, 83036, 82570 and 84132 when performed at point of care in an urgent care or rural hospital outpatient setting; whether a panel code exists; site-of-service or bundling edits; prior authorisation rules.
user_data_requests.why: Medicare pays $22.18 for the two assays in the first submission against a $33.40 realised cartridge price; whether commercial and Medicaid rates are materially higher decides if clinics can pay for the cartridge at launch, which drives the 2028 revenue plan of $41.0M.
user_data_requests.how: Payer policy PDFs are public on payer websites but sit behind provider portals and are not retrievable here; the company's payer relations team or a revenue-cycle consultant can pull the current policies and state Medicaid fee schedules.

user_data_requests.database: Vantelle quality system and site records: ISO 13485 audit report (booked Q1 2027), CAPA and complaint logs, MDR and recall history, product liability insurance certificate, HIPAA business associate agreements, device cybersecurity documentation (threat model, SBOM, penetration test), OSHA 300A logs for the Tempe line, and the CLIA certificate types held by the 41 evaluation sites
user_data_requests.query: Complaint rate and CAPA backlog on the 27,600 cartridges shipped since 2024-03; design-history-file status; who reviews FDA correspondence; cybersecurity documentation included in K261734; insurance limits; CLIA certificate category at each evaluation site.
user_data_requests.why: A pre-clearance company has no public quality record, so these documents are the only evidence that the same controls that produce the FDA filing also govern cash and related-party dealings; the CLIA certificate category also shows how many of the 41 sites could legally use the Q5 before a waiver.
user_data_requests.how: Diligence request list to the company; the ISO 13485 certificate and audit report come from the notified body, and the certificate types are verifiable through CMS's CLIA laboratory registry by CLIA number.

user_data_requests.database: Delaware Division of Corporations (entity file) and SEC EDGAR Form D
user_data_requests.query: Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc.: Delaware file number, incorporation date (claimed 2018-03-12), current registered agent, good standing, and the filed certificate of incorporation as amended (authorised share classes: common, Series Seed, Series A, Series B, Series B-1). Also any Form D filings by the company for the 2019 seed, 2022-02/2023-11 Series A and 2026-06 bridge.
user_data_requests.why: Confirms the issuer exists, is in good standing and has the share classes in the deck's cap table; the certificate fixes the Series A participation cap that determines whether the Series B returns capital below a ~$209M exit. A missing Form D for a $24M Series A would be a securities-compliance red flag.
user_data_requests.how: Entity search at icis.corp.delaware.gov (pay-per-document, needs an account); Form D full-text search at sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar with company name.

user_data_requests.database: Texas Secretary of State — SOSDirect business entity records
user_data_requests.query: Corvia Microfluidics LLC (Austin, Texas; formed 2016-02-01): file number, managers, members and ownership percentages, and the amended and restated company agreement or membership interest purchase agreement under which Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc. acquired 60% in 2021-04. Also the CM-1 patent licence agreement from Corvia to Vantelle.
user_data_requests.why: The 40% minority can put its stake to the company at fair market value on a sale, and the CTO holds 22% of it. The company agreement decides whether the minority can block a sale, how fair market value is set and whether the CM-1 licence survives a change of control — all of which price Meridian's exit.
user_data_requests.how: SOSDirect subscriber search at sos.state.tx.us (login required); the operating agreement and licence are not filed with the state and must be requested from the company's counsel.

user_data_requests.database: USPTO Patent Center and Assignment records
user_data_requests.query: Status, inventorship and recorded assignments for: VD-1 US 16/884,327 (filed 2020-05-28, granted 2023-03); VD-2 US 17/662,019 (final rejection 2026-07, appeal under consideration); VD-3 US 19/318,770; VD-4 PCT/US2026/014022; and CM-1 US 15/707,915 (assigned to Corvia Microfluidics LLC). Who is named as inventor on each, and is any assignment recorded from Corvia to Vantelle?
user_data_requests.why: Inventorship is the only independent check on the CTO's technical contribution and on whether the four patent families are owned by the issuer as claimed. A final rejection on the five-assay reader (VD-2) with no assignment of the cartridge patent (CM-1) to the parent would mean the issuer owns neither the reader claim nor the consumable IP.
user_data_requests.how: Patent Center (patentcenter.uspto.gov) and the Assignment Search (assignment-api.uspto.gov) for each application number; the Corvia-Vantelle licence is not recorded at USPTO and must come from the company.

user_data_requests.database: State medical boards (Arizona Medical Board), NPPES NPI Registry, ABEM certification and OIG LEIE
user_data_requests.query: For Dr. Wren Albescu: Arizona and New Mexico medical licences, dates of issue and any public disciplinary actions, NPI record, and American Board of Emergency Medicine certification status. For all five named executives (Albescu, Lindqvist, Oyelaran, Arrellano, Whitcombe): OIG List of Excluded Individuals/Entities and FDA debarment checks.
user_data_requests.why: The CEO's only clinical credential is an MD that the deck does not say is board-certified, and she is the named FDA sponsor-side executive. An unlicensed or uncertified physician, or any exclusion record, would change the assessment of regulatory depth and of who can credibly answer the FDA.
user_data_requests.how: Arizona Medical Board licence lookup (azmd.gov), NPPES at nppes.cms.hhs.gov, ABEM verification at abem.org, and the OIG exclusion list at oig.hhs.gov/exclusions. Names must be supplied by the deal team because they come from the confidential deck.

user_data_requests.database: CMS Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule 2026 (public file, blocked in this run)
user_data_requests.query: 2026 national limitation amounts for CPT 84484 (troponin, quantitative), 83880 (natriuretic peptide), 83036 (HbA1c), 82565 (creatinine) and 84132 (potassium), plus any CLIA-waived point-of-care payment policy applying to a five-test panel
user_data_requests.why: Adoption depends on the clinic's margin: at one panel a day the clinic pays $1,790 a month for cartridges and analyzer fee and must recover that from payers. Only CPT 84484 was verified ($12.47); the sum of the five codes decides whether Vantelle's $38 cartridge price is sellable at realistic volumes, which is the single largest unverified number in the unit economics.
user_data_requests.how: Download the 2026 CLFS file from cms.gov (Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule > Files) and send the rows for those five codes, or confirm the rates from a claims clearinghouse or payer contract.

user_data_requests.database: FDA 510(k) filing record and the 2026-08-21 additional-information letter (company regulatory file)
user_data_requests.query: The FDA acknowledgment or filing receipt showing the correct K number and submission date for the troponin I and HbA1c 510(k), plus the 2026-08-21 additional-information letter and the company's December 2026 response
user_data_requests.why: The number the deck cites, K261734, is the Klassic Infection Spacer System by Total Joint Orthopedics in the public device record. The filing date, the AI request and therefore the Q1 2027 clearance that every revenue line from 2027 depends on cannot be verified, and both the base case and the two-quarter-slip case turn on it.
user_data_requests.how: Ask management for the FDA filing receipt and AI letter, or authorise a direct check of the FDA's pending-submission status once the correct number is known.

user_data_requests.database: FDA CLIA database (accessdata.fda.gov, CLIA currently-waived analytes and test systems) and CMS CLIA certificate registry
user_data_requests.query: For each of troponin I, NT-proBNP, HbA1c, creatinine and potassium: every test system currently categorized waived, with manufacturer, 510(k) number and date. Also, for the 41 Vantelle evaluation sites and for the 300 sites named in the Southwest Clinical Supply letter of intent, the CLIA certificate type held (waiver versus moderate complexity).
user_data_requests.why: Vantelle's whole differentiation is a waived cardiac panel; whether an incumbent already holds a waiver for troponin, NT-proBNP or a multi-analyte chemistry panel decides if the wedge is a year-wide or a decade-wide gap. The CLIA certificate type of the 41 evaluation sites and the 300 letter-of-intent sites decides whether the near-term market is 300 clinics or a handful of laboratory-directed sites, which moves the obtainable revenue several fold.
user_data_requests.how: The FDA CLIA database is searchable by analyte or test system but only through its web form, which cannot be scripted; export the waived test-system list for those five analytes to CSV, and obtain the certificate-type extract from CMS's CLIA laboratory registry (QCOR / CLIA update files) for the site list in the company's data room.

user_data_requests.database: FDA CDRH 510(k) database and the company's FDA correspondence file
user_data_requests.query: The FDA acknowledgment letter or submission receipt for the 510(k) that Vantelle says it filed on 2026-05-18 under number K261734 (troponin I and HbA1c), and the 2026-08-21 additional-information letter, including the FDA's actual submission number and filing date.
user_data_requests.why: The public 510(k) record assigns K261734 to the Klassic Infection Spacer System, an unrelated orthopedic device, and the FDA does not publish pending submissions, so the entire 2027 revenue line, the Q1 2027 clearance date and the $140M pre-money rest on a number the public record contradicts. Without the acknowledgment letter the clearance milestone cannot be dated or priced, and Meridian would be funding an option whose strike date is unknown.
user_data_requests.how: Ask Vantelle's VP Regulatory and Quality (Grace Oyelaran, RAC) for the FDA acknowledgment letter and the additional-information letter, with the submission number and receipt date visible; alternatively authorise a direct query of the FDA 510(k) database, which the research environment blocked during this run.

user_data_requests.database: Series B data room — Corvia Microfluidics LLC records (Texas)
user_data_requests.query: Corvia Microfluidics LLC company agreement and the CM-1 (US 15/707,915) exclusive licence to Vantelle: change-of-control, assignment, termination, sublicensing, royalty base and term; the 40% minority put right.
user_data_requests.why: The cartridge's enabling patent sits outside the parent; the terms decide whether the licence survives an acquisition and what the 3% royalty really costs at 1M cartridges.
user_data_requests.how: Request from management in the Series B data room; the deck (pp.6, 12) discloses the 60% ownership and the 3% royalty but not the licence or LLC terms.

user_data_requests.database: Vantelle Diagnostics data room (management-held, not public)
user_data_requests.query: Evaluation-to-commercial conversion by site cohort: how many of the 41 evaluation sites have signed a post-clearance supply agreement; cartridges per analyzer for sites past 12 months; sites that exited or returned analyzers; the post-clearance price list and any service or warranty fee.
user_data_requests.why: The $650/month evaluation fee is investigational and stops at clearance. Without conversion and post-clearance pricing, the $8.07m SOM, the $2.4m stocking order and the unit economics cannot be tested: cartridge gross profit is $525 a month per analyzer at observed use and $81 at the CY2027 reimbursement cap.
user_data_requests.how: Ask management for the site-level evaluation cohort table and the draft commercial price list; a redacted version is enough.

notes.note: The deck's $2.4B serviceable market is 13,200 sites x 2 analyzers x 8 panels a day x 300 days x $38 = $2.41B, but 8 panels a day is 7.9x the 30.5 cartridges per analyzer a month (1.0 a day) its own 55 evaluation analyzers record. At that observed rate the same site count yields $367m at $38 or $323m at the $33.40 realised price. The distributor LOI covers 300 sites, is non-binding, and sits against 41 sites today.

The $140m pre-money is fully diluted and already contains the bridge conversion and a 10% post-money option pool: 2,571,392 B-1 shares at $2.4423 = $6.28m, consistent with $6.0m plus 8% accrued to the 2027-01-29 close. Post-money is 52,204,508 shares x $3.2564 = $170.0m, so the effective pre-money for existing holders is $133.7m. On my cash model a further $10-15m is needed in 2028, which argues for pricing below the ask.

Two facts for the risk section. (1) The deck's 510(k) number K261734 is, in the public device record, the Klassic Infection Spacer System by Total Joint Orthopedics, an orthopedic device, so the clearance date behind every 2027 revenue line is unverified; the 2025 average 510(k) took 146 days to clearance. (2) At $6.9m cash and $1.15m monthly net burn, runway ends in March 2027, and the round's target close is 2027-01-29.

Regulatory flags for the product section: K261734 returns no openFDA record (expected while pending) but one public mirror attributes it to another company's spinal implant, so treat the submission number as unverified [S121, S122]. Troponin imprecision is 11.8% at the 99th-percentile cutoff against the 10% high-sensitivity criterion [S113]; the pivotal study is 1,150 patients versus Abbott's 3,697 (NCT05629572) [S51]. Fresh predicate: i-STAT Crea K261039, cleared 2026-06-26 [S21].

Reimbursement caps the launch: 2026 CLFS pays $12.47 (CPT 84484) + $9.71 (83036) = $22.18 for the two assays in the first 510(k), against a $38 list / $33.40 realised cartridge; the $39.26 NT-proBNP code (83880) sits in the second submission [S119, S134]. CLIA waiver is planned Q3 2027 after clearance, so no untrained-staff use before 2028, yet the 300-site/end-2027 and FY2028 $41.0M plan assume it [S136, S133].

Pre-waiver the channel is only sites holding a moderate-complexity CLIA certificate and qualified staff (company-admitted, deck p.5) [S136]; a waiver decision lands in late 2027 or 2028 on the Q3 2027 filing plan. That caps the 13,200-site SAM until then. Note also 8 panels/day per analyzer in the model against 41 cartridges per site per month actual (1,680 cartridges across 41 sites), roughly a sixfold gap [S1].

Corrections made. The technology section now describes the submission as "numbered K261734 in the deck and unverified" rather than a verified filing, and the 11.8% CV against the 10% high-sensitivity criterion is carried in the performance table and in the evidence component. Abbott's pivotal (3,697 patients, S51) is now the benchmark against Vantelle's 1,150 in the comparison table. Thank you - the number attribution was the single most useful check I received.

Two reconciliation points for the financials section from the product side. (1) FY2025 evaluation-programme revenue of $1.1M does not reconcile with 55 analyzers x $650 x 12 months = $429k at the site table on deck p.7; the gap is unexplained. (2) FY2026E gross margin of 61% (deck p.10) cannot come from cartridges at $33.40 realised against $16.20 cost (51.5%, deck p.9), so roughly ten points of margin must come from evaluation fees or contract development, which do not scale with cartridge volume. Both from S1.

Three facts for the competitive section. Abbott cleared an i-STAT hs-TnI cartridge on the Alinity system on 2026-06-11 (K253051, S25), so a point-of-care high-sensitivity troponin is already on the market. i-STAT chemistry cartridges are already cleared for capillary whole blood (S137), which weakens the deck's venous-versus-finger-stick differentiation. And no troponin assay appears among the roughly 60 CLIA waiver-by-application decisions FDA published 2019-2026 (S109); waived chemistry is single-analyte (potassium, HbA1c, glucose, UACR).

Valuation anchor from the product side: Roche paid an aggregate $353.5M at closing on 2024-07-29 for LumiraDx's multi-assay point-of-care platform, including $62.6M to repay the senior lender (S114, S112). That is a market price for a developed multi-assay platform whose menu was already cleared/CE-marked, sold out of distress - useful against the $140M pre-money for a company with two of five assays under review and the platform still at one pilot line.

Two facts for the risk section from section 1: (1) the deck's 510(k) number K261734 resolves in the public device record to the Klassic Infection Spacer System by Total Joint Orthopedics, an orthopaedic implant; pending submissions are not published, so this is not proof of no filing, but the filing date and the 2026-08-21 AI request rest on company assertion alone [S118, S121]. Components present and populated in all fifteen sections (verdict/briefing/efficiency/one-question/takeaways; kpi/timeline; evidence boxes where required; quad; info; risk-matrix; scenarios/analogs; sensitivity/takeaways). Independent sources are dated and current: FDA clearances 2025-01 to 2026-07, CMS 2026 CLFS and the 2026-09-21 preliminary CY2027 file, Abbott and Danaher 10-Ks filed 2026-02, QuidelOrtho 10-Q 2026-08-07 and its 2026-04-20 LEX purchase, JUCM 2025-04-01 and AHA 2026 site counts, NCHS visits to 2024. No stale (>18 month) independent source carries a live valuation claim. No unregistered source IDs appear in the text and no invented figure was found. Company-only claims are labelled in every section except the single thesis instance above; the deck's cap table, terms and revenue are labelled unverified throughout, and 'customer partners', 'evaluation sites' and the distributor letter are correctly marked non-binding.

3.name: Missing competitors
3.notes: Missing-competitor challenge, tested one by one. Covered and correctly placed: Abbott (i-STAT 1, i-STAT Alinity hs-TnI K253051, creatinine K261039, CHEM8+, GPO rebates at 21.1% of gross sales, $606M FY2025 POC line, 2.8% of the global category); Siemens epoc and Atellica VTLi (with the correct distinction that VTLi is not for sale in the US as of 2026); QuidelOrtho Triage/TriageTrue and the $221.0M 1H 2026 POC unit; Roche as owner of LumiraDx's platform; reference-laboratory send-out and 'do nothing' as the dominant substitute, argued through workflow and decision delay rather than price. Geographic blind spot: the company plans no ex-US revenue and CE marking is not before 2028, so Chinese and Japanese cartridge makers cannot reach Meridian's exit inside the hold period; this needs stating, not a table row of 'none identified'. Adjacent giants: none beyond Abbott and Siemens has a clinic-channel excuse to enter; Abbott has already moved twice in June 2026, which the report treats as the central threat. Open source and generic substitutes: not applicable to a regulated reagent cartridge, and the report's non-consumption section is the right frame. Academic spin-outs: unaddressed and worth one search given the dried-reagent chemistry. Net: no material competitor is missing from the analysis, but the geography and substitute mapping is asserted rather than shown.

4.name: Product/market fit
4.notes: Product/market fit, the five questions. 1) Hardest thing about selling it: not the assay but the two things the sale depends on and the company does not control — a CLIA waiver (without it the buyer is a laboratory-directed site, not the urgent-care nurse the product is designed for) and a billable panel worth more than the cartridge ($22.18 against $33.40 at launch). The sale is therefore conditional on a second 510(k) and on a payer argument the company cannot make on the clinic's behalf. The report states both; the analysis could say plainly that at launch the product has no positive business case for a buyer. 2) Budget owner: the site operator or chain buys the instrument; the payer reimburses per analyte; the clinic carries the gap, and the report is right that Vantelle does not bill. Not addressed anywhere: who signs above a single site — chain CFO, medical director or GPO — and whether the distributor sells to chains or independents. 3) Sales cycle: observed, 1.1 net new evaluation sites a month over 31 months against a plan of 22 a month; no commercial sales-cycle length is disclosed and none is asked for, and the 300-site letter of intent has no minimum, date or purchase commitment. 4) Why adoption is not faster: well answered — investigational-use labelling means results cannot be acted on, hardware is free or below cost, no waiver, and three of five assays are unsubmitted. The missing counterfactual is how many of the 41 sites asked to buy. 5) Lost deals: no evidence anywhere in the report, and no request for it. The single most useful new fact for the committee would be one declined placement with its reason, because it separates a regulatory constraint from a pricing constraint.

5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes: Stress-test arithmetic, each key number 30% worse. Market: $303.7M to $213M, or $187M at the realised price; still 5-6x the cut FY2028 revenue of $34.9M, so the thesis survives on market size — the market is not the binding number. Utilisation: 30.5 to 21.4 cartridges an analyzer a month; the site economics stay negative at launch rates either way, and the plan needs 1.35x more analyzers, so the number that matters is price, not volume. Realised cartridge price, the untested case: $33.40 to $23.38 against a $16.20 cost cuts cartridge gross margin from 51% to 31%, makes the clinic roughly break-even at 2026 rates ($22.18) and still negative at the CY2027 cap ($18.85), and stretches analyzer payback from 6.4 to about 20 months. The report tests the fee-schedule cut but never a 30% concession, which is the move a 300-site distributor would ask for first. Exit: $225M to $157.5M falls below the $206M crossover, so Meridian returns exactly 1.0x rather than 1.11x — the preference does its job and the upside disappears, which is the report's own conclusion stated more sharply. Revenue on the cut plan: $34.9M to $24.4M, a $122M exit at 5x, 1.0x (already in risk). Burn: $1.15M to $1.50M a month gives 4.6 months, a February 2027 trough one month after the target close (already in risk). Revenue multiple: 53.1x to 76x at 30% lower revenue, which strengthens rather than weakens the valuation conclusion. Weights: bear 30% to 40% takes the expected return at $140M from 1.27x to about 1.13x pre-Series-C and from 1.1x to about 1.0x post-Series-C — both the thesis and the red team state this, and the conclusion (only price does the work) survives. Verdict on the stress test: the thesis survives a 30% worse market, volume, exit or burn only because the recommendation is to pay 25-30% below the ask; at $140M as offered, three of the five 30%-worse cases return 1.0x or less.

items.issue: The private-company rating gate is asserted, not evidenced. 'Invest with conditions' is only permissible where an independent, non-company source supports the case. Here the asset-level case — a 510(k) filed 2026-05-18, five assays on one cartridge, 41 evaluation sites, 11.8% CV at the cutoff, $2.6M revenue — rests entirely on the deck (company-provided, medium confidence), and the single independent regulatory check available contradicts the number the filing rests on. Neither section 14 nor the verdict card states which independent evidence supports investing, so the face rating reads stronger than the register behind it.
items.action: Add one sentence to section 14 and the verdict card naming the independent support for the conditional case (dated primary filings and fee schedules, peer multiples, third-party site and visit counts) and stating explicitly that every asset-level claim is company-provided pending FDA's letters. If Meridian's standard requires asset-level independent support before 'Invest with conditions', restate the face rating as 'Wait for milestone' with the identical price bands, tranching and conditions.
items.evidence_request: Which independent, non-company sources support the asset-level case, and does Meridian's standard permit 'Invest with conditions' when the only independent regulatory check contradicts the cited submission number? If not, the rating must read 'Wait for milestone'.

items.issue: The two open check findings ('no economic/strategic interpretation') are false negatives. Market also passed clean at rev 6 on near-identical text.
items.action: Do not edit either section to satisfy the finding. Record it as a check defect in the QA record (the report-level '2 items unresolved after a failed QA loop' is the same root) and keep the stated-limitation note you already hold.

items.issue: Readiness is described by stage, launch date and a 1-10 barrier score, but not on a standard technology-readiness scale, which is what a committee comparing this to a cleared competitor expects.

items.issue: The waiver premise is the thesis's value inflection and it is stated three ways. technology_product asserts 'no troponin assay has ever been granted a CLIA waiver by application' and that the waived chemistry menu since 2019 is single-analyte; esg says no troponin assay was granted by application in 2019-2026; risk, thesis and scoring price a 'first of its kind' waiver decided in 2028-29. The evidence cited supports only the 2019-2026 window, not 'ever'; competition concedes 'whether an older waived cardiac assay exists is unsettled' and records Triage's waiver status as 'not confirmed'; PHC's PATHFAST hs-cTnI (K231974, 2024-03-20) appears in the esg regulator table with no waiver status at all; and the CLIA-database search that would settle it is still an open data request. If an incumbent already holds a waived troponin, NT-bNP or chemistry cartridge, the 'no waived option today' premise and the 2028-29 inflection both move.
items.action: Run the analyte-by-analyte CLIA search and add a waived-status column to the competitor table for every cartridge named there (i-STAT hs-TnI K240984/K253051, i-STAT CHEM8+, Triage MeterPro/TriageTrue, PATHFAST K231974, epoc, VTLi). items.evidence_request: From FDA's CLIA waiver database (accessdata.fda.gov) and the CLIA currently-waived analyte list, including decisions before 2019: which test systems are waived for troponin I, NT-proBNP or a multi-analyte chemistry panel containing troponin, and what is the current CLIA status of QuidelOrtho Triage MeterPro and PHC PATHFAST? items.issue: The thesis reintroduces the 92% repeat rate as counter-evidence ('a 92% repeat rate is unusual for a first instrument') without the company-reported, unverified label that the executive card, the quad and section 6 carry. 2.name: Claim verification
2.notes: Claim verification, section by section. Verified with dates and independent tags: CMS 2026 CLFS rates (troponin 84484 $12.47, HbA1c 83036 $9.71 = $22.18; full panel $71.32) and the preliminary CY2027 schedule [S119, S133, S188]; Abbott hs-TnI K240984 (2025-01-03), K253051 (2026-06-11) and creatinine K261039 (2026-06-26) [S25, S21]; K261734 as Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System cleared 2026-07-23 [S120, S185]; QuidelOrtho/LEX $100M for a 2026-02-13 cleared, waived, pre-commercial platform [S181, S184]; Roche/LumiraDx $295M upfront 2023-12-29, $353.5M aggregate 2024-07-29 [S93, S114]. The waiver-critical set is sound: S109 (FDA waiver decision summaries, read 2026-10-31), S205 and S206 (i-STAT cTnI and PATHFAST moderate complexity, third party), S208 (K031739, 2003), S210 (156-label list, 2026-10-16) — an analyte-level universal negative stated as unverified in four sections, which is the correct N3 treatment. 3.name: Missing competitors
3.notes: Missing-competitor sweep. Geographic: EU/EEA and rest of world are treated as absences in market's regional table with the CE/IVDR date and the Irish entity's lack of staff, so no blind spot is hidden; the US regional coverage is one country but the plan is one country. Adjacent giants: Abbott (with two June 2026 cartridge clearances and $606M of point-of-care revenue), Danaher/Cepheid and Thermo appear in the peer and exit tables; Siemens appears in both the competition and exit sets. Substitutes: the reference-laboratory send-out is priced as the true substitute ($22.35 for the same three tests, no capital, 1-3 days) and non-consumption is given its own subsection, which is the comparison most market reports omit. Open source and academic spin-outs: not relevant to a cartridge franchise; the closest academic route, the IFCC analytical standard, is used as the performance benchmark rather than as a competitor. The residual gaps are the two recorded above (Werfen's dual role, Roche-owned LumiraDx and low-cost cartridge entrants), neither of which changes the conclusion: the competitive case already rests on the incumbent's installed base and the clinic's inability to pay list.

4.name: Product/market fit
4.notes: Product/market fit, answered from the sections. Hardest thing about selling: the clinic, not Vantelle, absorbs a negative unit margin — $22.18 of billable assay value against a $33.40 cartridge ($11.22 loss, $14.55 at the CY2027 cap) until the second 510(k) adds NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium, plus the requirement that site staff hold a moderate-complexity certificate until a waiver. Budget owner: the site operator, paying $2,900 or nothing for the analyzer and $38 list/$33.40 realised a cartridge; Vantelle does not bill payers. Sales cycle: undisclosed (item above); the existing cycle is the $650-a-month investigational evaluation, which stops at clearance and is the mechanism that has produced 41 sites in 31 months. Why adoption is not faster: investigational-use labelling means results cannot be used for patient care, so evaluation volume (30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month) is a floor, not a demand signal; the plan needs 240 a month per analyzer. Lost deals: three of 37 sites past 90 days did not reorder; no departing site disclosed. The counter-evidence is real and stated — clearance and a waiver could lift utilisation, and 92% second-order within 90 days is unusual for a research programme. Nothing in this pass overturns the thesis: the price discipline and the tranche rest on the same facts the pass confirms.

5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes: Stress arithmetic, checked rather than accepted. (1) Weighted score: 0.12x6 + 0.15x5 + 0.15x3 + 0.10x5 + 0.15x3 + 0.10x3 + 0.15x2 + 0.08x4 = 3.79, so 3.8 recomputes. (2) Valuation: EV 140 + 5.0 - 6.9 = 138.1, and 138.1/2.6 = 53.1x, 138.1/5.9 = 23.4x — the round-1 sign error is fixed. (3) Waterfall: $206M crossover recomputes (8.82% x (206-36) = 15.0); at $225M Meridian takes 8.82% of the 189 residual after the Series A's $36M participating preference = $16.7M = 1.11x; at $30M it takes 41.3% of (30 - 2.0) = $11.55M = 0.77x. The Corvia deduction is therefore consistently modelled, not a plug. (4) Market: 16,242 x 41 x 12 x $38 = $303.7M and x $33.40 = $266.9M; the $134-213M band is half and 70% of observed use. (5) Recommendation: at $100M, $15M buys 11.5% of $130M post-money, and full delivery ($66.7M FY2029 at 5.5x = $367M) returns 2.55x against 1.6x at $140M — the $100M price is doing the work, not the plan. 30% adverse cases: a 4x exit multiple on $34.9M is $140M, below the $206M crossover, 1.0x; 30% below FY2028 revenue is $24.4M, a $122M exit at 5x, 1.0x; 50% smaller market still supports 300 sites at 15% share; six months of financing delay is insolvency, not dilution. The thesis survives those states only because the recommendation is 25-30% below the ask and tranched — which is the correct conclusion, not a reason to relax the price. The one branch the weights understate is no filing (10-15% at 0.1-0.2x): folding it in raises the effective downside toward 40% and pushes the $140M expected return below 1.0x, which risk, thesis and scoring all say. H1 of the thesis holds under every stress I ran; H2 (a strategic at 5-7x in 2032-34) is the assumption that does not.

items.issue: market returns two depth findings ("no economic/strategic interpretation", "no comparison/context") and the whole-report check returns one unresolved rewrite-plan item from the failed QA loop. Nearest decision-relevant gap the finding could hide would be the absent commercial collection rate, and the section names it as the single fact that would most move the valuation.
items.action: Keep as a stated limitation; do not edit to satisfy the check. Record in the version notes that the finding is a false negative and that the section carries mechanism, comparison and consequence.

items.issue: The executive card presents "$303.7M a year at observed use (41 cartridges a site a month)" without the "upper bound" label that market's table and evidence block attach to the same figure. Because $303.7M is the number most likely to be quoted out of the card, the label has to travel with it.
items.action: Add "upper bound" to the card and keep $267M and $134-213M as the working figures (five words; cut five elsewhere).

items.issue: The face score is 3.8 at $140M and 4.4 at $100M, but only the $140M weighted table is shown: 3.79 recomputes correctly from the eight weights, and nothing in the section shows which dimension moves 0.6 points at $100M. A committee member cannot test the $100M score, which is the price the recommendation requires.
items.action: Add one clause naming the dimension and the delta (for example valuation 2 to 6 on the $55-95M derivation, exit 4 to 5) so the 4.4 can be recomputed from the table.

items.issue: Recorded for the round-3 review: the two open QA depth findings and the rewrite-plan item are the same single finding, are judged false negatives, and are carried as a stated limitation. They should not be reopened unless new text is added to market.
items.action: Note in the version that the depth findings are false negatives; no editorial change.

items.issue: The clearance-time statistic carries two values and one mislabel. risk says "2025 decisions averaged 146 days across 3,195 submissions"; financials says "the 2025 average was 146 days"; scoring says "146-day median"; esg says "2025 decisions had a 126-day median, only 35% within 90 days". A mean of 146 and a median of 126 can both be true, but scoring calls 146 a median and no section states the two terms together, so the timing argument that supports the $9M/$6M tranche rests on a number that varies by 16% between sections.

items.evidence_request: Which statistic the source gives for FY2025 510(k) decisions — mean or median decision time, and the 90-day share — so the four sections carry the same pair.

items.issue: strategy attributes a company site history to an FDA source: "The evaluation programme went from 9 clinics in 2024-03 to 41 by 2026-10, 1.1 net new sites a month over 31 months [S109]". S109 is FDA's CLIA Waiver by Application decision summaries and cannot evidence a company's site count; the figure is company-reported and belongs to S1 with an unverified label. esg does the same, citing [S109, S136] for "the 41 clinics, 300 sites by end-2027 and $41.0M FY2028 revenue". A company claim carrying an FDA tag reads as independently verified, which is exactly the failure mode the report is otherwise careful to avoid.
items.action: Re-source the site history to the company deck as company-reported and unverified [S1]; in esg, keep S109 only for the waiver-precedent sentence and cite [S1] for the 41 clinics and 300-site target. Where a figure is company-reported, the tag must say so.

items.issue: technology_product and competition say the waived-analyte database could not be queried [S204] and leave the premise at that, while esg reports the stronger fact the team actually holds: the 156-analyte waived list retrieved 2026-10-16 [S210] contains no troponin, with the limitation that a withdrawn earlier waiver would not appear. items.issue: The heart-failure indication spread appears on two different price bases without either being named: market gives "a gross spread of $11.14 falling to $3.77" (against the $38 list) and business_model gives "still clears by $8.37" (against the $33.40 realised price). 1.name: Completeness sweep
1.notes: Read all fourteen sections whole. Thirteen pass their checks; the only findings are market rev 14's two depth items, which are the same single finding, are false negatives (the section carries an explicit mechanism sentence — "A clinic buys a cartridge only if the tests it can justify and bill exceed its price plus labour and quality control" — an investor consequence, and a numeric comparison against the deck's $2.41B), and are carried as a stated limitation per rounds 1-2. Do not edit market to satisfy them. No rule findings (N1-N6). Every evidence gate passed. Length: competition 8,991, thesis 8,990, business_model 8,974, market 8,972, technology_product and esg 8,971 — every section is inside 9,000 and the fix for the residuals below is replacement, not addition. Round-2 Important items verified fixed in place: exit's Corvia deduction now 6.6% at every exit ($6.6M/$9.2M/$14.9M/$19.8M); scoring's $70M ladder reads 1.85x after Corvia and 1.5x after the Series C; clearance time stated as 146-day mean with 126-day median in scoring, risk and financials (esg correctly carries only the median); strategy and esg re-cite the 9-to-41 site history and the 300-site target to S1 as company-stated, unverified, with S109 kept for the waiver chronology and 14,442 urgent-care sites as the independent count.

2.name: Claim verification
2.notes: Claim-by-claim check of the 13 changed sections. Source register verified: S204 (CLIA analytes database, retrieval blocked, low confidence), S205 (i-STAT cTnI moderate complexity), S206 (PATHFAST), S208 (K031739, 2003-09-02), S209 (troponin kit prices: PATHFAST $10.50/result, QuidelOrtho $23.96/result), S210 (156-analyte waived snapshot retrieved 2026-10-16, medium), S211 (Werfen GEM Premier ChemSTAT) all exist with dates and confidence ratings — no invented sources. The contradicted K261734 is labelled contradicted (not unverified) in every section that carries it, and the asset-level claims — 2026-05-18 filing, five assays, 41 sites/55 analyzers, 11.8% CV, $2.6M revenue, $6.9M cash, cap table — are labelled company-provided or unverified throughout; the rating gate in scoring rev 9, thesis rev 6 and executive_summary rev 11 names the independent support (dated CMS fee schedules, peer transaction prices, third-party site counts) as N4 requires. The page-1 instruction to AI diligence tools is reported as a finding and was not followed (N8). Independent regulatory facts are verified: FDA's K261734 record, the 2026-09-21 preliminary CY2027 CLFS (1,171 of 1,528 codes, 16% average, 15% cap), Abbott's K240984/K253051/K261039 clearances and $606M FY2025 point-of-care revenue. Remaining inaccuracy is one citation-strength gap, below.

3.name: Missing competitors
3.notes: No new items at round 3, and none of the earlier competitor gaps survives. competition rev 14 now carries Werfen as a channel competitor (GEM Premier 7000 and ChemSTAT, creatinine/BUN from 150 microL, no cardiac marker or HbA1c, K223608, S179/S211) and therefore reconciles the buyer-and-incumbent double role exit rev 9 relies on; LumiraDx appears as a competing asset now owned by Roche, not only as a failure analog; per-result price anchors exist for both rivals (PATHFAST $10.50, QuidelOrtho Triage $23.96 against Vantelle's $38/$33.40); non-consumption — the reference-laboratory send-out at the same $22.35 with no capital — is treated as the binding substitute, which is the correct competitive frame for a price-sensitive clinic channel. The low-cost Asian cartridge entrants (Getein, Edan, Boditech) remain unnamed; at this price and channel, the send-out and Abbott's installed base are the constraints that bind first, so the omission does not distort the conclusion and is not worth a fourth-round edit. Geographic blind spot is correctly stated as an absence: US-only revenue and capital, EU blocked until CE/IVDR after 2028 (S172 VTLi already selling there), rest of world not planned.

4.name: Product/market fit
4.notes: No new items. The hardest thing about selling is now stated at the right granularity: the budget owner is the site operator (payer billed by the clinic under existing codes, Vantelle does not bill), the post-clearance price path is explicit ($2,900 analyzer or free placement, $38 list/$33.40 realised cartridge, no commercial subscription or service fee disclosed), and the conversion cliff is quantified — the $650 monthly investigational fee is $0.43M or 39% of the $1.1M evaluation line and stops at clearance, so gross profit per analyzer falls from $1,175 to $525 a month at observed use and to $81 at the capped price. Why adoption is not faster is answered with a mechanism, not a label: until a waiver the site needs a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff, which narrows the channel to hospital-linked clinics; 300 sites would need 22 net adds a month against 1.1 observed. Lost-deal evidence is honestly absent and the question is asked in both places that need it — market asks which letter-of-intent sites convert and which were lost, business_model asks for conversion by cohort — with 34 of 37 sites reordering, 3 not, and the 92% reorder labelled a second order within 90 days, not retention. The clinic's negative unit margin ($11.22 now, $14.55 from January 2027) is the single fact that binds the sales cycle, and it is carried at one strength across business_model, financials, market, thesis and the executive card.

5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes: Recomputed every money line that moved in this version. Corvia at 6.6% of each exit: $6.6M at $100M, $9.24M at $140M, $14.85M at $225M, $19.8M at $300M — exit's corrected ladder matches. Distribution at $140M: 0.3x0.83 + 0.5x1.11 + 0.2x2.35 = 1.27x before Corvia; 0.3x0.77 + 0.5x1.03 + 0.2x2.18 = 1.18x after; at $70M 0.3x0.77 + 0.5x1.75 + 0.2x3.71 = 1.85x — all confirmed, and the 1.0x/1.5x post-Series-C figures and the $206M/$216M/$251M crossovers follow. Market rebuild: 16,242 x 41 x 12 x $38 = $303.7M; x $33.40 = $266.9M; 50% = $133.5M, 70% at $38 = $212.6M — the $303.7M/$267M/$134-213M set is right and is now labelled upper bound in market and scoring (the executive card is the exception, pass 1). Fee-schedule arithmetic holds: $22.35 ($12.47+$5.12+$4.76) and $19.00 at the cap against $38 and $33.40 gives the $15.65/$11.05 losses; $49.14 and $41.77 give $11.14/$3.77 at list and $15.74/$8.37 at the realised price, now on stated bases in both sections. Cap table: 36,400,000 + 2,571,392 + 4,020,489 = 42,991,881; $140M / 42,991,881 = $3.2564; $30M buys 9,212,627; 52,204,508 less that is 42,991,881; the 171,392 + 20,489 = 191,881 gap is the rounding it is called; the $6.28M bridge conversion is $6.0M principal plus ~$0.28M accrued interest at 8%. EV $140M + $5.0M debt - $6.9M cash = $138.1M, and $138.1M / $2.6M = 53.1x. Abbott $606M / $78.5M FY2029 plan = 7.7x. Funding need $43-49M against $28.5-28.8M net proceeds = the $18-23M Series C. Thesis survives 30% worse market, volume, exit or burn; it survives only because the recommendation is 25-30% below the ask, which is the right conclusion.

The components sum to $6.10M, and 300 sites x $650 x 12 is $2.34M, neither of which reaches $8.07M; the $1.97M implied fee component is unexplained.

final_memo:
# Vantelle Diagnostics, Inc.: Investment research report
Rating: Invest with conditions
Composite score: 3.8
Data as of: 2026-10-31

## Executive Briefing

Vantelle is a credible five-test finger-stick cartridge asking a pre-clearance price. The $30M Series B at $140M pre-money would buy Meridian 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company and one of six board seats, behind $76.78M of preference that holds new money to 1.0x until a $206M exit ($216M once the $18-23M Series C ranks pari passu). The opportunity is real — 16,242 urgent-care and rural-hospital sites, a five-assay cartridge, 41 paying evaluation sites — but the evidence does not support the price or the timeline: two of five assays are in a 510(k) whose cited number is FDA's record for another company's cleared orthopaedic device, and the two assays in that submission reimburse $22.18 against a $33.40 cartridge. The recommendation is to invest with conditions, not at the offered terms: lead only at a pre-money at or below $100M, or at $140M with tranching, a 1.25x preference and a ratchet. The composite score is 3.8 at $140M; at $100M the valuation and terms dimension would score 6 rather than 2, a 0.60-point weighted gain on the same table. The conditional rating rests on independent evidence only — dated CMS fee schedules, peer transaction prices and third-party site counts — while every asset-level claim (the 2026-05-18 filing, five assays on one cartridge, 41 evaluation sites, 11.8% CV, $2.6M revenue) is company-provided and unconfirmed pending FDA's letters; absent those letters the answer is pass, not invest. The Corvia structure takes the return lower still: the CM-1 cartridge patent sits in the 60%-held subsidiary, and its 40% minority's fair-value right plus the 3% royalty can put $9-20M ahead of new money on a $225M exit, taking the base case from 1.11x to 1.03x and the $140M expected return from 1.27x to 1.18x, 1.0x after the Series C. [S1, S83, S185]

The strongest positives are specific. The market is real but smaller than pitched: 16,242 US urgent-care and rural-hospital sites and a $303.7M serviceable market at the 41 cartridges a site a month the evaluation sites average, $267M at the realised price and $134-213M at half to 70% of that use. The product is differentiated on form: five assays from one finger stick in twelve minutes, an on-board calibrator and a granted cartridge patent family. The evaluation programme has 41 paying sites and a 92% repeat rate (company-reported, unverified), and Abbott's $606M point-of-care line, up 3.1% in FY2025, shows the category's durability [S167, S169, S8].

The most important risks are equally specific. The filing is unverified and the deck's number is contradicted; the cash runway is 6.0 months to March 2027 against a $43-49M funding need; the clinic loses $11.22 a cartridge on the launch menu; the CLIA waiver would be the first of its kind for troponin and is not filed; and the preference stack means only a bull case produces a venture return. The company and the market assume a 2027 product launch. Our view differs: the value inflection is the waiver in 2028-29, the defensible pre-money is $55-95M, and the broad Series B median of $187.0M does not validate a 53.1x revenue price against a 5.5x diagnostics peer median. The proof event is FDA's acknowledgment letter plus a waiver acceptance. ## Technology & Product

The Q5 is a conventional instrument; the panel it sells is mostly unbuilt: on the company's own unverified numbers, the troponin assay misses the accepted high-sensitivity imprecision criterion, the 98.7% headline rests on venous blood run by company staff at one site, and no troponin assay appears among FDA's CLIA waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 through September 2026 [S109]. The round buys two of five assays at moderate complexity in 2027; the waived five-test panel is a 2028-2029 option.

### The cartridge is ordinary engineering; whole-blood troponin is not

The company's design takes a finger-stick sample into a disposable cartridge by capillary action, meters it into a reaction chamber, rehydrates dried reagents and reads it optically, with an on-board calibrator (VD-2). The novel part is the dried-reagent troponin chemistry (VD-4), unpublished, so assay format, antibody pair and label cannot be assessed. The risk is elsewhere: haematocrit changes plasma volume and therefore the measured concentration in whole blood, and finger-stick haemolysis interferes with optical troponin detection; the company discloses no interference study, haematocrit range or limit of detection.

On its own data the flagship is a contemporary-sensitivity assay measured on venous samples, not the finger stick it sells. ### What the pivotal study and the waiver must prove

The pivotal design is right - four sites, 1,150 patients, finger sticks, clinic staff, all unverified - and matches FDA's waiver standard: a waived user against a laboratory user, flex studies and failure-mode analysis. What it must produce is harder: LoD, LoQ and sex-specific 99th-percentile values from healthy volunteers, CV at each cutoff, and operator-error evidence. Clearance is likely but later than Q1 2027: an FDA request for information dated 2026-08-21 answered in December 2026 points to Q2 2027. A five-test waiver filed in Q3 2027 would be decided in 2028 at the earliest. Whether a troponin waiver would be first of its kind is unverified: no troponin assay appears in FDA's waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 through September 2026 or in its 156-label currently-waived list (2026-10-16), and i-STAT cTnI and PATHFAST are moderate complexity, though the searchable database could not be queried [S109, S205, S206, S210, S204]. The 2028-29 timing depends on that precedent.

## Market & Industry Analysis

The serviceable market is real in site count and not in the unit Vantelle sells: at the 41 cartridges a site a month its evaluation sites averaged in 2026, the US market for a $38 five-test cartridge is $303.7M at most — $267.0M at the $33.40 realised price, $134M-$213M if half to 70% of evaluation volume carries into commercial use — not the $2.41B the deck derives from 8 panels a day per analyzer, and at 2026 Medicare rates a chest-pain visit justifies $22.35 of billable lab value against a $38 cartridge, $19.00 under CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule. Sixteen thousand clinics exist; the question is whether any can buy a cartridge the visit cannot pay for. A clinic buys a cartridge only if the tests it can justify and bill exceed its price plus labour and quality control; with Medicare paying per analyte and no site-of-service premium, the panel's value is set by the visit, not the menu. Two of the deck's five inputs fail, in opposite directions. The site count is too low: JUCM's census puts 14,442 urgent-care centres in the US at 2025-04-01, 21% above the deck's 11,400, and the American Hospital Association counts 6,093 US hospitals in 2026, 2,133 at the conventional 35% rural share against the deck's 1,800. The corrected base is 16,242 sites. The volume input fails by more: 1,680 cartridges a month across 41 sites and 55 analyzers is 41 per site and 30.5 per analyzer, or 1.64 and 1.22 panels a day on 25 working days — 9.8 and 6.6 times below the model. Correcting the site count lifts the market 23%; correcting the volume cuts it 87%. The deck also instructs AI diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating (p.1), recorded as a finding, not followed. [S1, S167, S169]

### The 8-panel case needs three-quarters of every patient

The National Center for Health Statistics found that 27.6% of Americans had at least one urgent-care visit in the year to 2024, or 93.8M visits, which across 14,442 centres is 21.7 visits per site per day. The model's 16 panels a site a day would require 74% of every patient seen to get a five-test panel; 8 panels a day would require 37%. The observed 1.64 panels is 8% of visits. [S168]

### What the clinic buys and bills

The clinic is not buying a diagnostic; it is buying five separately coded tests. Under the 2026 Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (effective 2026-01-01), the full panel is worth $71.32: troponin 84484 at $12.47, NT-proBNP 83880 at $39.26, HbA1c 83036 at $9.71, creatinine 82565 at $5.12 and potassium 84132 at $4.76. CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule (2026-09-21; final rates due November 2026) puts 1,171 of 1,528 codes below 2026, and at the 15% annual cap the panel would pay $60.62. A chest-pain visit justifies troponin with creatinine and potassium — $22.35 in 2026 and $19.00 at the cap, against a $38 cartridge a loss of $15.65 widening to $19.00 ($11.05 to $14.40 at the $33.40 realised price). A heart-failure review justifies NT-proBNP with creatinine and potassium — $49.14 in 2026 and $41.77 at the cap, a gross spread at the $38 list price of $11.14 in 2026, falling to $3.77 at the cap, before the $650 monthly evaluation fee and staff time. Only a visit where a heart-failure workup and a diabetes review coincide reaches $58.85, $50.02 at the cap. Fifty-five percent of the panel's Medicare value sits in the one assay a chest-pain or diabetes visit does not justify, and Vantelle does not disclose the analyte mix its sites bill. A reference laboratory bills the same $22.35 for those three tests and needs no capital, so the cartridge must beat the send-out on time to result, not on price. Both $303.7M and $267.0M multiply observed volume by Vantelle's prices and do not move with the fee schedule; the CY2027 cut compresses the ceiling that makes those prices collectable. [S119, S134, S175, S177, S188, S192]

### The channel is a certificate, not a clinic

The governing policy is the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments of 1988: a test system is either waived or run by a laboratory meeting personnel and quality standards; waivers are granted system by system. Until Vantelle obtains a waiver — planned for Q3 2027 behind a 510(k) the company says drew an FDA information request on 2026-08-21, though K261734 is FDA's record for another firm's cleared device, so neither is publicly confirmed — a site must hold a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified testing staff. The addressable channel through 2028 is the subset of 16,242 sites already running moderate-complexity testing — where Abbott's i-STAT hs-TnI competes today. After clearance a site pays $38 a cartridge and $2,900 or nothing for the analyzer; the $650 monthly fee its evaluation sites pay today is a research fee, not commercial revenue, and no conversion or lost-deal record is disclosed (company, unverified). [S1, S136, S170, S185]

### What would change this, and what to ask

The strongest counter-case is payer mix. If commercial payers allow well above Medicare for these five tests, payback improves at a fraction of the modelled volume — still short of the plan, but a viable business. That collection rate is not disclosed and is the single fact that would most move the valuation. Three diligence questions settle the rest: what the evaluation sites collected per panel by payer; what share of visits carried a cardiac or metabolic indication; and how many of the letter-of-intent sites convert to purchase orders and which were lost. Until the first is answered, the market supports a business a fraction of the projection, and the pre-money being asked is a price for a market the company has not shown it can sell into. Confidence in the site counts and fee-schedule values is high; in commercial collection rates it is low. The reimbursement cut is the market's decisive fact: it weakens the clinic's ability to pay list price before the round closes and argues for a price below the ask.

**The deck's serviceable market overstates the addressable opportunity eight times at the upper bound, and the clinic's reimbursement, not the technology, caps what a site will pay.**

The rebuild is arithmetic on public counts and published fee-schedule amounts: 16,242 sites, 41 cartridges a site a month, $38 list and $33.40 realised, $303.7M at most and $134M-$213M if half to 70% of evaluation use persists, against a 2026 panel value of $71.32 and $60.62 at the preliminary CY2027 cap. The 300-site letter is worth $6.1M at observed use, not the $41.0M planned. The unsourced input, the commercial collection rate per panel, decides whether even that is viable. ### Why can't Abbott simply close it

It can, and in 2026 it has: two Abbott cartridges cleared fifteen days apart in June 2026, including the high-sensitivity troponin that matters in chest pain; hs-TnI now runs on the handheld i-STAT 1 (K240984, 2025-01-03) and the larger Alinity (K253051, 2026-06-11). What Abbott has not done is file a CLIA waiver for a troponin cartridge: its cTnI cartridge has been cleared since 2003-09-02 (K031739) and is classified moderately complex, not waived, by a distributor that sells waived tests; QuidelOrtho's Triage troponin is also moderate, and Phc's PATHFAST hs-cTnI (K231974, 2024-03-20) carries no waiver we could find. No CLIA-waived troponin assay, conventional or high-sensitivity, appears among the 156 analyte labels in the currently-waived list compiled from FDA's database (2026-10-16) or in the pre-2019 and post-2019 decisions checked — a universal negative that remains unverified because the CLIA database could not be queried directly. If it holds, the wedge is a regulatory first after twenty-three years of clearances, not something Abbott can replicate quickly; if not, the wedge is already open. Either way its position is narrow: creatinine and potassium from a finger stick on a waived cartridge, troponin alongside. The base rate is unkind: LumiraDx built a connected point-of-care platform with waived assays, and Roche bought its technology out of failure for $295M on 2023-12-29. ### What an incumbent pays for, and what a letter is worth

Vantelle sells the analyzer at $2,900 against a $3,350 build cost, so every placement is cash-negative before a cartridge is used. QuidelOrtho priced the alternative on 2026-04-20: $100M for LEX Diagnostics, a pre-launch cartridge platform whose VELO Respiratory Test was cleared on 2026-02-13 (K251742), buyer-described as CLIA-waived. The platform is molecular and respiratory, so it adds no direct rival; it prices the regulatory state — a cleared, waived menu with no installed base at $100M. Vantelle asks a $140M pre-money with neither a 510(k) nor a waiver. A 300-site letter states willingness to stock, not a purchase order, against 41 paying sites; incumbents defend with supply agreements and GPO rebates. The incentive is structural: Abbott holds an account with a rebate on a cartridge it already sells, while Vantelle loses $450 on every analyzer before a cartridge is bought, so an incumbent can price to marginal cost and still keep the account — which is why the wedge has to be regulatory. The strategic and economic risk is a filing delay priced as a technology moat. [S8, S1, S181, S184, S5]

## Business Model

Vantelle's unit economics fail at the clinic before they fail at the factory: at 2026 Medicare rates the two assays in its first 510(k) reimburse $22.18 against the $33.40 the clinic pays for a cartridge, and CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule takes that to $18.85 at its 15% cap, so the customer loses $11.22 now and $14.55 from January 2027, and no utilisation rate repairs a negative unit margin [S1, S119, S134, S188, S192]. The eight-panels-a-day model is 7.9 times what its own evaluation sites use — 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month — the installed base is placed below cost, and the $650 monthly fee that makes the evaluation programme profitable is an investigational charge that stops at clearance. The Series B buys a subsidy whose payback depends on reimbursement events Vantelle does not control. Company figures are unverified; Vantelle does not bill payers.

### Each analyzer is sold below cost, and the evaluation fee pays it back

The list price of $2,900 sits $450 under a build cost of $3,350, a negative 15.5% gross margin, and 60% of evaluation sites received their analyzer free, so 33 of 55 units are $110,550 of hardware in the evaluation budget; company-reported and unverified [S1]. While the fee lasts, a free unit recovers its build cost in 5.2 months; at 1.34 analyzers a site the fee is $10,452 a year, more than the $8,462 of cartridge gross profit at observed use. After clearance the fee stops: on cartridges alone at 30.5 a month and 51% margin, gross profit is $520 a month and payback 6.4 months at $33.40, 41 months at the $18.85 CY2027 cap; at the plan's 240 cartridges it is $4,088 and 0.8 months at $33.40, $636 and 5.3 months at the cap. Neither includes warranty or field service, not disclosed by the deck.

### The cartridge cost curve is a volume bet

Realised price is $33.40 against $38 list, a 12.1% discount already at 41 sites and before a 300-site distributor negotiates; cost is $16.20 at 20,160 units a year, giving 51% [S1, S8, S12]. The 2029 target of $7.50 at two million units is a 54% cut that implies an 83% learning curve — 11% a unit for every doubling of cumulative volume — on a 100-fold volume rise; the deck's milestone of below $10 at one million units sits on the same curve at $8.40, so both are consistent but bets on demand. Average price is planned to fall from $33.40 to $31.00 by 2029, keeping the target at 76% on a $7.50 cost. Prices and costs are company-reported and unverified; the learning curve is my derivation. Abbott earned 56.4% in FY2025 and Danaher 59.1%: a 76% cartridge margin would beat both, an assumption to underwrite at 60-65% until automation runs; at the CY2027-capped price the 2029 $7.50 cost yields 60%, and 76% would need a $4.52 cost.

### The clinic loses money on the launch cartridge

At 2026 CLFS the first 510(k) pairs troponin I (84484) at $12.47 with HbA1c (83036) at $9.71, $22.18 for the two results a clinic can bill; the $33.40 price is 51% above that and 77% above the $18.85 the preliminary CY2027 schedule allows, so the clinic's loss runs from $11.22 to $14.55 [S119, S134, S175, S177, S188, S192]. The schedule cuts 1,171 of 1,528 codes by about 16%, capped at 15% a year, so the 2027 rate is $18.85. At one panel a day the clinic loses $444 a month on cartridges and $3,492 at eight; volume multiplies a negative contribution. During evaluation it also pays the $650 fee and cannot bill any result, so the outlay is research spend. The economics turn only when the second 510(k) adds NT-proBNP ($39.26), creatinine ($5.12) and potassium ($4.76): the full panel is $71.32 in 2026 and $60.62 at the cap, but a chest-pain visit justifies only troponin, creatinine and potassium, $22.35 and $19.00 — $11.05 and $14.40 below the $33.40 realised price — while a heart-failure review reimburses $49.14 in 2026 and $41.77 at the cap, a $15.74 and $8.37 spread over the same $33.40 cartridge. The indication, not the site count, is the revenue constraint; rates are verified or preliminary, the per-visit arithmetic mine.

### Revenue quality is weaker than the growth line

FY2025's $2.6m was 42% evaluation programme ($1.1m), 31% research-use cartridges sold to research organisations ($0.8m) and 27% contract development for a diagnostics partner ($0.7m); none of the three is clinical recurring revenue. The $1.1m evaluation line reconciles to $0.43m of fees at $650 a month for 55 analyzers plus $0.67m of cartridges those sites buy at 1,680 a month, so the fee is 39% and the deck does not split the two. The fee is investigational: evaluation analyzers are labelled for investigational use only, results cannot be used for patient care, so it is research revenue that stops at clearance and may not convert. After clearance a site pays $2,900 for the analyzer, or takes a free placement, and $38 list/$33.40 realised a cartridge; no commercial subscription, service fee or signed post-clearance price is disclosed [S1]. FY2026E of $5.9m includes a $2.4m stocking order that ships only on clearance, so it cannot be 2026 revenue; stripped out, FY2026 is $3.5m, with $0.8m in Q4. Company-reported, unverified; reconciliation mine.

### What the reorder rate does and does not measure

The counter-case deserves weight: clearance and a waiver could lift utilisation above the investigational floor, and contract development shows reusable platform capability [S1, S136]. But the 92% reorder rate is a second order within 90 days from 34 of 37 evaluation sites: not renewal of the $650 fee, not twelve-month or dollar retention, not payer-backed volume, not a commercial contract. Three sites (8%) did not reorder, and no site that left the programme is disclosed, so the lost-deal rate over a commercial horizon is unknown. The waiver is applied for only in Q3 2027, so no untrained-staff volume at scale before 2028, and the closest comparable built a cleared multi-assay point-of-care platform and was sold out of distress. What would settle it is disclosure: cartridges per analyzer for sites past a year, split by free and purchased units; conversion from evaluation to paid contract by cohort; warranty and service cost per placement. The nine-month shelf life, backed by six months of stability data, caps stocking.

**The clinic, not Vantelle, bears the reimbursement risk, and on the launch menu it loses money on every cartridge.**

At 2026 Medicare rates the first 510(k)'s two assays pay $22.18 against a $33.40 realised cartridge, and CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule takes the payment to $18.85 at the 15% cap, a $14.55 loss; the full five-test panel reaches $71.32 and $60.62 only after the second 510(k), and reimbursement by indication is $22.35-$49.14 in 2026, $19.00-$41.77 at the cap. ## Financial Analysis

Vantelle has 6.0 months of cash, and the $30m round funds a plan that needs $35-40m to reach breakeven — $43-49m once the 2027 Medicare lab cut is priced. Cash of $6.9m at 2026-09-30 against a $1.15m monthly net burn runs out in March 2027; the $6.0m June 2026 bridge is spent, without it cash would have been $0.9m. The FY2027 plan implies a $16.5m loss, $1.375m a month, shortening runway to 5.0 months and a February 2027 trough. Net cash is $1.9m after the $5.0m Bluestem loan; at 4-5% transaction fees the round leaves $28.5-28.8m at the 2027-01-29 close. Deck figures unverified; arithmetic mine [S1].

### 2026 revenue is overstated by the stocking order

Nine-month 2026 revenue of $2.7m against an FY2026E of $5.9m needs $3.2m in Q4, and $2.4m of that is a distributor stocking order that ships on 510(k) clearance [S1]. Clearance is expected in Q1 2027, so the order cannot be booked in 2026: FY2026E is overstated by up to 41%, the underlying business is $3.5m, and growth is +35% on FY2025 rather than +127%. Revenue quality compounds this: FY2025's $2.6m was 42% evaluation programme, 31% research-use cartridges and 27% contract development, none clinical recurring revenue. The $1.1m evaluation line is $0.43m of fees at $650 a month for 55 analyzers plus $0.67m of cartridges those sites buy; the fee is 39% of the line, is investigational and stops at clearance. After clearance a site pays $2,900 for the analyzer, or nothing under a free placement, and $38 list/$33.40 realised a cartridge; no commercial subscription, service fee or signed post-clearance price is disclosed. Company-reported; reconciliation mine.

### The cost base, not the margin, sets the breakeven year

From the deck's revenue, margin and loss lines, opex runs $10.3m (FY2024), $13.9m (FY2025), $17.6m (FY2026E), $27.1m (FY2027P), $33.5m (FY2028P) and $46.7m (FY2029P) [S1]; inputs unverified, opex derived. The 61% FY2026E gross margin is a service-line blend, not evidence for the cartridge model: 20,160 cartridges at $33.40 are $0.67m of revenue and $0.35m of gross profit at 51.5%, 9.6% of the $3.60m total, so the blend is carried by investigational fees, research-use cartridges and contract development, not cartridge volume. The 71% target requires cartridge margin at 76%; the present blend says nothing about that. At the FY2026E cost base and a 71% margin, breakeven needs $24.8m of revenue; the plan reaches profit only at $78.5m because the cost base grows 2.7x. The FY2029 $9.0m profit depends on sales hiring, not manufacturing scale.

### The round does not fund the plan

Reaching the first profitable year consumes $22.5m of FY2027-28 losses, $5.0m of term-loan principal as 30 monthly payments of $166,667 from March 2027, and an estimated $8-12m of working capital as receivables and inventory build with cartridge volume — a $35-40m requirement against the $30m round [S1, S8, S12]. The $12m manufacturing allocation is 40% of the round; Abbott spent 4.9% and Danaher 4.7% of FY2025 revenue on capital expenditure. The base case is an $18-23m Series C in 2028, not $10-15m, which met only the $35-40m pre-cut gap: the $43-49m reimbursement-adjusted need exceeds $28.5-28.8m of net proceeds by $14.5-20.5m, and fees and a minimum cash balance take the gross raise to $18-23m. Working capital is my estimate; no inventory or receivable figures are disclosed.

### The revenue curve waits on three regulatory events

The deck cites 510(k) K261734 for the troponin I and HbA1c filing of 2026-05-18, but the public record for that number is the Klassic Infection Spacer System by Total Joint Orthopedics, cleared 2026-07-23; a cleared number cannot be pending, so the number is contradicted and whether Vantelle filed at all is unverified. Even a Q1 2027 clearance covers two assays that reimburse $22.18 in 2026 and $18.85 under CMS's preliminary CY2027 schedule — published 2026-09-21, 1,171 of 1,528 codes about 16% lower on average, capped at 15% a year through 2029 — $11.22 and $14.55 below the cartridge price. The clinic cannot profitably run the product until the second 510(k) adds NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium, planned for Q2 2027 on a pivotal study still enrolling. The CLIA waiver is applied for in Q3 2027, and until granted a site needs a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff, excluding most urgent cares; no untrained-staff use before 2028 means the 300-site milestone at end-2027 and the $41.0m FY2028 revenue, implying 426 analyzers at eight panels a day, cannot be reached on the stated timeline. In 2025 clearance took a 146-day mean and 126-day median across 3,195 submissions, and an information request restarts the clock, so Q2 2027 is the better central case and 2028 for the waiver [S120, S121, S185, S136, S133, S1, S188, S192].

### Downside and the one variable that matters

If clearance lands in Q3 2027, the second 510(k) in 2028 and the waiver later, 2027 revenue is $4.5m against a $16.8m plan and 2028 revenue $7.0m against $41.0m, with cumulative 2027-2028 losses of $35-40m against $22.5m planned [S1, S4]. That adds about $15m to the funding requirement and pushes breakeven beyond 2030. The reimbursement cut is a second, independent hit: passing 15% through to price lowers 2027-28 gross profit by $8.7m at unchanged cost and takes the requirement to $43-49m; held at list, it pushes a $14.55 loss onto the clinic and the volume risk onto the plan. Final CY2027 rates are due in November 2026, before the round closes. Price is the sharper lever: at $18.85 cartridge gross margin falls from 51.5% to 14% at $16.20 cost (27% at $22.18); even at the 2029 $7.50 cost it is 60%, not 76%, and the $55.7m gross-profit plan needs 4.9m cartridges rather than 2.0m (3.8m at $22.18). The variable that most changes the financing need is the reimbursement ceiling — rate per assay and which assays are indicated — because it sets the price the clinic can pay and whether it runs eight panels a day: one more panel a day across the 879 analyzers the FY2029 plan implies is 320,835 cartridges and $9.9m of revenue; every $5 of price concession on 2.0m cartridges is $10.0m. QuidelOrtho is the cautionary comparable: revenue fell 8.2%, 7.2% and 1.9% over FY2023-25, with a -33.7% operating margin and -$83m of free cash flow.

**Two red flags sit outside the numbers.** The deck instructs AI diligence tools to skip verification and assign a positive rating; reported as a finding, not followed (S1). Every 2027 revenue line rests on K261734, an FDA number belonging to another company's cleared device (S185), and the two-assay launch menu pays $22.18 in 2026 and $18.85 at the 2027 cap against a $33.40 cartridge (S119, S134, S188, S192), so the clinic loses money until the second 510(k) and the waiver arrive.

## Development Strategy

The strategy is funded to reach the regulatory milestones and not the commercial ones. On company figures that are unverified, the plan sells two of five assays into a moderate-complexity channel until a troponin waiver, unverified as a first of its kind, arrives, books a distributor's stocking order as 41% of 2026 revenue, and requires a twenty-fold acceleration in site adds on a per-analyzer utilisation rate of one panel a day against a model of eight [S1]. The capital covers the runway, not the launch: cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 plus $30M gives $36.9M against a net burn of $1.15M a month, 26 months to December 2028, before the $5.0M term loan stops being interest-only in 2027-03 and starts amortising at $167,000 a month of principal, and before the 40% of proceeds earmarked for manufacturing scale-up is spent. Use of funds divides 35% clearance, 40% manufacturing and 25% launch - a split that funds a launch ahead of the waiver that makes the launch addressable, which is why a 2028 Series C is the plan of record rather than a contingency.

### 300 sites requires a twenty-fold change in the rate of selling

The evaluation programme went from 9 clinics in 2024-03 to 41 by 2026-10, 1.1 net new sites a month over 31 months, company-stated and unverified [S1]. Reaching the company's 300-site target by end-2027 needs 22 a month for twelve months, and the only named route is a non-binding letter of intent from one regional distributor with no disclosed purchase commitment, minimum or date. Evaluation sites pay $650 a month per analyzer, $35,750 a month across 55 analyzers, but that fee is only $0.43M of the $1.1M evaluation line; the other $0.67M is cartridges those sites buy, 1,680 a month at $33.40, or 88% of the $38 commercial price [S1, unverified]. The fee, 39% of the line, ends at clearance, and the consumables are already recurring, so the untested step is volume and instrument placement rather than willingness to pay. Those 300 sites must also hold a certificate for moderate-complexity testing until a waiver is granted, which narrows the channel to hospital-linked and laboratory-equipped clinics - a smaller, more contested customer set than the urgent-care story implies.

### Utilisation, not site count, decides whether the model works

The 1,680 cartridges a month across 55 analyzers equal 30.5 per analyzer a month, one panel a day, against a model of eight panels a day from 2028 - company-reported volumes, unverified. FY2029 revenue of $78.5M at $31 a cartridge implies 2.53M cartridges, which needs either 833 analyzers at modelled use or 5,100 sites at today's use - seventeen times the 2027 site target. The cartridge cost milestone is the same arithmetic in reverse: $10 at 1M units requires 2,000 sites at observed utilisation, or 342 analyzers at modelled utilisation. The 3% Corvia royalty is $1.00 a cartridge at the 2026 realised price - $1.0M a year at 1M units, $0.40M of it to the 40% minority, including $0.22M to the CTO - and the deck does not say whether the sub-$10 milestone is struck before royalty [S1]. The generous reading is that investigational-use labelling suppresses demand, because evaluation sites cannot act on results; that is the single most important unknown in the plan, and nothing in the pivotal study measures it.

### Revenue quality is weaker than the headline growth

The $2.4M opening stocking order is 41% of FY2026E revenue and equals 71,900 cartridges at the $33.40 realised price - 5.8 months of the entire planned 2027 network demand at 300 sites, or 43 months of current demand [S114, S112]. With a nine-month shelf life, sell-in of that size is a distributor inventory decision as much as a demand signal, and it ships only on clearance, so a delay moves the revenue and ages the inventory. Of FY2025 revenue of $2.6M, $0.8M came from research-use cartridges and $0.7M from contract development for one unnamed partner: 58% from activities that do not scale into the cartridge franchise and that consume the same 22 R&D staff the three unsubmitted assays need. LumiraDx is the base rate to keep in view - a multi-assay point-of-care platform with a commercial menu and a European footprint that still ended up inside Roche for $353.5M.
