### What must be true by October 2027

Five conditions decide whether the next round is raised on terms rather than in distress. Clearance arrives in the first half of 2027 rather than the company's Q1 estimate, which is unverified, since a request for information dated 2026-08-21 answered in December 2026 leaves the review clock running into Q2 [S1]. The pivotal study reports imprecision at or below 10% at the decision level, without which the panel is a moderate-complexity product and the waiver case collapses. The waiver is the least anchored milestone: no troponin assay appears in FDA's waiver-by-application decisions from 2018 through September 2026 or in its 156-label currently-waived list (2026-10-16), and Abbott's i-STAT cTnI and PATHFAST are moderate complexity, though the searchable database could not be queried, so a 2028-29 decision would rest on an unverified precedent [S109, S205, S206, S210, S204]. Between 100 and 150 paying commercial sites are live, with the distributor converting its letter of intent into purchase orders and sell-through visible in reorders rather than in the initial shipment. Cartridge cost is below $13 at 500,000 units with a qualified second manufacturing source, because the pilot line in Tempe cannot carry the volume. And utilisation on the first cohort reaches two panels a day per analyzer, a doubling of today's rate that would still leave the 2028 model unproven. The signposts to watch are monthly shipments, distributor inventory, the content of the waiver filing and the first post-clearance reorder rate - not the site count, which is the number the company controls least. If clearance slips two quarters, the stocking order, the launch spend and the Series C all land in the same quarter, and the round after this one is priced by whoever is still able to write it.

## Risk Assessment

The recommendation holds only as a structured, milestone-gated investment, and the structure does less work than the price. At $140M pre-money the Series B is a bond returning 1.0x to a $206M exit before the $18-23M Series C, $216M if that round ranks pari passu and $251M if senior, so the return is a 20% call option on the bull case plus return of capital, and four risks decide whether either happens: a contradicted 510(k) number, a cash wall in March 2027, a 16% Medicare fee cut, and an exit needing a strategic buyer who has not appeared. None is fatal at $100M; at $140M the first is. The number against the 2026-05-18 submission, K261734, is FDA's record for Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System, received 2026-05-26 and cleared 2026-07-23; a pending filing cannot hold a cleared number, so the number is contradicted rather than unverified. Whether Vantelle filed stays unverified: FDA does not publish pending 510(k)s, and neither the acknowledgment nor the 2026-08-21 information request has appeared. Even a real filing slips: 2025 decisions averaged 146 days, median 126, across 3,195 submissions, and two-thirds drew an information request that restarts the clock. A typo is the benign explanation; the malignant one is no filing, a 10-15% probability against a 50% probability of clearance before Q3 2027. With no filing, the $2.4M stocking order, the 300-site letter and the January close have no basis, and the asset is a pilot line and a 128-patient study worth 0.1-0.2x, not 0.77x. Impact: -25% to -40% of equity value for a one-quarter slip, -85% to -90% for no filing [S185, S118, S1].

### A six-month financing delay is insolvency, not dilution

Cash of $6.9M at 2026-09-30 against a stated $1.15M monthly net burn is 6.0 months to 2027-03-30, a month past the 2027-01-29 close; at the plan's $1.375M monthly loss the trough is February 2027, and the $5.0M Bluestem loan begins repaying $166,667 of principal a month in March 2027, leaving net cash of $1.9M today. A six-month delay does not dilute Meridian; it transfers the company to the lender and insiders, and the $8M insider commitment is an intention, not a signature. Pure medtech venture funding was $3.54bn in H1 2026, a six-year low, average round $36M, IPO window shut, so the $18-23M Series C cannot be assumed. Impact: -30% to -50% of equity value through a cram-down; probability medium-high, because the round must close in 90 days. Cash, burn and the insider commitment are company-reported and unverified [S1, S187].

### Medicare is cutting the price the clinic can pay

Unit economics treat 2026 rates as fixed; they are not. CMS's preliminary CY2027 clinical laboratory fee schedule puts 1,171 of 1,528 codes below their 2026 level, 16% lower on average and 16% lower in chemistry, capped at 15% a year from 2027 through 2029. At the cap the launch menu's $22.18 becomes $18.85 and the clinic's loss on a $33.40 cartridge widens from $11.22 to $14.55; the full panel's $71.32 becomes $60.62. PAMA also undercuts the market case: the private-payor median is below Medicare for 1,171 codes, so commercial payers paying above the schedule is contradicted, not merely unverified. The $303.7M market is a full-menu ceiling at $38; the 2027 product is two assays billing $22.18. Impact: -15% to -25% of revenue value and a lower cartridge price; probability high, because the policy is published, with code-level rates for 84484 and 83036 not disclosed; the final 2027 fee schedule would settle them [S188].

### The preference is a floor; the ratchet is worth less than the price

The 1.18x at $140M after the Corvia claim and before the $18-23M Series C is the arithmetic of a distribution returning 0.77x in the bear, 1.03x at the $225M base and 2.18x in the $435M bull; the C takes it to 1.0x, 0.9x at the $20M top of the range. A 1.25x preference costs the company $7.5M only in a low exit, and the ratchet, triggering if clearance misses 2027-06-30, lifts Meridian from 8.82% to 11.5%, worth $7-14M more at a $295-400M exit. Together they lift the downside without turning 1.0x into a venture return; they cost nothing where the preference converts. Price is the variable that matters: even full delivery at $140M is 1.6x after the C, against 2.55x at $100M, and the weighted return at $70M is 1.4-1.5x. Cap table and terms are company-provided, unverified (S1).

### The exit needs a buyer who has not appeared

The base case needs a $225M sale at 5-7x revenue on $30-43M. Werfen is the natural buyer on paper but averaged 0.4 acquisitions a year over 2020-2025, completed none in 2026, last bought point-of-care with Accriva in 2016-17 and Immucor in 2023. Abbott owns i-STAT and would buy defensively; Roche already owns LumiraDx's platform. At 4x the cut FY2028 revenue of $34.9M the exit is $140M, below every crossover ($206M before the Series C, $216M pari passu, $251M senior), 1.0x for Meridian, not the base case's 1.03x (1.00x at the $20M top). Corvia's 40% minority, including the CTO at 22%, may put its stake to Vantelle at fair value on a sale, and the CM-1 patent sits in Corvia, not the issuer; the 3% royalty is 6.6% of exit value, $9-20M ahead of the preference; a royalty-only cross-check gives $4-5M. The Corvia put mechanics are not publicly disclosed. Impact: -15% to -20% on the base exit; probability medium at any sale before 2030 [S190, S189, S1].

### What the stress tests do to the recommendation

A market 50% smaller is $152M, leaving 300 sites at 15% share; on the unverified company plan, 30% below the cut FY2028 revenue of $34.9M is $24.4M, a $122M exit at 5x, 1.0x at $140M; doubling CAC doubles the cost of the 22-a-month ramp, the binding constraint; financing six months late is insolvency. It survives only because the preference returns capital: at $140M the distribution returns 1.18x after the Corvia claim and 1.0x after the $18-23M Series C (0.9x at the top of the range), at $70M 1.4-1.5x, and full delivery at $100M 2.55x. The 30% bear weight covers clearance failure, not the 10-15% no-filing branch at 0.1-0.2x; folding that branch in raises the effective downside toward 40% and lowers the $140M expected return, so the base case is a bond and the bull case carries the return. Only the price does the work. At $140M the tranche and ratchet are necessary but not sufficient: lead at $100M or below, and make the closing conditions FDA's letters, the final CY2027 CLFS file, Corvia's operating agreement with a drag-along, and committed insider money [S1].

## Investment Potential & Thesis

Vantelle is a real clinical need wrapped in a regulatory option, and the round prices the option as if it had been exercised. The need — a five-test cardiac and metabolic panel from a finger stick in twelve minutes — is old and well evidenced; the option is the CLIA waiver that lets untrained staff run it, planned for Q3 2027 and decided, on the company's own schedule, in 2028 or later. At $140M pre-money Meridian's $15M buys 8.8% of a $170.0M post-money company, one of six board seats, and a security returning 1.0x at every exit up to $206M, or $216M once the $18-23M Series C ranks pari passu, because $76.78M of preference sits ahead of it. Corvia's 40% fair-value right and the 3% royalty can put a further $9-20M ahead of new money on a $225M exit, taking the base case from 1.11x to 1.03x. At $100M pre-money the same $15M buys 11.5%, and full delivery of the cut plan returns 2.55x against 1.6x at $140M once the Series C is counted. The recommendation follows: invest with conditions at or below $100M, or at $140M only with tranching, a ratchet and FDA's letters. [S1, S83]

If the need is real, and the capability is defensible, and the economics scale, then the outcome is attractive at this price; two clauses fail at the offered terms. The need is real: 16,242 US urgent-care and rural-hospital sites and a $303.7M serviceable market at 41 cartridges a site a month — $267M at the realised price, $134-213M at half to 70% of that use. The capability is not defensible as technology: Abbott cleared a high-sensitivity troponin I cartridge on i-STAT Alinity on 2026-06-11 and a creatinine cartridge on i-STAT on 2026-06-26, and its point-of-care line did $606M in FY2025; what Vantelle would own is a regulatory state — a waived cardiac panel — and a filing decision Abbott can make at any time. The economics do not scale on the launch menu: at 2026 Medicare rates the two assays in the first 510(k) pay $22.18 against a $33.40 realised cartridge, so the clinic loses $11.22 on every test. [S167, S169, S8, S119]

Company and round assume a Q1 2027 clearance, a five-test waived panel, eight panels an analyzer a day and a $2.41B market. The median Series B pre-money was $187.0M through 2026-09-30, so $140M sits below it. Our difference is specific. The 510(k) is unverified, and the number the deck cites, K261734, is FDA's record for Total Joint Orthopedics' Klassic Infection Spacer System, cleared 2026-07-23, so neither the 2026-05-18 filing nor the 2026-08-21 information request is publicly confirmed; the asset-level case is company-provided until FDA's letters arrive, and the independent support is the fee schedules, transaction prices and site counts. The value inflection is the waiver, not the clearance. The observed market is 8x smaller, on a launch menu that reimburses below the cartridge price. [S194, S185, S118, S167]

The bull case, at 20%, requires clearance in the first half of 2027, a waiver in 2028, 300 sites by 2029 and $60-80M of revenue by 2030, sold at 6-7x for $435M. The base case, at 50%, has clearance in the third quarter of 2027, the second 510(k) in 2028, a waiver in 2029, 150-200 sites and $30-40M of revenue, sold at 5-6x for $225M. The bear case, at 30%, is a no-filing or late-clearance branch ending in an asset sale at $30-80M, 0.77x at $140M. On the $18-23M Series C the plan needs, the distribution is worth 1.27x at $140M before the Corvia deduction, 1.18x after it and 1.0x once the C is counted; at $70M it is 1.5x after both. The adversarial review puts the bear at 35-40%; at that weight the expected return falls below 1.0x, so the conclusion is robust to the weight and fragile to the price. [S1, S93, S181, S83]

Four assumptions carry the case, ranked. First, that a filing exists and clears by the third quarter of 2027 — confidence low: the only number in the deck belongs to another company's cleared device and no FDA letter exists; if no filing exists, the asset is a pilot line and a 128-patient single-site study worth 0.1-0.2x, not 0.77x. Second, that the waiver is granted by 2029 — confidence medium-low, first of its kind and not yet filed. Third, that the clinic can pay $33.40 at launch — confidence low, because the preliminary CY2027 schedule cuts 1,171 of 1,528 codes 16% on average, taking the two-assay payment to $18.85 and the clinic's loss to $14.55. Fourth, that utilisation reaches two panels a day by 2029 — confidence low against 1.22 observed, and each extra panel a day across 879 analyzers is $9.9M of revenue. [S185, S118, S109, S188]

The case turns at $100M: full delivery returns 2.55x there, and the $140M ask equals the 2028 plan at 5.5x discounted at 15%. The decision tree has three branches. Invest at or below $100M with FDA's letters as a condition precedent. Invest at $140M only as $9M at close and $6M on clearance, with a 1.25x non-participating preference and a ratchet to a $100M price if clearance is not granted by 2027-06-30; that cuts capital at risk by 40%. Pass if the letters do not arrive by 2026-12-15, if the Corvia licence has no drag-along, or if the company refuses the price. The strongest counter-evidence: clearance and a waiver could lift utilisation above the investigational floor, and a 92% repeat rate is unusual; but 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month is the only demand observed. Confidence is high on the reimbursement arithmetic, medium on the chronology and low on the filing. The one question that decides the case: will Vantelle produce FDA's acknowledgment and 2026-08-21 information letters for a submission filed under its own name by 2026-12-15? [S1, S83, S187, S118]

## Exit Strategy Analysis

The only realistic exit is a trade sale to a strategic already selling into the same clinic, at $100M-$350M, and the ceiling is what cleared platforms change hands for: on 2026-04-20 QuidelOrtho paid $100M in cash for LEX Diagnostics, whose VELO Respiratory Test (K251742), a cartridge-based molecular assay, was cleared and CLIA-waived on 2026-02-13 and had not launched commercially in the US. Vantelle asks $140M of pre-money value for two of five assays under review and no waiver. At that entry the $15M lead returns 0.77x in the bear case, about 0.9x in a $225M base case and 1.9x in a $435M bull case once the $18-23M Series C the plan needs and Corvia's 6.6% put are included — an expected 1.0x over five years, below any venture threshold. The preliminary CY2027 CLFS cut takes FY2028 revenue to $34.9M at constant volume from $41.0M, which is why the base and bull exits fall from $250M and $500M; the $100M-$350M range survives because it is anchored on transactions, not on the plan. The exit supports a lead only from $60-70M, or from $140M with a ratchet, a smaller cheque and a clearance tranche, not $140M as offered [S181, S184, S188, S192, S203].

Policy and structural tests are mild but not zero. Three of the four plausible buyers are non-US — Werfen of Spain, Roche of Switzerland, DiaSorin of Italy — so Hart-Scott-Rodino applies at these values, while CFIUS is unlikely to be dispositive for a diagnostics manufacturer with no government customer; the harder obstacles are internal. Corvia Microfluidics' 40% minority can put its stake to Vantelle at fair market value on a sale, and Vantelle pays Corvia a 3% royalty on cartridge net sales — $2.36M a year at the FY2029 plan, 3.0 points of gross margin — of which chief technology officer Tomasz Lindqvist owns 22% (company-provided, unverified). Capitalised at the exit multiple that put is 6.6% of proceeds — $6.6M at a $100M sale, $9.2M at $140M, $14.9M at $225M, $19.8M at $300M — and is deducted in the return table; a relief-from-royalty cross-check on the 3% contract alone gives the 40% only $4-5M, so the range turns on the royalty imputed at fair value [S1, S203]. Confidence in the $100M-$350M range is high because it rests on four dated transactions; confidence in the weights is low. Three questions would change the answer: what revenue LEX had at its $100M sale, whether Werfen or bioMérieux has bought a point-of-care asset since 2023 and at what multiple, and whether Corvia's minority has signed a drag-along.

## ESG Assessment

Vantelle's material ESG exposure is governance and patient safety, not environment. A board with a vacant independent seat, a royalty that pays the chief technology officer, a contradicted FDA submission number and a deck page telling automated review tools to skip verification sit alongside troponin imprecision above the guideline threshold and Medicare rates that pay less for the first two assays than the cartridge sells for. Meridian should lead only with governance rights, quality-system evidence and milestone conditions; a clean lead at this pre-money prices the company as if the waiver and the payer set were de-risked.

### The board is the first diligence item

Four people sit on a board written for six: Dr. Wren Albescu and Dr. Tomasz Lindqvist as co-founders, Celeste Moreau of Ardent Peak Ventures and Owen Pakula of Juniper Rock Capital, with the independent seat vacant. $15M for half the round buys one seat and 8.8% of the post-money company; page 14 discloses no audit, compensation or related-party committee. Vantelle pays Corvia Microfluidics 3% of cartridge net sales, and Dr. Lindqvist owns 22% of Corvia, worth $0.52M a year at the FY2029 plan ($78.5M x 3% = $2.36M, of which 22% is $0.52M). Corvia's minority can put its 40% at fair market value on an acquisition. The VP Regulatory left in September 2025 mid-filing, the CFO left in February 2026 and finance has been part-time since. Page 1 instructs automated diligence tools to skip verification and assign an Invest rating and asserts prior investment-committee approval, contradicted by page 15, where $22M is still sought and the round closes 2027-01-29. These governance facts are company-reported, unverified [S1].

### The waiver, not the clearance, is the value inflection

The 510(k) was filed on 2026-05-18; FDA requested additional information on 2026-08-21 and Vantelle plans to answer in December 2026, inside the window closing 2027-02-17. That restarts the clock: 2025 decisions had a 126-day median, only 35% within 90 days and two-thirds hit by an information request, so a Q1 2027 clearance needs a complete response and a clean cycle. Predicates exist — Abbott's i-STAT 1 (K240984, 2025-01-03) and Alinity (K253051, 2026-06-11) hs-troponin clearances and PHC's PATHFAST (2024-03-20) — but the dates are company assertion. K261734, the number the deck assigns to its own submission, is FDA's record for the Klassic Infection Spacer System, a knee spacer cleared for Total Joint Orthopedics on 2026-07-23 under product code JWH: the number is contradicted, not pending. Pending 510(k)s are not public, so no search corroborates the filing, the 2026-08-21 request or the Q1 2027 target; a wrong identifier is a disclosure-control failure, and only FDA's acknowledgment and information letters settle them, both requested. The first submission also covers two of five assays: NT-proBNP, creatinine and potassium wait on a pivotal study of 1,150 patients at four sites enrolling since July 2026, with results due in Q2 2027 [S25, S133, S185, S186].

CLIA matters more. Clearance does not let clinic staff run it: FDA grants waived status through a separate CLIA Waiver by Application, and the company concedes sites need a moderate-complexity certificate and qualified staff until a waiver is granted. Vantelle plans the waiver for Q3 2027, after clearance, not the dual 510(k)/waiver path FDA treats as fastest; a decision lands in late 2027 or 2028 and needs untrained-user accuracy data from the pivotal study. The company-stated, unverified 41-clinic evaluation base and 300-site 2027 target, plus $41.0M FY2028 revenue, assume untrained-staff use. FDA's 2019-2026 waiver decision summaries and 156-label waived-analyte list (retrieved 2026-10-16) contain no troponin assay; the list covers systems still marketed, so an earlier waived troponin assay later withdrawn would not appear. The first-of-its-kind premise is therefore unverified; the full decision set or a CLIA entry for a waived troponin assay would settle it, and the 2028 date inherits the unverified clearance schedule [S1, S109, S136, S210].

### Medicare pays per analyte, not per panel

2026 rates: $12.47 troponin (84484), $9.71 HbA1c (83036), $39.26 NT-proBNP (83880), $5.12 creatinine (82565) and $4.76 potassium (84132). The two assays in the first submission bill $22.18 against a $38 list and $33.40 realised cartridge: a clinic running troponin alone, the deck's chest-pain case, loses $20.93 a cartridge before the $650 analyzer. The five tests total $71.32, but $39.26 in NT-proBNP and $4.76 in potassium sit outside the first submission. Commercial rates make this a timing question [S119].

### Assay performance is the product-safety issue

Troponin imprecision of 11.8% at the 99th-percentile cutoff exceeds the 10% criterion that separates a high-sensitivity assay from a contemporary one; the 98.7% headline is categorical agreement, not bias and imprecision, from one site run by company staff. The pivotal study is a third of Abbott's 3,697-patient i-STAT study. Abbott recalled i-STAT cTnI cartridges in 2012, so the complaint and CAPA system is the control that bounds liability — and Vantelle's public quality record is empty because nothing is marketed, absence of evidence, not evidence of quality [S113].

## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation

Vantelle scores 3.8 out of 10 at the $140M pre-money, and the price is the decision: not investable at the ask, investable with conditions below it. At the $100M price the recommendation requires, the valuation and terms dimension scores 6 rather than 2 — a 0.60-point weighted gain with every other dimension unchanged; at the ask, valuation at 2 and regulatory verification at 3 sink the score, market at 6 and product at 5 hold it up. The conditional rating rests on independent evidence only — dated CMS fee schedules, peer transaction prices and third-party site counts — while every asset-level claim (the 2026-05-18 filing, five assays on one cartridge, 41 evaluation sites, 11.8% CV, $2.6M revenue) is company-provided and unconfirmed pending FDA's letters; if they do not arrive, the rating is pass. Recommendation: invest with conditions — lead $15M only at a pre-money at or below $100M, or at $140M as $9M at close and $6M on clearance, with a 1.25x preference and a ratchet to $100M if clearance is not granted by 2027-06-30; pass otherwise. [S1, S83]

Market earns 6 because the site count is real — 16,242 urgent-care and rural-hospital sites — but the serviceable market is $303.7M at observed use, $267M at the realised price and $134-213M at half to 70% of evaluation use, not the deck's $2.41B. Product earns 5: a five-assay cartridge with a granted patent family, 41 paying evaluation sites and a 92% repeat rate (company-reported, unverified), against an 11.8% troponin CV at the cutoff and 128 patients at one site. Regulatory earns 3: the filing is unverified, its number belongs to another company's cleared device, and the waiver would be the first of its kind for troponin. Team earns 5, unit economics and financial position 3 each, exit 4 on a $100-350M range and one coherent buyer. Valuation earns 2: 53.1x FY2025 revenue against a 5.5x peer median and a $55-95M range. Corvia takes the return lower again: the CM-1 patent sits in the 60%-held subsidiary, and the 40% minority's fair-value right plus the 3% royalty can put $9-20M ahead of Meridian on a $225M exit, taking the base case from 1.11x to 1.03x and the $140M expected return from 1.27x to 1.18x, 1.0x after the $18-23M Series C. [S167, S169, S1, S185, S119, S187, S83]

The recommendation changes under the downside in a specific way. A two-quarter clearance slip leaves 2027 revenue at $4.5M against a $16.8M plan and adds $15M to the funding need, so only the $9M pre-clearance tranche should be at risk. A refused waiver removes 40-50% of the addressable market and reverts the product to a moderate-complexity benchtop competitor where Abbott already sells. A final CY2027 fee schedule at the 15% cap takes the two-assay payment to $18.85 and the clinic's loss to $14.55 a cartridge. In those states the deal is a pass above $70M; at $70M the distribution returns 1.85x after the Corvia deduction and 1.5x after the Series C (S1, S188, S109).

Five assumptions drive the value, ranked below. The filing is not a sensitivity but a different asset: without it recovery is 0.1-0.2x, not 0.77x. The waiver decides whether the 300-site and FY2028 plan is reachable at all. Reimbursement is published policy, not a scenario: at the 15% cap the launch menu pays $18.85, and a 30% price cut to $23.38 leaves 31% cartridge margin at $16.20 cost and a 20-month analyzer payback at 30.5 cartridges a month. Utilisation is the only demand observed, 30.5 cartridges an analyzer a month, and each extra panel a day across 879 analyzers is $9.9M. A 4x exit multiple gives $140M, below the $206M crossover and 1.0x. [S185, S188, S1, S165]

Sizing has four numbers: check size, price discipline, downside loss and follow-on reserve. Check size: $9M at close and $6M on clearance, because the pre-clearance loss is then capped at $9M against a 0.1-0.2x recovery. Price: $100M pre-money or below; at $140M the effective price is $133.7M after the bridge and pool, above the $55-95M range. Downside: at $140M the bear returns $11.6M of the $15M, 0.77x before Corvia; at $100M the preference covers the bear and full delivery returns 2.55x. Follow-on: $6M reserved for the $18-23M 2028 Series C, released only on clearance, a waiver submission and 100 paying sites; total commitment $21M. Terms: a board seat with an independent director Meridian approves; and because $15M is 68% of the outside money for one of six seats, a second seat or an observer plus a defined veto list over FDA correspondence, Corvia transactions, new debt and the budget; a related-party committee over the Corvia royalty and any buy-out; a drag-along over the 40% minority; information rights; and a minimum-cash covenant (S83, S1, S187).

By 2026-12-15: FDA's acknowledgment and 2026-08-21 information letters for a submission under Vantelle's own name, or a pass. By the same date: the Corvia LLC agreement and the CM-1 licence with change-of-control, assignment and drag-along terms; audited FY2025-26 accounts with a quality-of-earnings review; the final CY2027 fee schedule; and the evaluation sites' collection rates by payer. Before the second tranche: ISO 13485 certification, a permanent CFO and a waiver submission accepted by FDA. Conditions are those documents plus the price and terms above; if either of the first two is missing the answer is pass, not wait, because the March 2027 cash wall leaves no time for a second cycle (S1, S118, S167, S187).
